entry.title: Single Material for Sales Order Stock (E) and Project Stock (Q)
entry.content:
Dear SAP Experts,

I need your advice on the following scenario in SAP S/4HANA 2025 Private Cloud.

My client is an asphalt manufacturing company. They produce the same asphalt product for two purposes:

  1. Internal Project Consumption: Asphalt is produced and consumed in internal construction projects using Project Stock (Special Stock Q), valuated against the respective WBS element.

  2. External Customer Sales: Asphalt is produced against customer orders using Make-to-Order (MTO), with Sales Order Stock (Special Stock E).

Both scenarios use the same material code.

My Questions:

  1. Is it possible to manage the same material under both Special Stock E and Q?

  2. Can SAP determine different requirements types dynamically based on the business process (Sales Order vs. WBS)?

  3. Can this be achieved through standard configuration without creating separate material codes?

  4. What is the recommended best-practice approach?

I would appreciate your suggestions and guidance on the standard SAP solution.

Thank you.

silambarasan R

entry.title: From Analytical Model to S/4HANA Table: Automating Field-Level Data Lineage in SAP Datasphere
entry.content:
We Lost a Friday to One Field. So We Built Something That Finds the Answer in Seconds.

One Client question — “where does this field actually come from?” — turned into a tool that answers it automatically, for every field, across a hundred data models. Here’s how.

It started with a fairly ordinary-sounding ask. The client wanted to know, for every Analytical Model in their SAP Datasphere system, which S/4HANA table and column each field actually comes from. And if a field isn’t a direct copy, exactly how it’s calculated.

Reasonable request. Sounded like a short piece of work.

Then someone actually counted the Analytical Models. About a hundred of them. A good number were self-service models — built directly by business users in Datasphere, with nobody gatekeeping how many fields got added along the way. Some had a handful of fields. Some had thousands. And the deadline was days, not months.

Somewhere in there, the client stopped calling it “lineage” and started calling it a “data dictionary” instead. Same scope, better name, same amount of work waiting for us.

This is the story of what the team built to get through it, the real engineering problems along the way, and exactly how to pull the input files together if you want to try something similar.

The Shape of the Problem

Datasphere’s own lineage view gives you a diagram — object A connects to object B connects to object C. Useful for understanding one model at a time. It does not scale to a hundred models, some with thousands of fields, on a deadline measured in days.

So the plan was to automate the trace itself: start at a field on an Analytical Model, and walk backward through everything that field depends on, until reaching something with no further source behind it.

One thing worth calling out about that diagram, because it trips people up: Replication Flows live entirely inside Datasphere. They’re built and configured there — their only job is reaching into S/4HANA to pull data back. It’s easy to assume they sit “in between” the two systems, but they don’t. Everything up to and including the Replication Flow is a Datasphere object. The actual border only gets crossed once, right at the CDS View.

On Graphical View vs. SQL View — most views in this landscape were built with Datasphere’s graphical editor, the usual drag-and-connect approach. But every so often, something the data model needed — a specific join condition, a calculation the graphical properties panel just didn’t expose — wasn’t achievable that way, so the team dropped into a SQL View and wrote it directly instead. Both had to be treated as valid starting points and valid intermediate steps.

Getting the Input Files

Before any resolution logic matters, you need the raw files. Three different sources, three different ways of getting them.

Datasphere objects — Analytical Models, Graphical/SQL Views, Local Tables, Replication Flows — export as JSON two ways. For a one-off check, open the object in its Data Builder editor and use the Export toolbar button: Export to CSN/JSON File. It downloads  <Object_Name>.json straight to your browser — standard, documented Datasphere behavior.

For a hundred models, clicking “export” a hundred times is not a plan. That’s what the Datasphere CLI is for:

npm install -g @SAP/datasphere-cli
datasphere config auth login

datasphere objects analytic-models read \
  --space <SPACE_ID> \
  --technical-name <MODEL_NAME> \
  --output <MODEL_NAME>.json
Same pattern works with views, local-tables, and replication-flows as the object type. Loop it over your list of model names, and an afternoon of clicking becomes a five-minute batch job.
CDS view definitions on the S/4HANA side are a different animal, because Datasphere has no idea what’s inside them — it just hands you a reference by name, and you have to go get the actual SQL yourself. For a one-off look, SE11, SE80, or ABAP Development Tools will show you the source directly. For bulk extraction across hundreds of views, a small custom ABAP report looping through your view list and reading the compiled DDL source (stored in the standard dictionary table DDDDLSRC) does the job — writing each view’s full definition out as one row. One row per view, the entire DDL text in a single column. That’s exactly the shape the tool expects.
S/4HANA table and field metadata is the easy one, and genuinely safe to share, because this query only touches SAP’s own standard system catalog — no customer data anywhere in it:

SELECT
    T.TABNAME,
    T.FIELDNAME,
    T.POSITION,
    T.ROLLNAME,
    T.DATATYPE,
    T.LENG,
    T.DECIMALS,
    TXT.DDTEXT
FROM DD03L AS T
LEFT JOIN DD04T AS TXT
    ON TXT.ROLLNAME = T.ROLLNAME
    AND TXT.DDLANGUAGE = 'E'
WHERE T.TABNAME IN ( 'BKPF', 'EKKO', 'MARA' )   -- swap in whatever tables you actually need
ORDER BY T.TABNAME, T.POSITION​

DD03L holds the field-level structure of every table in the system. DD04T holds the short description text for the data element each field points to. Run it through SE16/SE16N’s download option, or wrap it in a small report — either way you get one row per field, across every table you listed, with exactly the columns above.

How the Folders Are Laid Out

Once you’ve got all three categories of files, the tool expects one predictable structure, repeated per business area:

That’s genuinely most of the operational complexity. Organize the inputs predictably, and the resolution logic does the rest. Drop in a new model’s export, rerun, done.
 
Two Completely Different Parsing Problems

This is the part that made the project genuinely hard.

On the Datasphere side of the diagram, every object exports as structured JSON with a defined grammar — select statements, joins, unions, calculated columns, references to other objects. Resolving a field here means walking that structure backward: follow a reference to wherever it points, step into joins, split into multiple branches when a conditional expression genuinely has more than one possible source, and stop the moment something has no further definition behind it. Fiddly in places, but tractable — it’s structured data, with rules you can code against directly.

Once the trace crosses into S/4HANA, the problem changes completely. A CDS view’s real definition is free-form text, written by people, over years, with no structural guarantee beyond “this is roughly SQL.” A simple pattern match on straightforward field references handles most of it. Not all of it. A few things that actually turned up, lightly genericized:

-- a type conversion wrapping a function wrapping the real field
cast( abs(some_raw_field) as amount_type ) as DisplayAmount

-- a multi-branch condition where each branch pulls from a different field
case
  when change_date is not initial then change_date
  else creation_date
end as LastModified

-- a custom field using a namespace prefix - the forward slash is a
-- legitimate part of the field name in ABAP, not a typo
cast( /custom_ns/raw_field as target_type ) as /custom_ns/ExposedField

Each needed different handling. The first two needed the logic to look past the outer function and find the field actually buried inside it — including correctly recognizing when there’s no real field at all, because sometimes a “calculated” value turns out to be a hardcoded constant wearing a cast as a disguise. We genuinely found one that was just a cast wrapped around another cast wrapped around the number 1. An elaborate way of writing “1.” The third example needed field-matching extended to handle identifiers containing a forward slash, which standard pattern matching treats as a hard stop and simply refuses to cross.

The One Rule That Mattered More Than Any Other: Never Guess

Early on, there was a tempting shortcut available in several places: when something was ambiguous, just pick the most likely answer and move on. The team deliberately avoided this, for a plain reason — a wrong answer in a data dictionary is worse than a missing one, because a wrong answer looks confident. Nobody double-checks a cell that already has something written in it.

So the rule became: resolve a field only when the evidence actually supports exactly one answer. If a conditional expression has three possible source fields, report all three, plainly, rather than silently picking a favorite. If a field is a hardcoded constant, say so directly instead of leaving an unexplained blank. And if the input data genuinely isn’t there to resolve something, leave it blank and say why, instead of filling the cell with a guess that merely looks reasonable.

If you know Sheldon Cooper from The Big Bang Theory, this will sound familiar — the man has never once stated something as fact without being able to back it up, and treats “I don’t know yet” as a complete and acceptable answer. More discipline than most production systems manage, honestly.

Three Real Bugs, Three Different Fixes

A full run against a real export came back with a few hundred unresolved fields. Chasing them down split into three distinct causes, each needing a different kind of response.

Version-suffix mismatches. The exact same physical table, referred to two different ways — once by whatever created it, once by whatever loads it — with a small version tag present on one side and missing on the other. A strict comparison fails here, even though any engineer looking at both names would instantly recognize them as the same object. The fix was a two-step match: try an exact comparison first, since it’s fast and correct almost all the time, and only on a miss, strip known suffixes from both sides and compare again.

Missing reference files. In one test run, a single missing input file turned out to be responsible for roughly a third of everything unresolved downstream of it. This wasn’t a defect in the logic at all — the tool correctly reported “I can’t find this.” The actual fix wasn’t a code change. It was going back and sourcing the file that should have been there in the first place.

Incomplete intermediate definitions. A field would correctly resolve one hop — down to a specifically named CDS view — and then stop, because that view’s own definition simply wasn’t included in the set of files being scanned. From the outside, this looks identical to a parsing bug: a blank cell. It needed a completely different response: go find the missing definition, don’t touch the code.

What You Get, and What You Don’t

The genuine upside:

  • A field-level answer, not just an object-level diagram — “this exact field” rather than “these two things are related somehow”
  • Business name and technical name recorded at every single step, not just the final answer
  • A run that takes minutes across a hundred models, repeatable on demand, instead of a one-time manual effort that’s stale within a month
  • Honesty about what it can’t resolve, with a stated reason, instead of a silent or invented answer

The real limitations:

  • It’s only as complete as what you feed it. A missing CDS view or a missing Replication Flow export means a genuine, honest gap in the output — not a tool failure, but still a gap someone has to go close by hand.
  • Parsing free-form CDS text is chasing a moving target. However far this gets extended, developers will keep finding new, creative ways to write SQL, and something will eventually show up that isn’t handled yet.
  • It’s a snapshot. If the underlying models or views change, you need to re-export and rerun it — this isn’t a continuously synced, always-current view.
  • It doesn’t yet trace through Data Flows or Transformation Flows, which brings us to the next point.

 What It Doesn’t Cover Yet

Being upfront about this: the tool currently doesn’t trace lineage through Data Flows or Transformation Flows. This particular landscape doesn’t use either one, so that part was never built or tested, and it would be dishonest to claim otherwise. The underlying approach — read the structured side, make sense of the free-text side, bridge the two — should extend to cover them without starting over. If your landscape uses either one and you’d like to help push this further, we’d genuinely like to hear from you.

Why Any of This Was Worth Doing

For one model with a handful of fields, none of this matters much. Click through the screens, done in a few minutes.

For a hundred models, several with thousands of fields, on a deadline that didn’t care how large the models were, this was the difference between a deliverable that was achievable and one that wasn’t. It’s also the difference between documentation that goes stale the week it’s written, and a report that gets regenerated on demand whenever anyone — including the client — needs the current answer, rather than relying on what someone remembers from six months ago.

Over to You

Does your landscape run on Data Flows or Transformation Flows, and would it help to extend this approach to cover them? Have you hit a CDS pattern this wouldn’t catch? Let us know in the comments — and if there’s enough interest, we’ll follow this up with a more technical post covering the actual resolution logic behind this: how the tree-walking works on the Datasphere side, the real parsing strategy on the CDS side, and working code for both.

entry.title: Re: Single Material for Sales Order Stock (E) and Project...
entry.content:
To support different planning behaviors for the same material, consider differentiating the process using Item Categories and/or Schedule Line Categories. SAP determines the resulting Requirement Type based on the combination of the material's MRP strategy and SD determination logic (including Item Category and Schedule Line Category).

Therefore:

  • Customer sales orders can be configured to determine a requirement type that creates Sales Order Stock (Special Stock E).
  • Project-related scenarios can follow a different process flow that results in Project Stock (Special Stock Q).
  • If different requirement types are needed for the same material, the distinction should be driven through the sales and planning configuration (e.g., different Item Categories and/or Schedule Line Categories) rather than creating separate material masters.

entry.title: Why Emails Show as Delivered But Cannot Be Found in the Recipient's Mailbox
entry.content:
When Delivery Logs Show Success But the Recipient Cannot Find the Email

This article addresses a specific situation: an email sender confirms that a message was sent and accepted by the receiving mail server, but the recipient cannot find the email anywhere in their mailbox — not in the inbox, not in the spam or junk folder, and no bounce was recorded.

This situation is uncommon but does happen. It occurs because "delivered" in email terminology means that the receiving mail server accepted the message — it does not guarantee that the message was placed in the recipient's inbox. After a mail server accepts an email, several processes can redirect, quarantine, or delete it before the recipient ever sees it.

The causes fall into two categories: recipient-side mailbox rules that the recipient may have configured themselves, and server-side security filters — particularly in business email environments — that quarantine messages without notifying the recipient. This article explains both, and provides a troubleshooting process for identifying and resolving the issue.

Recipient-Side Causes: Mailbox Rules and Settings That Can Hide or Delete Emails

Modern email applications allow users to create rules and filters that automatically process incoming emails. While useful for managing a busy inbox, these features can cause emails to be moved, deleted, or forwarded without the recipient being aware. The following are the most common recipient-side causes of missing delivered emails.

Emails Redirected to Specific Folders

Recipients may have rules that automatically move certain emails to folders other than the primary inbox — for example, routing newsletters, promotional emails, or messages from specific senders into dedicated folders. An email that appears "delivered" to the sender may be in a folder the recipient does not routinely check.

Automatic Deletion Rules

Recipients may have rules that automatically delete emails matching certain conditions — for example, deleting all messages containing a specific word in the subject line. If a legitimate email matches one of these conditions, it will be deleted without the recipient ever seeing it.

Forwarding with Deletion

A recipient may have configured their mailbox to forward incoming emails to another address and delete them from the original mailbox. If the forwarding address is incorrect or no longer active, the email can be lost entirely — deleted from the original mailbox and undeliverable at the forwarding destination.

Compromised Mailboxes

In cases where a mailbox has been compromised by an unauthorised third party, the attacker may have created rules to delete or redirect incoming emails. This is a tactic sometimes used to hide malicious activity, such as sending spam replies or auto-replies from the compromised account. The recipient may not be aware that rules have been added to their mailbox.

Server-Side Cause: Business Email Security Filters That Quarantine Delivered Emails

This is the most common cause of "delivered but missing" emails in business environments, and the one that is hardest for the sender to diagnose without the recipient's cooperation.

Business email systems — such as Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace — provide email and IT administrators with advanced security filtering that goes beyond what personal email services offer. These filters can accept an incoming email at the mail server level (so the sender's logs show a successful delivery) but then quarantine the message before it reaches the recipient's mailbox or spam folder.

Quarantine means the email is held in a separate security area, visible only to email administrators, where it can be reviewed before being released or deleted. This allows IT teams to monitor potential spam, phishing, or impersonation attacks without the emails reaching end users.

Why Business Email Filters Quarantine Legitimate Marketing and Transactional Emails

Business email security rules can be highly customised — by domain, by user group, or even at the individual mailbox level. This means an email might be quarantined for one recipient within an organisation while others in the same organisation receive it without issue.

The following table shows examples of detection methods from Microsoft 365 Defender (now part of Microsoft Defender for Office 365) that result in emails being quarantined. These are real examples from quarantine logs:

Detection Method Confidence Level Action Taken

Phishing: Impersonation domain + Spam: Advanced filterNormalQuarantine
Phishing: URL malicious reputationHighQuarantine
Phishing: Mailbox intelligence impersonationNormalQuarantine
Phishing: URL detonation reputationHighQuarantine
Phishing: File detonation reputation + Spam: Advanced filterHighQuarantine
Phishing: Impersonation userNormalQuarantine

Email messages that trigger these detection methods at a confidence level of "Normal" or "High" are quarantined and will not appear in the recipient's mailbox. Microsoft provides documentation on these detection methods — for example, "URL detonation" refers to a process where Microsoft Defender opens and analyses links in a sandboxed environment to check for malicious behaviour.

Why Test Emails from Your Own Organisation Are Especially Likely to Be Quarantined

A common scenario: a sender tests their marketing or transactional emails by sending from their sending subdomain (for example, sender@marketing.example.com) to their own corporate mailbox (name@example.com). If the company's email security filters are configured to prevent domain impersonation or phishing attacks — and the IT team has not been asked to trust the marketing or transactional sending subdomain — these test emails are likely to be flagged as suspicious and quarantined.

This can cause confusion because the sender believes the email was not delivered, when in fact it was accepted by the mail server and quarantined by the company's own security filters.

How to Troubleshoot Missing Delivered Emails: Step-by-Step

The following process applies whether the missing email was sent to your own mailbox, to a colleague within your organisation, or to an external customer or recipient.

Step 1: Confirm That the Email Was Delivered Successfully

Check your bounce and delivery reporting with your Email Service Provider (ESP) to verify that the message was accepted by the receiving mail server and no bounce was recorded. If the message shows as bounced, the issue is a delivery failure — not a missing delivered email — and should be investigated as a separate deliverability problem. If delivery logs confirm acceptance with no bounce, proceed to the next steps.

Step 2: Ask the Recipient to Check All Folders, Including Spam

Ask the recipient to use their mailbox's search function, entering the sender address or subject line to locate the email. The message may have been sorted into a folder other than the inbox. If the email is found in the spam or junk folder, the issue is a spam classification problem rather than a missing email — this should be investigated separately as a deliverability or sender reputation issue.

Step 3: Ask the Recipient to Review Their Mailbox Rules

Ask the recipient to check their mailbox for any rules that may be redirecting, deleting, or forwarding incoming emails. Common areas to review include:

  • Inbox rules or filters that automatically sort emails into folders
  • Automatic deletion rules based on subject line, sender, or keywords
  • Forwarding rules that may be sending emails to another address and deleting them from the original mailbox

Step 4: For Business Recipients — Ask Their IT or Mail Administrator to Check for Quarantined Emails

If the recipient uses a business email account, the most likely cause is quarantine by the organisation's email security filters. Ask the recipient to contact their IT staff or mail administrator and provide the following details:

  • From: the sender address used to send the missing email (for example, sender@marketing.example.com)
  • To: the recipient's email address where the message should have been delivered
  • Subject line of the missing email

The IT administrator can use these details to search the organisation's quarantine logs and determine whether the message was intercepted and why.

Step 5: If the Email Still Cannot Be Found

If all previous steps fail to locate the message, provide the recipient with your sending logs confirming that the message was accepted by the receiving server. The recipient should then contact their mailbox provider or mail administrator with this evidence to seek further investigation on the receiving side.

How to Find and Release Quarantined Emails

If the investigation confirms that the email was quarantined by a business email security system, the IT administrator can use the platform's quarantine management tools to locate and release the message. The two most common business email platforms provide documentation for this process:

  • Google Workspace: Google provides documentation on how to find and release quarantined messages through the Google Workspace admin console.
  • Microsoft 365: Microsoft provides documentation on how to manage quarantined messages through the Microsoft Defender portal.

Other business email security tools may have similar quarantine features — consult the relevant platform's documentation for instructions.

What to Do After Finding the Cause of Missing Emails

Once the cause has been identified, the next steps depend on what was found.

If the Email Was Quarantined by Business Security Filters

The appropriate resolution depends on the organisation's security policy. Options to consider include:

  • Add the sending address to the safe senders list. This allows future emails from the sender to bypass the security filter that triggered the quarantine. This should only be done if the sending address is trusted and verified.
  • Review the email content. Identify which elements of the email — links, attachments, subject line wording, or sender domain configuration — may have triggered the quarantine detection rule. Adjusting these elements may prevent future quarantines.
  • Work with your Email Service Provider's (ESP's) deliverability support team. They can help identify what aspects of the email may be triggering business security filters and recommend changes.

If the Email Was Moved, Deleted, or Forwarded by Mailbox Rules

The recipient should review and correct any rules that are causing emails to be misrouted or deleted. If the mailbox has been compromised, the recipient should immediately change their password, review all mailbox rules for unauthorised additions, and report the compromise to their IT security team.

Summary: What to Know About Delivered Emails That Cannot Be Found

"Delivered" in email means that the receiving mail server accepted the message. It does not mean the message was placed in the recipient's inbox. After acceptance, several processes — both on the recipient side and the server side — can prevent the email from reaching the recipient.

  • The most common cause in business environments is quarantine by email security filters. Business email platforms such as Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace can accept an email at the server level and then quarantine it before it reaches any folder visible to the recipient.
  • Recipient-side mailbox rules can also cause emails to disappear. Inbox sorting rules, automatic deletion rules, forwarding with deletion, and compromised mailboxes can all result in a delivered email not being visible to the recipient.
  • The sender cannot diagnose most of these causes without the recipient's cooperation. Once the receiving server has accepted the email, the sender has no visibility into what happens next. The recipient — or their IT administrator — must investigate on their side.
  • Test emails sent within the same organisation are especially at risk. Sending from a marketing or transactional subdomain to a corporate mailbox will often trigger the organisation's own security filters if the subdomain has not been trusted by the IT team.

When this situation occurs, the troubleshooting process is: confirm delivery success in your logs, ask the recipient to search all folders and review their mailbox rules, and — for business recipients — escalate to the IT or mail administrator to check quarantine logs.

entry.title: CAP Agents that collaborates with humans - Announcing `cap-agents-sdm-backend` plugin
entry.content:
In my earlier articles, we explored how CAP agents can remember useful information across conversations and find relevant passages in documents using vector stores. But knowledge work often continues beyond finding an answer.

A project assistant or a manager may need to read last week's report, follow a reporting template, prepare this week's update, and save it where the team can review it. The result needs to become a document people can continue working with.

Enterprise Content Management has been a central piece in enterprises for document collaboration through role-based access control and audited work through versioning.

In this post, I'm introducing @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend: an open-source add-on that lets CAP agents work on content and collaborate with humans via SAP Document Management or any compliant CMIS 1.1 repositories through an unified access layer.

SDM as a filesystem for knowledge work

With CAP v10 and the @cap-js/agents plugin, developers can build Calesi-pattern agents within CAP applications. CAP provides the application framework, while the underlying agent harness coordinates the model and its tools.

Tools such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex offer a useful illustration of this working style. An agent explores folders, reads instructions, finds relevant files, and saves its work. The filesystem gives it a practical way to organise and revisit content.

That pattern is useful for business content too. Imagine a workspace containing the following folder layout:

File content layout for agentic work

 The agent can read the instructions (AGENTS.md), discover how to prepare a report (via Agent Skills), inspect earlier work (previously created files), and write a new document. With this backend, the content lives in SAP Document Management rather than on the application's local disk, accessed as a virtual filesystem.

These file operations do not require a shell or a code-execution tool. Hence, this is a better and a more secured approach. The backend translates them into requests to the document repository via the CMIS 1.1 protocol.

A filesystem view for the agent, with content stored in SAP Document Management

@mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend implements the Deep Agents filesystem backend interface for SAP Document Management via CMIS Browser Binding. It is designed to be used with CAP Node.js 10 or later.

It gives the agent familiar operations to:

  • Browse folders and read files (ls command)
  • Create files, including missing parent folders below its configured workspace. (mkdir and >> operations)
  • Edit text within existing files (>> operation)
  • Find files by path patterns and search for literal text in their contents (grep command)

This is direct file access. This is in stark contrast to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) through 'Semantic retrieval' using a vector store.

The CMIS Browser Binding approach also makes compatible CMIS repositories a possible backing store or virtual filesystem, subject to their supported capabilities and connection setup.

The source code is open-source and MIT licensed.

A shared workspace for people and agent collaboration

The most useful part is that the documents remain available with people too.

An agent can prepare a report, a team member (human) can review and revise it, and a later conversation can use the saved report as its starting point. The document becomes a shared work product that remains useful beyond the chat.

Content Management Interoperability Services v1.1 (CMIS) brings the content-management layer. Depending on the repository and configuration, this includes role-based access and document or folder permissions, version history, and the auditing capabilities. SAP's Document Management has in-built access controls and versioning for supported repositories.

Collaboration here means people and agents contributing to content in the same repository, through their respective interfaces i.e. UI for humans, while filesystem interface for agents.

People and agents collaborate together on documents

Example: Project Reporting Assistant

I added a basic reports assistant example in the repository demonstrating this pattern in a CAP application with an embedded SAPUI5 Document Management ReuseUI and an agent chat.

The workspace contains agent instructions, reporting skills, and templates. A user supplies a few updates:

Create this week's project status report for Northstar.

Integration testing is complete.
Environment access is still pending.
Carry forward the open actions from the previous report.

The agent reads the relevant instructions and template, consults the previous report, and saves a new text report in the repository. The user can then open the output report for review.

The example includes project status reports, incident reports, and executive briefings. For instance, an incident report can become the source for a later leadership briefing.

In the demo, instructions (AGENTS.md) and skills (Agent Skills) also live in SAP Document Management. Teams can update that content in the repository and start a new chat to load the revised instructions.

Team begins a conversation with an agent, and collaborates on the content

 Demo of Project Reporting Assistant

Getting started

Install the package in your CAP agent application:

npm install @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend

The SdmBackend backend can automatically use the service-binding flow if having an SDM instance binding or can use a configured Cloud SDK destination. And the configured root folder lets the application expose a selected part of the repository as the agent's workspace.

There is no additional CDS persistence model or cds add step for document storage. The package README explains configuration, and the complete example shows the CAP integration and document UI.

Start with text-based content such as instructions, templates, and reports. Access to a file does not automatically provide native editing of Word documents, spreadsheets, or PDFs. Likewise, prompt instructions asking for confirmation or protecting templates need enforceable application controls when those are business requirements.

With this add-on, a CAP agent can leave behind more than a chat response: a report, a working draft, or an updated document that the team can pick up and continue.

Try the example, adapt the workspace to your use case, and share feedback or issues in the repository.

entry.title: #Demystifying AI Series — Ep 4: # "SAP BTP's AI Foundation — The Engine Room Nobody Shows You"
entry.content:
DEMYSTIFYING AI SERIES  ·  EPISODE 04 

"SAP BTP's AI Foundation — The Engine Room Nobody Shows You"

 

💡  Every time Joule answers a question or runs a task, something invisible makes it possible. SAP calls it AI Foundation. Nobody talks about it — but it's the reason enterprise AI at SAP actually works, and the reason your job will change in ways you can't see yet.

 

The Room Behind the Stage

You've been to a theater.

The performance is up front — lights, actors, dialogue. It all looks seamless. But somewhere backstage there's a generator, a lighting rig, a sound system, crew members running cue sheets. Without all of that, there is no performance.

Joule is the performance.

SAP BTP's AI Foundation is the room behind the stage.

When Joule answers your question about an overdue purchase order, or an agent autonomously routes an approval workflow, or the system summarizes a supplier contract in seconds — none of that happens because of Joule alone. It happens because AI Foundation is running underneath it, managing the models, routing the requests, governing the data access, logging every decision.

Most people never see it. That's by design. But if you work in the SAP ecosystem — as a consultant, an architect, a functional expert — understanding what's back there will change how you think about everything SAP is building.

What Is SAP AI Foundation?

SAP positions AI Foundation as the "operating system for AI" on BTP.

That framing is intentional. Just as an operating system abstracts the hardware from the application, AI Foundation abstracts the complexity of AI infrastructure from the teams building on top of it. You don't need to manage GPU clusters, handle model versioning, or wire up security frameworks from scratch. The platform does it.

At its core, AI Foundation is a set of services that run on SAP BTP — services that Joule, SAP's business applications, and custom extensions all use to do anything AI-related.

It covers three things your organization needs before AI can actually work at enterprise scale:

Access to models —  a governed, unified way to use large language models without every team reinventing authentication, rate limiting, and cost tracking from scratch.

Infrastructure to run AI workloads —  a managed runtime that handles the scaling, deployment, and lifecycle of AI models and agents in a secure, compliant environment.

A governance layer —  the audit trails, access controls, metering, and monitoring that enterprise customers require before they'll let AI anywhere near regulated processes.

Without these three, AI in an enterprise isn't a product. It's a prototype.

The Key Components

Let me walk through what's actually inside AI Foundation — in plain terms, not product documentation.

SAP AI Core — The Runtime Engine

Think of AI Core as the power plant.

It's the managed execution environment where AI workloads actually run. When you deploy an AI model, when Joule executes a skill, when a custom extension calls a language model — AI Core handles the underlying compute. It manages scaling, model lifecycle, and deployment pipelines.

Developers and architects care about AI Core when they're building or deploying AI-powered applications. Business users almost never interact with it directly — but every AI capability they use runs through it.

Generative AI Hub — The Model Switchboard

Here's a practical problem: different AI use cases need different models. A model that's great at summarizing legal contracts might not be the best for coding assistance or customer sentiment analysis. And the best model today might be replaced by a better one in six months.

Generative AI Hub solves this by providing a single, unified API to multiple large language models — from SAP, from third-party providers, and from the open-source ecosystem. Teams build against one consistent interface, and the hub handles which model gets called, how, and under what constraints.

It also provides orchestration capabilities: prompt management, reusable prompt templates, content moderation, and grounding integrations. This is where the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine plugs in — documents and business data can be embedded and retrieved to ground AI responses in your actual business context, not just general model knowledge.

For anyone building custom AI capabilities on BTP, the Generative AI Hub is where most of the interesting work happens.

SAP AI Launchpad — The Operations Panel

AI Core and the Generative AI Hub are developer and platform tools. AI Launchpad is what the humans running AI in production use to manage what's deployed, monitor what's running, and experiment with what's possible.

It provides a UI for model lifecycle management, deployment oversight, and experimentation — including a prompt editor and chat interface for testing models before they go into production flows.

Think of it as the cockpit for the AI runtime.

Joule Studio — Where Business AI Gets Built

Joule Studio is the newest and most visible piece of the AI Foundation picture.

It's the low-code, business-facing environment where organizations can build custom Joule skills and AI agents — without writing platform infrastructure code. An HR team can build a skill that drafts offer letters from a role profile. A procurement team can build an agent that tracks supplier risk across open orders.

These capabilities are built on top of AI Foundation — they use AI Core to run, they call models through the Generative AI Hub, they ground answers through the Vector Engine. Joule Studio abstracts all of that behind a composable, business-oriented interface.

This is where SAP's vision of "thousands of AI agents across the enterprise" becomes buildable by people who understand the business process, not just the platform.

How It Connects to What You Already Know

Here's the picture assembled.

S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba —  your business applications. When Joule runs inside them, it's calling AI Foundation services to fulfil your request.

HANA Cloud —  provides the data storage and the Vector and Graph engines that enable grounding. When you AI Agent gives you an answer specific to your business, HANA Cloud's Vector Engine retrieved the relevant context.

AI Core —  runs the models. Generative AI Hub routes the model calls. AI Launchpad monitors it all.

Joule Studio —  where your organisation can extend all of this with custom skills and agents, without rebuilding the infrastructure layer.

And sitting under all of it, handling security, compliance, access control, and audit: the governance layer that makes it defensible to your legal team and your auditors.

Why This Matters Even If You Never Touch It

Here's the honest answer to the question in every prior episode: why should I care about this?

Most SAP professionals will never write a line of code for AI Core. Most will never configure a Generative AI Hub deployment. That's fine.

But here's what you will do:

  • Advise clients on whether to adopt AI capabilities.
  • Scope projects that include Joule-powered workflows.
  • Evaluate whether an SAP AI feature is ready for production in a regulated environment.
  • Explain to a steering committee why their SAP investment now includes an "AI Foundation" they've never heard of.

Understanding what's in the engine room doesn't make you a mechanic. It makes you the person in the room who knows why the lights are on — and what it takes to keep them on.

That's not a niche skill. That's the work.

 

Your Turn

In your current SAP landscape — whether it's a customer project, your own organisation, or a system you support — where do you see the first realistic use case for a custom Joule skill or agent? Not theoretical. Something someone is already doing manually that takes longer than it should.

That's probably where AI Foundation will show up first.

Drop your answer in the comments. I'm curious whether the gap is in the process, the data, or the organisational readiness to trust the output.

⏭  Next episode: HANA Cloud's Vector and Graph engines — what they actually do, and why they're the difference between AI that knows your business and AI that just sounds like it does.

entry.title: Choosing an SAP BW Modernization Strategy — Your Questions Answered (Migration Strategy & Timeline)
entry.content:
Are you responsible for an SAP BW or SAP BW/4HANA application? Do you like to move on to a new platform designed not only for pre-defined questions, but also for providing a data fundament suitable for fuzzy requests that are typically processed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents and Machine Learning (ML) tools? Probably, you have heard about SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) as such a platform as SAP's strategic data platform.

Do you now wonder how and when you should move your BW models?

 

Here you find answers for really asked questions about the

Migration Strategy & Timelines

Question: What is the best migration path to SAP Datasphere? 

Answer:  A phased approach is recommended. First, Lift & Shift SAP BW 7.5 to SAP BW/4HANA on PCE — this is low-risk and preserves your data models. Once on BW/4HANA, use the modernization tools (data product generators, migration assistant) to move objects to SAP Datasphere selectively. The BW Bridge is no longer recommended because of its feature limitations in comparison to Business Data Cloud and BW (PCE).

 

Question: We run SAP ECC and SAP BW 7.5 on PCE, with an S/4HANA upgrade planned soon. We use traditional BW DataSources and want to use SLT-based HANA calculation views and new BDC data products in a parallel (mixed model). 

Answer: Given the pending S/4HANA upgrade,, make sure that you convert to BW/4HANA either before or after the migration. Either way, whitelisted BW extractors still work with S/4HANA, so your extraction logic is protected. Avoid a direct BW 7.5 to SAP Datasphere greenfield migration — the tooling maturity is not there yet for that path. Once your source is converted to SAP S/4HANA, use more and more SAP-managed data products directly in SAP BDC. Use SAP Datasphere to combine the different models.

 

Question:  If a customer refuses to do a Lift & Shift, do they only have until end of 2027 to find an alternative?

Answer: Not quite. The 2027 deadline applies specifically to SAP BW on HANA running on-premise or on legacy SAP-hosted infrastructure (PCE/HEC contracts that SAP is not renewing). With SAP BDC,  maintenance is promised until 2030, which may be extended until 2033. Customers on SAP-hosted infrastructure who refuse Lift & Shift do face urgency. In all cases, delaying increases risk — tooling, partner expertise, and migration support resources diminish over time. 

 

Question:  Should all SAP BW data flows be lifted and shifted at once, or can migration happen in phases — Finance first, then HR and Procurement?

Answer: A phased approach is not only possible but generally recommended. Migrating domain by domain reduces risk, lets teams build experience, and limits business disruption. SAP's tooling supports selective migration, so you choose which data flows and InfoProviders to move in each phase. Maintain clear cutover plans and run parallel operations where needed to keep data consistent across domains during the transition.

 

Question:  Once the Lift & Shift to SAP BW/4HANA is done, is the SAP BW component no longer needed? 

Answer: Not immediately. After Lift & Shift, the BW component is still fully active — you have simply moved the existing system to a newer platform. It becomes optional only after you have completed the subsequent steps: migrating BW objects to native SAP Datasphere artifacts and decommissioning BW-specific data flows. Lift & Shift is step one of the journey, not the finish line. 

 

Further Resources

- SAP Road Map Explorer: https://roadmaps.sap.com — Check current and planned features for SAP BW/4HANA, SAP Datasphere, and SAP Business Data Cloud
- SAP BW/4HANA product page: https://www.sap.com/products/technology-platform/bw4hana.html — Overview of SAP BW/4HANA capabilities and modernization options
- SAP Datasphere product page: https://www.sap.com/products/technology-platform/datasphere.html — Overview of SAP Datasphere features, architecture, and use cases
- SAP Business Data Cloud product page: https://www.sap.com/products/technology-platform/business-data-cloud.html  — Overview of the BDC portfolio: SAP Datasphere, SAC, SAP Databricks, and SAP BW/4HANA PCE
- SAP Business Accelerator Hub: https://api.sap.com  — Explore data products, APIs, and pre-built integrations for SAP solutions

entry.title: SAP TM Clean Core extensibility, API-first integration, and intelligent logistics automation
entry.content:
Introduction

Follow my previous blog  SAP Transportation Management Clean Core Evolution - SAP Community. As  part of the continuous  evolution of SAP  TM SAP S/4HANA  marks a pivotal milestone for SAP Transportation Management (TM). This release delivers a cohesive set of innovations that collectively advance three strategic imperatives: Clean Core extensibility, API-first integration, and intelligent logistics automation. The 49 SAP Notes documented in this blog represent the authoritative reference for architects, developers, and functional consultants who need to understand what has changed, why it matters, and how to act on it.

The notes are organised into eight thematic areas — each with a curated list of notes and an architectural commentary that frames the changes within the broader SAP Logistics landscape. A full reference table at the end provides a one-page summary of all 49 notes.

1  CDS Views & Virtual Data Model (VDM)

The Virtual Data Model is the foundation of SAP's Clean Core strategy. C1-released CDS view entities provide stable, versioned interfaces that partners and customers can consume without risk of breaking changes at upgrade. S/4HANA 2025 introduces new VDM artefacts for the Transportation Order model and for the Material and Location business objects.

  • SAP Note 3840080  New V2 view I_MaterialFreightGroup_2 (C1 released)
  • SAP Note 3838137  VDM Foundation layer for TOR Party node
  • SAP Note 3780776  TM: Enable enhancement of BO Material root via CDS view entity
  • SAP Note 3756405  TM: Enable enhancement of BO Location root via CDS view entity

Architectural Commentary

SAP Note 3840080 elevates I_MaterialFreightGroup to a V2-stable, C1-released interface, making it safe to consume in BTP extension projects, fiori apps, and analytical queries without worrying about undocumented changes at upgrade time. SAP Note 3838137 delivers the VDM foundation for the Party node of the Transportation Order — a prerequisite for downstream data product and API capabilities introduced elsewhere in this release.

Notes 3780776 and 3756405 are architecturally significant: they expose the Material and Location business object roots as CDS view entities, enabling BAdI-based enhancement in a fully Clean Core-compliant way. This replaces the need for implicit enhancements or custom dictionary includes, and aligns with the SAP BTP extensibility model where side-by-side extensions interact with the core through stable, released interfaces.

2  Location & Organisational Units Data Products

Data Products represent SAP's next-generation approach to master data consumption: semantically annotated, OData-ready, and governed through a formal release contract. S/4HANA 2025 completes the Location and Organisational Unit data product foundation for SAP TM, delivering the full stack from core CDS views through data provider infrastructure to service exposure.

  • SAP Note 3677186  S/4HANA 2025 Development – TM Clean Core Location CDS view foundation
  • SAP Note 3696891  S/4HANA 2025 Development – Location core CDS views, Data Product and Data Provider views
  • SAP Note 3747480  S/4HANA 2025 Development – Location Data Product – boolean annotations
  • SAP Note 3727007  S/4HANA 2025 Development – Service Development for Location and Org Units Data Products

Architectural Commentary

The four notes in this group follow a deliberate layering pattern. SAP Note 3677186 creates the stable CDS-view foundation for Location master data — the single source of truth. Note 3696891 builds the data product and data provider views on top, while Note 3747480 corrects boolean annotation semantics that affect downstream OData filter and search behaviour. Note 3727007 completes the picture by exposing Location and Org Units through OData services.

The Org Units data product in Note 3727007 is particularly valuable for organisations integrating SAP TM with SAP S/4HANA Central Finance or SAP Analytics Cloud, as it provides a standardised, API-accessible interface to the organisational hierarchy without custom BAPI wrappers.

3  Transportation Order (TOR) & Clean Core Extensions

The Transportation Order is the central business object in SAP TM, orchestrating the full freight lifecycle from order entry through carrier assignment to proof of delivery. S/4HANA 2025 delivers a wave of Clean Core enhancements — new data products, remote APIs, and creation types — that deepen the TOR model while preserving a clean, stable core.

  • SAP Note 3803774  BDC/Data Product – TOR (S/4HANA 2025)
  • SAP Note 3688875  BDC/Data Product – TOR (S/4HANA 2025)
  • SAP Note 3675348  Clean Core TOR TP Enhancement & Remote API
  • SAP Note 3691780  Clean Core TOR Foundation Enhancement
  • SAP Note 3791310  New TOR Creation Type for Local API

Architectural Commentary

Notes 3803774 and 3688875 deliver the Business Document Composition (BDC) data product for the TOR, enabling standardised document exchange in SAP Business Network for Logistics scenarios and providing a governed read interface for the full TOR payload.
Note 3691780 provides the Clean Core foundation that every subsequent TOR extension builds on — without it, custom fields and logic added via BTP extension projects cannot attach cleanly to the TOR. Note 3675348 introduces Remote API capabilities for Transportation Planning enhancements, allowing side-by-side BTP extensions to interact with TOR planning logic on the S/4HANA backend. Note 3791310 adds a dedicated TOR creation type for local API-driven scenarios, relevant for event-driven architectures and integration via SAP Integration Suite.

4  Order Management — Advance Developments

S/4HANA 2025 introduces a significant cluster of advance developments in Order Management, delivered through a coordinated set of SAP Notes. These notes extend Freight Order and Transportation Order capabilities with new fields, UI improvements, and process logic — collectively raising the bar for end-to-end order lifecycle management in SAP TM.

  • SAP Note 3841367  Advance Developments for S/4HANA TM – Order Management
  • SAP Note 3841186  Advance Developments for S/4HANA TM – Order Management
  • SAP Note 3840156  Advance Development in the Area of Order Management
  • SAP Note 3839471  Advance Developments for S/4HANA TM – Order Management
  • SAP Note 3837052  Advance Development in the Area of Order Management
  • SAP Note 3839570  Advance Developments for S/4HANA TM – Order Management
  • SAP Note 3805411  Enhancements in freight order management
  • SAP Note 3418826  TM: Cumulative enhancements (S/4HANA 2025)

Architectural Commentary

The volume of Order Management notes in S/4HANA 2025 reflects the strategic importance of this domain. Notes 3841367, 3841186, 3840156, 3839471, 3837052, and 3839570 form a coordinated advance development package — each addressing a specific aspect of order lifecycle management such as status handling, document flow, and carrier integration. These notes should be applied as a set; partial application may leave the system in an inconsistent state.

Note 3805411 targets Freight Order management specifically, adding UI fields and processing logic that support the expanded order scenarios introduced in this release. Note 3418826 is the cumulative enhancement note — it consolidates corrections and incremental improvements and should be a standard part of any S/4HANA 2025 maintenance patching checklist.

Recommendation:  Review all Order Management advance development notes (3841367, 3841186, 3840156, 3839471, 3837052, 3839570) together with your SAP TM functional lead before applying. Regression testing on Freight Order creation, status transitions, and carrier assignment workflows is strongly advised.

5  Event Reporting & Trigger Handling

Real-time visibility and event-driven processing are critical capabilities for modern logistics networks. S/4HANA 2025 advances both areas with dedicated developments for Event Reporting and Trigger Handling within SAP TM.

  • SAP Note 3840749  Advance Developments for S/4HANA TM – Event Reporting
  • SAP Note 3839577  Advance Development for S/4HANA TM – Trigger Handling

Architectural Commentary

SAP Note 3840749 extends the Event Reporting framework within SAP TM — enabling richer, more granular shipment event capture and reporting. For organisations running SAP Track and Trace or integrating with SAP Business Network for Logistics, this note is a key enabler of real-time visibility dashboards and exception-based alerting.

SAP Note 3839577 targets Trigger Handling — the mechanism by which SAP TM reacts to upstream events (e.g. goods issue, delivery creation, EWM transfer order confirmation) and initiates downstream TM processes automatically. Enhanced trigger logic reduces manual intervention and improves end-to-end process automation, supporting the Autonomous Enterprise vision.

6  Transportation Planning Enhancements

Transportation Planning is at the heart of TM's value proposition — optimising freight consolidation, route determination, and carrier selection. S/4HANA 2025 brings targeted UI improvements, engine enhancements, and a significant refactoring of the VSR engine activity model.

  • SAP Note 3759273  Enhancements in Transportation Planning
  • SAP Note 3758381  Freight Unit UI enhancements
  • SAP Note 3734234  MTR Determination Facade and VSR
  • SAP Note 3481260  ABAP VSS: Engine Activity Model Refactoring

Architectural Commentary

Note 3759273 is the umbrella note for planning enhancements — it should be reviewed alongside the release documentation to understand the full scope of changes in Freight Order and Freight Booking planning. Note 3758381 improves the Freight Unit UI with new field additions and list view improvements that streamline day-to-day planner operations.

Note 3734234 updates the MTR (Mode of Transport Routing) Determination Facade and its interaction with the VSR (Vehicle Scheduling and Routing) engine — a critical integration point for customers using TM optimisation. Note 3481260 performs a deep refactoring of the ABAP-side engine activity model within the VSS. While transparent to end users, this is important for technical consultants who have implemented custom BAdIs or enhancements in the planning engine. A thorough regression test of optimisation runs and manual planning is strongly recommended after applying this note.

 

7  API Enhancements & Consumption

API-first design is central to SAP TM's evolution. S/4HANA 2025 significantly expands the available API surface — introducing Configuration APIs, a new Agent API framework, performance improvements in ASR Read APIs, and important authorisation controls. This section covers 14 notes across five API sub-domains.

7.1  Configuration APIs

  • SAP Note 3804213  TM TOR Configuration API
  • SAP Note 3804214  TM Configuration API

The Configuration APIs expose TM customising objects through stable OData V4 interfaces, enabling automated landscape management, CI/CD pipelines for configuration transport, and integration with SAP Cloud ALM. These are particularly valuable for customers managing multiple system landscapes.

7.2  Agent APIs

  • SAP Note 3800652  TM CO creation Agent API should support PKG & APM items
  • SAP Note 3752950  TM Agent API – Consignment Order (V1)
  • SAP Note 3770079  New Authorization Object T_AGTAPI

The Agent API framework is a new class of SAP TM integration — designed for AI-agent and autonomous process orchestration. Note 3752950 introduces the V1 Consignment Order Agent API, while Note 3800652 extends CO creation to support Packaging (PKG) and Autonomous Planning Module (APM) items. Note 3770079 creates the dedicated authorisation object T_AGTAPI to govern access to these endpoints — a critical control for security architects reviewing the API attack surface.

7.3  ASR Read APIs — Performance & Data Quality

  • SAP Note 3759451  ASR Read API performance improvements
  • SAP Note 3765315  ASR Read API performance improvements – Part 2
  • SAP Note 3676599  TM ASR Read APIs: Correction for empty Freight Orders

Availability and Schedule Resource (ASR) Read APIs are high-frequency endpoints in planning-intensive deployments. Notes 3759451 and 3765315 deliver two rounds of performance optimisations — critical for customers running large-scale carrier availability checks where API response time directly impacts planning cycle time. Note 3676599 fixes a data quality issue where empty Freight Orders were incorrectly returned in API responses.

7.4  Read APIs — Delivery, DG, and Lazy Assignment

  • SAP Note 3679607  Read APIs extension for the lazy assignment scenarios
  • SAP Note 3737225  API for stage information per delivery
  • SAP Note 3743773  Provide packaging instructions to DG Check API
  • SAP Note 3781229  Prevent passing of stages without locations to PC API
  • SAP Note 3716814  Unnecessary Product Compliance API calls for non-relevant documents

Note 3737225 adds stage-level delivery information to the API surface — closing a visibility gap for customers tracking multi-leg shipments in external systems. Note 3743773 enriches the Dangerous Goods (DG) Check API with packaging instruction data, essential for chemical, pharmaceutical, and hazardous materials shippers. Note 3716814 eliminates redundant Product Compliance API calls for non-relevant documents, reducing integration load and improving performance.

7.5  API Governance & Supported Versions

  • SAP Note 3703361  Support status of TM OData APIs in S/4HANA Private Cloud and On-Premise
  • SAP Note 3567395  Supported APIs – Private Cloud, Public Cloud, On-premise S/4HANA versions

Notes 3703361 and 3567395 are governance references — they map every TM OData API against its support status across deployment models. Every API integration project should validate against these notes before committing to an API as a stable interface.

8  Settlement Integration & GTS Extension

Two strategically important notes expand the integration footprint of SAP TM — one into financial settlement via lean service frameworks, and one into global trade compliance through a new GTS integration capability.

  • SAP Note 3802781  BAdIs for TM Settlement Integration using Lean services
  • SAP Note 3448484  New Feature: GTS-Integration in Decentralized Advanced Shipping and Receiving

Architectural Commentary

SAP Note 3802781 introduces a set of BAdIs that allow custom logic to be injected into the TM Settlement integration flow when using lean (lightweight) service frameworks. This is particularly relevant for organisations with complex charge calculation or settlement approval workflows that require customer-specific logic at the point of financial posting.

SAP Note 3448484 is a significant functional addition: it integrates SAP Global Trade Services (GTS) into the Decentralized Advanced Shipping and Receiving (ASR) process. For companies operating across international trade lanes with export compliance requirements, this note brings GTS-driven compliance checks directly into the ASR workflow — reducing the risk of non-compliant shipments leaving the warehouse without the required trade documentation.

 

9  Technical Corrections & BAdI Extensions

Every release cycle includes targeted corrections and BAdI additions that address issues found post-GA and fill extensibility gaps reported by customers. These notes are operationally important for system stability and for closing known functional gaps without waiting for a full feature release.

  • SAP Note 3809059  On-The-Fly Data Conversion during Release and Support Package upgrade
  • SAP Note 3733352  Technical correction, TM BOBF Navigator 12
  • SAP Note 3773548  BOBF buffer may not correct when calling TOR OData V4 API
  • SAP Note 3728224  BAdI for controlling the change documents related to charges
  • SAP Note 3671117  BAdI missing for additional LINC error categories

Architectural Commentary

SAP Note 3809059 describes On-The-Fly (OTF) data conversion behaviour during Release and Support Package upgrades — critical reading for Basis teams and upgrade project managers to avoid data inconsistencies during patching windows.

SAP Note 3773548 resolves a BOBF (Business Object Processing Framework) buffer inconsistency when the TOR is accessed via OData V4. This can cause stale data to be returned in API responses — a high-priority fix for any customer using the TOR OData V4 API in a production environment.

Notes 3728224 and 3671117 introduce new BAdI implementations: Note 3728224 provides fine-grained control over charge-related change document creation, useful for compliance and audit trail requirements; Note 3671117 closes a gap in LINC (Logistics Integration and Collaboration) error handling. Both are additive and require explicit activation in the BAdI framework.

S/4HANA is a strategically coherent release for SAP Transportation Management. The investments cluster around four themes:

1.  Clean Core & Extensibility — VDM notes, data product notes, and BAdI extensions collectively advance TM's Clean Core readiness, enabling customers to extend and integrate without modifying SAP code.

2.  API Breadth & Quality — 14 API notes signal SAP's commitment to an API-first integration model. The Agent API framework anticipates AI-driven logistics orchestration.

3.  Order Management Depth — The largest note cluster in this release, covering advance developments, cumulative corrections, and freight order management improvements.

4.  Event-Driven Intelligence — New Event Reporting and Trigger Handling capabilities lay the groundwork for autonomous, event-driven TM processes.

Priority Actions for S/4HANA Projects

  • API Strategy Validation:  Review SAP Notes 3567395 and 3703361 early to confirm API availability in your deployment model before committing to an integration architecture.
  • Immediate Production Fix:  Apply SAP Note 3773548 (BOBF buffer inconsistency with TOR OData V4 API) immediately if the TOR V4 API is used in production.
  • Planning Engine Regression:  After applying SAP Note 3481260 (VSS engine activity model refactoring), run a full regression test on optimisation and manual planning scenarios.
  • Order Management Note Set:  Apply the Order Management advance development notes (3841367, 3841186, 3840156, 3839471, 3837052, 3839570) as a coherent set, not individually.
  • Agent API Readiness:  Begin evaluating the Agent API framework (3752950, 3800652) as a foundation for AI-assisted and autonomous logistics automation scenarios.
  • GTS Compliance:  If operating international trade lanes, evaluate SAP Note 3448484 (GTS-Integration in Decentralized ASR) to close compliance gaps in the shipping and receiving workflow.

entry.title: Meet the Case Management Assistant: SAP Service Cloud Q3 2026 Highlights
entry.content:
This quarter marks a real milestone in our journey toward autonomous service. With the Case Management Assistant, SAP Service Cloud brings autonomous AI agents to customer service. Register for our Q3 Release Webcast to see the agents in action.

The Case Management Assistant introduces three AI agents, each playing a distinct role in moving cases from triage to resolution, faster. These agents actively coordinate to prepare cases, process them, and recommend the right actions in real time.

With AI handling the routine work, your people can focus on what actually requires human judgment. Everyone benefits: cases move without friction, service reps get to do the more interesting work, and customers get their issues sorted faster.

See a preview of the Case Management Assistant in this video. The Case Management Assistant is now available for early adopter customers. 




Financial Services Delivery: A Complete Financial Picture, Right in the Service Rep’s Workspace

In financial customer service, every delay has a cost — not just to the customer experience, but to your receivables. Financial Services Delivery brings SAP Cloud ERP financial data directly into the service reps' hands — contract accounts, collections history, payment behavior and payment arrangements. Service reps can handle inquiries and resolve cases on the spot, with the data they need right in front of them. The result is fewer delays, faster resolutions, and payments that land where they should.
 

 


Case Management: Faster Workflows, Less Manual Work

Beyond the Case Management Assistant, we have also been refining the everyday experience of case management. With Auto Complete Conditions for Input Steps, administrators can now define the conditions under which input steps in a case flow complete automatically — no action required from your service reps. With Auto Trigger for Case Approval Step, approval steps can be configured to auto-submit when the right conditions are met, removing another point of manual intervention from the workflow.

Case management also gets smoother this quarter. We have added expanded Business Information Extraction support for case categorization, greater copy control for admins in case copying and sub-case creation, and more accurate email-to-case matching for organizations with multiple email channels, ensuring replies always reach the right case.

Utilities: A Fuller View of Every Customer Account

For utilities service teams, the quality of every customer interaction depends on having the right information at hand. SAP Service Cloud already puts a wealth of that context at the service rep's fingertips — and this release adds to it.

 A new dedicated Point of Delivery tab on the Premise page gives service reps a complete view of all points of delivery associated with a premise, including installation details, contracts, and service history. Customer Account Balances — including due amounts, open and payable items, and scheduled payments — are now visible directly in the Contract Account panel.

Contract Account Entity Extraction takes another manual step off the table: the system automatically identifies and populates contract account IDs from the case subject and description.
