entry.title: Delete the Training Pipeline
entry.content:
Delete the Training Pipeline

1. The retrain you can't stop

Structured data for AI has been a hot topic for a few years now, yet the progress in the data management world and in the AI practitioner world has happened in silos, rarely informing each other.

The data management community focused on producing a fresh, governed, query-ready lakehouse that ingests data continuously. The architecture converged: an open table format (Iceberg) over one catalog (Polaris), so every consumer reads the same governed data in place, with no copies, as fresh as the last commit. Data scientists and analysts then pulled their own extracts from it and worked on them in dashboards and notebooks.

The Machine Learning community, meanwhile, addressed structured data by training models on frozen extracts. Those models moved to a serving stage that ran one model per tenant per use case. Models were retrained on a schedule, or on events such as drift, but the update cycle ran to days or weeks. The freshest data in the company reached the model through the slowest, stalest path in the stack.

The result is a contradiction: your lakehouse is fresh, your models and your predictions are not.

Imagine NorthBound, a fictitious multi-tenant SaaS platform. NorthBound sells one thing to three thousand retail merchants: tell each merchant what next week looks like. To deliver it, the team spent three years building a single governed lakehouse where every tenant's sales, inventory, and returns land continuously and stay query-ready. The demand forecast that turns all that fresh data into a number a merchant can act on is the one feature that never feels fresh, because it depends on a retrain pipeline that rebuilds training data every few days.

That pipeline is the one we are deleting. Deletion does not make the work go away, but we will see that the modern data stack can deal with it much more elegantly.

What makes the deletion possible is a new kind of model that predicts without training at all. That is where we start.

2. Training-free models already win

In the last year or two, a class of technology has matured that changes what is required for tabular prediction: no training runs, no per-dataset tuning at the model level. These tabular foundation models have been overshadowed by progress on large language models, but on the data most predictive products actually run on they now win the head-to-head against classic ML with no training run at all.

A tabular foundation model is trained once, up front, to do regression or classification of cells in a relational table. At inference it takes your labeled rows as context and predicts new ones in a single forward pass, much like an LLM answers from a prompt, without a per-dataset training run. The model is just a big singleton; data serves as context, not as training input.

From the use-case owner's perspective both sides show only what you do to get a prediction. a) Classic ML has you train on your labeled rows, then serve. b) A foundation model takes those same labeled rows as context at request time; the training is the provider's, done once, off your diagram. For a use case owner, the data is context, not a training input.

How good are these models today? What matters for this article is not how good one such model is among its peers but how far a single forward pass pulls ahead of classic ML tuned hard.

The late-2026 numbers make the gap concrete. On TabArena (51 datasets, 816 tasks), the tabular foundation model TabPFN-3.5 scores 1866 Elo against 1404 for a tuned-and-ensembled LightGBM, 1394 for CatBoost, and 1352 for XGBoost in the same configuration, a lead of roughly 460 Elo over the best gradient-boosted tree. It even clears a four-hour AutoGluon ensemble (1786) by about 80 Elo while fitting in under two seconds per thousand rows against that ensemble's fourteen, and its Thinking variant wins 79% of individual splits head to head against that same AutoGluon. The lead is sharpest in the small-data regime, where a model has few rows to learn from: on the smallest TabArena datasets (500 to 10,000 rows, 36 of them) TabPFN-3.5 still sits about 420 Elo clear of the best tuned trees.

This is not a clean sweep. With many rows and careful tuning, the trees close much of the gap, so the win is decisive on small data rather than everywhere. And on the data boosting was always strongest at, grouped or temporal splits and text-heavy, high-cardinality tables, earlier foundation models trailed tuned trees; as we see from TabPFN-3.5, tabular FMs are now getting competitive here as well. The field is moving fast regardless, next to established models like RPT-1, TabPFN, etc., new players such as Google's TabFM entering the same benchmarks and converging on the same training-free approach.

The pace of progress on these models is remarkable in its own right. From an architectural standpoint, though, the more interesting question is not accuracy but what happens to your architecture once the model needs no training.

3. Predictive ML is priced by a multiplication

There is a further, decisive complication in most realistic predictive scenarios today.

You often cannot pool all your data into one model. In a multi-tenant SaaS, data residency forbids it, contractual isolation forbids it, and even when pooling is legally allowed the distributions diverge enough that one model serves no one well. The same holds for the subsidiaries, regions, and business units of a single enterprise, which are logically separate tenants that often live on different stacks. So you train one model per tenant (or subsidiary, region, unit), and each run wants its own isolated compute, because one tenant's training job must not read another tenant's data or contend for its resources. Then you repeat that for the next use case, and the next, because a churn model and a demand forecast share nothing. Then you repeat all of it every few days to keep up with a changing world. The bill is a multiplication: N tenants times M use cases times R retrains.

That multiplication is more than a compute bill; it is a lifecycle burden. Each of the N times M cells is an artifact that ages on its own schedule and carries its own operational load: a training run, a validation gate, a registry entry, a drift monitor, a retrain trigger, a rollback path. A new predictive feature becomes a project rather than a configuration, because it repeats all of that work, and even when the work is tooled and automated it stays error prone.

The serving side is hard on its own. Each model faces a sparse, spiky workload: most sit idle most of the time, handling a handful of requests, until one suddenly gets flooded when a tenant runs a batch or a business day peaks. The serving infrastructure has to scale each model up and down quickly, across thousands of independently bursty models at once. Keeping N times M models warm is wasteful, keeping them cold is slow, and no single policy fits all of them. Commodity serverless inference softens this for CPU models, but in practice many models need GPUs: a cold start means grabbing a scarce accelerator and loading gigabytes of weights, while scale-to-zero and GPU scarcity pull against each other. Serving N times M bursty GPU endpoints is exactly the workload it handles worst, and that whole problem exists only because there are so many separate models to serve.

To feed each training run you extract the data and materialize a frozen snapshot into a feature store, because a batch training job reads the same rows thousands of times and wants them local and stable. That snapshot is a copy. The data platform spent a decade removing copies: one open table format, one catalog, read the data in place. The ML pipeline is where the copy quietly returns. So the multiplication is not only N times M models, it is N times M frozen copies of a substrate that was designed to have none.

NorthBound runs the multiplication in plain sight. Three thousand merchants, four use cases (demand, churn, DSO risk, ticket escalation), retrained on a rolling schedule. That is twelve thousand live model artifacts before a single retrain, each with its own frozen slice of the lakehouse in the feature store. The lakehouse the team was proud of now carries twelve thousand shadow copies alongside it.

Cold-start

Consider one situation more closely: onboarding a new tenant. A newly launched use case, or a low-volume long-tail tenant, rarely has enough labeled rows to train on. In the classic retraining pipeline your options are limited, and often you simply disable the prediction. The tabular foundation models from the last section are strongest exactly where classic training is weakest, on small data.

Merchant 3,001, one more on top of NorthBound's three thousand, signs up on Monday with three weeks of history. The classic stack has nothing to offer until enough rows accumulate to train a per-merchant model, so the flagship forecast stays dark through the merchant's first quarter. The product underperforms in the very window when a new customer is paying closest attention.

Skills, and the accessibility flip

A second issue hides along the use case axis. Scaling across tenants is mostly a machine problem: once a use case is modeled, an automated pipeline produces the per-tenant models with no person in the loop at runtime. Scaling across use cases is a people problem. Every new use case is a fresh modeling problem: what to predict, which features carry signal, which metric matters, how to validate. That work needs data scientists, and good ones are scarce. So predictive features stall on talent per use case long before the per-tenant machinery becomes the constraint.

The automated retraining pipeline carries its own cost. Optimal per-tenant results would need human judgment applied to each tenant's data, the cleaning, feature choices, and validation someone does by looking. You cannot staff that per tenant, so the pipeline has to anticipate it: every judgment a person would make live must be pre-encoded into rules that run blind and unattended across tenants and data no one has looked at. That is a harder, more brittle task than doing it live, and it is why building a pipeline that survives production is real engineering: detect drift, refresh features consistently, retrain, revalidate, promote or roll back, version every artifact, all without silently shipping a worse model. A use case therefore waits on two kinds of scarce people: the practitioners who frame and validate it and the engineer who makes retraining safe to run on its own.

Training-free loosens this bottleneck. In internal head-to-head work on a real imbalanced classification problem (genericized here, no figures), a training-free tabular model reached a usable predictor in about thirty seconds and two decisions, call fit and pick a threshold, with no ML expertise in the loop. The tuned AutoML and gradient-boosting baseline took roughly fifteen minutes and a practitioner's judgment (metric choice, threshold calibration, output parsing, infrastructure) to reach a comparable point, and it did so at worse precision-recall on the metric that matters most under heavy imbalance. AutoML removes the manual labor of tuning gradient boosting but still needs a data scientist to frame the problem. Training-free lowers that framing bar too, so a new use case stops being a hiring decision.

NorthBound automates the per-merchant models fine; the retraining pipeline handles three thousand tenants without three thousand people. What it cannot cheaply do is add the fifth use case, because that is not more of the same pipeline, it is another modeling problem waiting on a data scientist NorthBound has to find first.

4. The architecture that produces it: pipeline-centric ML forces the copy

The costs in the last section are systematic outcomes of the architecture the industry standardized on. Let's draw this architecture explicitly to make cost become visible.

The classic predictive-ML reference architecture is a pipeline that flows in one direction:

Purple nodes run as a preparation step, at design time or in an explicit re-training step in production. Green nodes run at request time.

The architecture is built around the model as its central artifact, so every new predictive capability enters near the left and travels almost the full length of the pipeline before it produces anything. Author the feature engineering, land the frozen extract in the feature store, run training, pass the validation gate, register the model, deploy it to serving, and only then does a prediction come out. Onboarding a use case is a real project.

The feature store deserves a second look. Structurally it exists for one reason: a training job needs a stable, local, repeatedly-read copy of the data, so the pipeline materializes one. That makes the feature store a second source of truth beside the lakehouse, and now someone has to keep the two consistent, fresh, and governed.

In practice, the feature store rarely survives to production at its original scope. The offline store that feeds training and the online store that serves inference drift apart in freshness, schema, and definition. Keeping training-time and serving-time features identical (avoiding train/serve skew) is a problem teams fight continuously. The feature store promises one consistent definition across both; sustaining that promise at scale is where many never arrive.

The pipeline-centric ML architecture and the zero-copy lakehouse therefore pull in opposite directions. One was designed to remove copies and read data in place; the other reintroduces a copy and reads from it. Freshness, lineage, and access policy quietly fall out of agreement.

Trace merchant 3,001's demand feature through NorthBound's version of this diagram. It enters at feature engineering, gets its own partition materialized in the feature store, waits for a training run, waits for the validation gate, gets a registry entry, and finally lands on a serving endpoint. Every merchant already onboarded sits somewhere in that same pipe. The lakehouse team owns the fresh source of truth on the left; the ML pipeline owns a growing pile of frozen copies in the middle, and the gap between them is exactly where NorthBound spends its incident time.

5. Training-free deletes the multiplication

What happens if we delete the training pipeline from that architecture? The change is easiest to see as a recoloring of the same diagram. In the classic pipeline almost every node is purple, prepared ahead of the request. In the training-free architecture almost every node turns green, done at request time against the live lakehouse.

The same architecture recolored. What the classic stack prepared ahead of time (purple) the training-free stack does at request time (green): no feature store, no per-tenant training. The one shared foundation model answers from a context assembled per request, read from source data in place. Monitoring moves up a level, from watching a per-tenant model for drift to watching the context that feeds the shared model. The center of gravity moves from design time to request time.

With no per-tenant training run, there is no per-tenant model to train, register, monitor, and retrain. One shared, stateless tabular foundation model stands in for all N times M of them. Each prediction runs the same model against a different context assembled at request time, containing this tenant's rows and this use case's columns. Instead of N times M artifacts to manage, you have one model plus a set of context specifications, where a specification describes a query rather than a trained thing that ages.

That changes what onboarding requires. In the classic stack a new tenant or use case re-enters the pipeline at full size: author features, materialize an extract, train, validate, register, deploy. Training-free replaces that project with a declarative context specification: which tenant, which columns, which window. Adding a tenant becomes defining a query scope. The unit of work drops from a pipeline to a spec.

Onboarding merchant 3,001 needed the merchant to accumulate enough history, then run a training job, register the model, and attach a monitor before the forecast turned on. The training-free stack points the shared model at merchant 3,001's rows and answers on the first request. The marginal cost of the next tenant fell from a full train-register-monitor cycle to one query scope.

Failures have one place to look

A less obvious benefit shows up when a prediction is wrong. In the classic pipeline the fault could sit in many places: a feature transform, an outdated extraction, a bad retraining, a validation gate that did not catch a regression, a serving-time skew. Debugging needs to look at a lot of places. With a shared foundation model the model is fixed and the same for every tenant, so a wrong prediction almost always traces to one thing, the context it was given. In order to debug we don't need to look at many scattered places of a pipeline but to a single question: were these the right rows?

Drift gets cheaper to answer, not easier to see

Drift does not disappear because training was deleted. Detecting that a tenant's world has shifted is exactly as hard in both architectures; nothing about a shared model tells you sooner that a distribution has changed.

What changes is the cost of reacting. The classic stack reacts by retraining: schedule a run, refresh the frozen extract, revalidate, promote or roll back, and repeat per tenant across the whole surface. Training-free reacts by reading fresher rows or adjusting the specification. The reaction is a re-query, not a retrain.

One piece of the drift problem survives the move: once a distribution shifts, the question of which rows are the right rows to show the model now becomes live, and that question relocates into context construction (see below).

A NorthBound merchant runs a holiday promotion and its demand curve jumps. The classic stack notices the error climb and schedules a retrain of that merchant's model. The training-free stack notices the same error climb and re-queries against the fresher rows, or narrows the context window to the post-promotion period. Same detection problem, a far cheaper answer.

The feature store has no job left to do

Deleting training also removes the reason the feature store existed. The sections above traced that reason to one thing: a batch training job wants the same rows local and frozen, so the pipeline materializes a snapshot. With no training job, there is nothing to materialize. The duplicated, scheduled, second source of truth blamed above for the seam has no job left to do.

What remains is inference that reads in place. Every prediction is one governed query against the live lakehouse, resolved at request time. That is exactly the shape the modern lakehouse was built for: one open catalog, read the data where it lives, no frozen slice on the side.

NorthBound's feature store for demand forecasting disappears. There is no per-merchant frozen partition to keep consistent with the lakehouse, because each forecast is a governed query against the live merchant tables at the moment it is asked. The twelve thousand shadow copies from earlier have nothing left to copy.

In summary, the two worlds do not merely differ by model count; they ask different things of the data layer beneath them.

RequirementPer-tenant (classic)Shared training-free
Data materializationfrozen per-tenant training snapshot (a copy)read-in-place, per-request query
Isolation mechanismphysical separation into N artifactsfederation/semantic-layer policy at the source
New tenant onboardingnew extract + new training jobnew query scope (a spec)
Reproducibilityfrozen training set (side effect)Iceberg snapshot + tag (deliberate)
Freshnessas of last retrainas of last commit to the lakehouse

The right column has a clear pattern: it is the column a zero-copy Iceberg lakehouse is already good at. Read in place, isolated at the source, onboarded by query scope, addressed by a snapshot, serving the last commit. The modeling choice dictates the data-layer shape, and the training-free shape is the one the modern data architecture fits perfectly to.

The isolation row is the most significant, because real multi-tenancy is rarely one table with a tenant column. It is table-per-tenant, system-per-tenant, the same logical view instantiated N times, often across regions for residency. Classic per-tenant ML mirrors that fragmentation and treats it as destiny: N physical sources become N feature pipelines become N trained models, so the storage-layer split has tremendous effects on the whole lifecycle. With a federation layer, the physical sources stay separate, because residency and ownership demand it, but assembling tenant k's context becomes one governed query against the logical layer, and the shared model consumes the assembled table regardless of where its rows physically live. The messier the physical layout, the more that layer is worth. Isolation relocates: instead of being enforced by physical separation, it is enforced by the semantic layer at query time.

Deleting the training pipeline takes the multiplication, the onboarding project, and the reintroduced copy with it. That is a clean story on the modeling side. The question is whether it holds against a real, physically fragmented, multi-tenant data layer, and whether the properties the classic stack got for free survive when nothing is materialized.

Experiments

To test whether the properties hold against a real model and a real, physically fragmented lakehouse, we ran three small experiments, each aimed at one claim: (1) accuracy, whether one shared model matches per-tenant models; (2) federation, whether isolation survives physically separate tables behind one view; and (3) reproducibility, whether a past prediction can be recovered from a snapshot. They map onto NorthBound through a public dataset: the merchants are retail stores, the demand feature is store-sales forecasting, and the dataset holds 1,115 stores treated as 1,115 tenants. 

One stack is used in all three experiments: TabPFN is the training-free model, the data lives as Iceberg tables on S3 behind a Polaris catalog, and Dremio federates and queries them, assembling each context and serving point-in-time snapshots. This setup is not a controlled scientific study, but the experiments are strong enough to make an architectural point.

The experimental method, compact code, detailed results, and caveats are included in the appendix.

On accuracy

We ran the multiplication and its replacement side by side. On 36 stores we built a classic ML architecture, one LightGBM trained per store on that store's rows, against a training-free arm of one shared TabPFN handed the same store's rows as in-context data at request time. To draw a tenant-size axis, we truncated each store's context to budgets from 20 up to 640 most-recent rows, giving 181 (store, budget) units.

The shared foundation model matched or beat the per-tenant model on 85% of units. It held on small tenants (80.6% win, median normalized RMSE 0.160 against 0.194) and on large ones (91.9% win, 0.120 against 0.135). Plotted against size, both lines run roughly flat with the shared model consistently below; the per-tenant model is simply noisier where rows are scarce. A pooled model trained across all stores was competitive, sometimes best, but pooling ignores tenant isolation, which multi-tenant SaaS forbids: a tenant could rightly object that its data was used to help a competitor. The foundation model reached near-pooled accuracy while keeping every tenant isolated at inference.

The conclusion: deleting the per-tenant training multiplication cost nothing on accuracy here. From an architectural standpoint, what does a shared-model world ask of the data layer beneath it? The caveat is that this experiment ran on a single physical table, so it proved the model claim, not yet the data architecture claim. The next experiment moves onto a real, physically fragmented one and tests the isolation row, then reproducibility follows.

On federation

This experiment wrote five stores as physically separate Iceberg tables on S3 and exposed them through a single Dremio view, then handed TabPFN each store's context assembled through that view. Across all five, the federated context was cell-by-cell identical to a single-table read and the predictions matched to the last decimal, while a WHERE Store=k returned only that tenant's rows. The federated path is invisible to the model: physical fragmentation stops at the layer, and everything downstream can treat the substrate as one table. Classic ML hid the same fragmentation by copying the scattered tables out into a per-tenant training set, another frozen dataset to build, store, and keep in sync; the training-free path skips the copy and federates in place instead.

On reproducibility

The one thing classic ML got for free by materializing a frozen training set was reproducibility: the training data sat right there, frozen, for as long as you kept it. Delete training and nothing is materialized, so who owns the point-in-time snapshot of what a prediction actually read? 

The mechanism is built in: Iceberg's AT SNAPSHOT returns the same bytes it stored, and a deterministic model handed the same bytes returns the same prediction. Predict at the original snapshot S1 (320 rows), RMSE 875. Append four rows through pyiceberg, creating snapshot S2. Re-predict naively on the current state and the result drifts hard, RMSE 10,076. Query AT SNAPSHOT S1 through Dremio and the original prediction returns exactly, a timestamp cross-check one second before S2 resolving to S1 as well.

Reproducibility survives the deletion of training but changes owner and character. In classic ML it was a free side effect of materializing a frozen training set, sitting there for as long as you kept it. Here it worked only because S1 still existed, and Iceberg expires old snapshots by default; even the durability tag we pinned S1 with carries a maximum age. So reproducibility relocates from an automatic byproduct of materialization to a deliberate retention and tagging policy that someone needs to owns. Cheaper to govern than a warehouse of frozen training sets, but no longer free. That relocation of responsibility is why reproducibility needs to be designed for, not assumed.

↳ This closes the drift thread from earlier. After merchant 3,001 runs its promotion and changes its catalog, reproducing the forecast served last Tuesday becomes a snapshot query, not a hope that the training set still exists.

What this buys: freshness

The three experiments do not each stand alone; together they resolve the contradiction the blog opened on, a fresh lakehouse feeding stale models, the freshest data reaching the prediction through the stalest path. The tabular foundation model reads the same governed, live tables on every prediction, reading in place, and across accuracy, federation, and reproducibility we showed those reads staying correct and point-in-time addressable through the real federated layer.

Model freshness collapses into data freshness, and the lakehouse already owns data freshness. The data platform stops being upstream of a bottleneck and becomes the serving layer directly.

↳ Back to the opener's dashboard: NorthBound's forecast is now as fresh as the last order that landed, because it reads the same live tables the dashboard does. The opening contradiction resolves.

The textual world made this exact move years ago, and that is worth a remark before we conclude.

6. The textual world already went stateless-and-shared

The emerging training-free architecture, built on a modern data layer, mirrors the move the LLM world already made for unstructured data. In that world you do not train separate models for separate use cases or tenants, though fine-tuning still has a place in some niche areas. The dominant, economically winning pattern is one shared stateless foundation model plus per-tenant context retrieved at inference.

Stateless requests made LLMs accessible and easy to consume, and made model access scalable across tenants and use cases. Tabular workloads are now getting the same treatment.

The parallel points to more than "stateless is better." Training-free inference converts per-task learned state into per-task declarative state. In the classic stack, the state that defines a tenant's predictions is a set of weights in a registry, produced by a training run. In the training-free stack, that state is a context specification: which rows, which columns, which window, governed as data alongside the policies that scope it.

Declarative state is cheaper to govern and to evolve: you change a policy once and it applies everywhere, with no retrain across N times M models. A rule about which window counts as recent is edited in one place, not baked into thousands of frozen artifacts.

It is not automatically cheaper on every dimension though. A trained model is self-contained: its weights plus the frozen set it learned from fully determine how it behaved in the past. A query result is not self-contained, because the rows it read live in tables that keep changing. On artifact count the declarative approach is plainly simpler; on reproducibility it can look harder. Reproducing a past prediction needs two things: the context specification and a point-in-time snapshot of every table it touched. The specification is easy, but the snapshot is where classic ML had an advantage, because materializing a training set froze the exact inputs as a side effect, and without training nothing is materialized.

The reproducibility experiment above showed the substrate closing that gap: Iceberg records every commit as an immutable, addressable snapshot, so the exact inputs a prediction read become a snapshot id you can query back through the serving path. This is the second place training-free fits the modern data layer rather than fighting it. The first was read-in-place inference, where every prediction is a governed query against the live lakehouse.

Borrowing the LLM architecture also borrows its known failure mode: retrieval quality. A shared model is only as good as the context it is handed. Bad retrieval yields confident, wrong output, and no training-time validation gate stands in the way to catch it, because there was no training.

This does not invalidate the architecture; it relocates where failures need to be caught. The risk that used to live in the training run now lives in context selection: choose the wrong rows and the model returns a confident wrong answer, with no gate to catch it. That failure surface has to be governed at inference time, and how to do it well is an open problem, the third of the four the next section takes up.

Point the shared model at the wrong recent window for merchant 3,001, say a promotion week treated as a normal baseline, and it will forecast next week confidently and wrongly. No gate catches it, because the only thing that decides quality now is which rows you chose. The merchant that opened the piece carries out the new failure mode as clearly as it carried the old one.

7. The new challenges

Deleting the training pipeline did not make the work vanish. It moved, and where it moved is the point.

Four hard problems relocated, each worth stating plainly as an open question.

First, which examples are the right examples once a distribution shifts. We saw earlier that drift reaction gets cheaper, a re-query instead of a retrain, but that left a residue: choosing which rows to show the model now becomes the live problem, and it lives in context construction. How to build that context well is the actual challenge.

Second, point-in-time reproducibility of a query result. The experiment above showed it is solvable on the substrate through Iceberg snapshots and tags, but only as an explicit retention and tagging policy that someone owns and pays for. Which snapshots to keep, for how long, and who governs the policy stays open.

Third, retrieval and selection quality as a new silent-failure surface. With no training-time gate, the wrong context produces confident wrong output and nothing stops it. Governance has to move to inference time.

Fourth, online-serving latency under an SLA, together with the freshness contracts context assembly now has to honor. The federated fetches in our experiments ran in seconds, not milliseconds, and the re-query paradigm re-reads source rows in place on every prediction, which turns expensive and wastes database compute as contexts grow. Where the same context is queried repeatedly, caching the assembled context (through a materialization layer like Dremio's reflections) is the natural mitigation. Caching the model's state over a fixed context (KV caching) is a further option on the serving side.

Deleting training does not remove the work, it relocates it left, into the assembly, governance, and semantic correctness of the table you hand the model. That relocation promotes the federated semantic lakehouse from a convenience layer to the critical path.

NorthBound deleted the training pipeline for its demand forecast, and the twelve thousand model artifacts collapsed into one shared model plus a set of specifications. The four relocated problems are now NorthBound's real backlog: which rows to show merchant 3,001 after its promotion, how to reproduce last Tuesday's forecast, how to catch a bad context before it ships, and how to answer inside an SLA.

The fit is not incidental

A training-free model needs exactly what an Iceberg lakehouse served by Dremio already provides: live governed tables to read in place, tenant isolation at the source, and addressable snapshots for point-in-time recall. What one side requires at inference time, the other supplies as a native property. The model removes the per-tenant training multiplication; the lakehouse carries what relocated when training was deleted, from context assembly to reproducibility.

This is the combination we put to the test, and the one we are bringing together, tabular foundation models (RPT-1, TabPFN, etc) on SAP AI Core reading in place through Dremio, as part of the SAP Business AI Platform, shown end to end at SAP TechEd.

Each side provides what the other assumes. And that is why it works.

Appendix: experiment details

The snippets below preserve the essential method and checks without requiring a separate code archive. They are shortened for readability; setup, authentication, retries, and result serialization are omitted.

A. Accuracy: shared versus per-tenant

For each store we held out the latest 20% of rows, gave both models the same most-recent history, and changed only the context budget:

budgets = [20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640]

for store in stores:
    rows = data[data.Store == store].sort_values("Date")
    split = round(len(rows) * 0.8)
    train, test = rows.iloc[:split], rows.iloc[split:]

    for budget in budgets:
        if budget > len(train):
            continue
        context = train.iloc[-budget:]

        per_tenant = LightGBM().fit(context[features], context.Sales)
        classic_prediction = per_tenant.predict(test[features])

        shared = TabPFNRegressor().fit(context[features], context.Sales)
        training_free_prediction = shared.predict(test[features])

The implementation fixed categorical encoding, excluded prediction-time leakage such as Customers, and recorded RMSE and MAE for every unit.

Context rowsUnitsTabPFN win rateMedian normalized RMSE: LightGBM Median normalized RMSE: TabPFN
203683%0.2030.187
403683%0.2170.164
803675%0.1700.146
1603692%0.1440.127
3203692%0.1360.122
6401100%0.1030.092

Each point is one store at one context budget; the lines show median normalized RMSE. Lower is better. The 640-row result contains only one store and should be treated as anecdotal.

B. Federation: separate tables, one logical view

The logical layer was a union over independently stored tenant tables:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW retail.tenants AS
SELECT * FROM retail.store_644
UNION ALL SELECT * FROM retail.store_455
UNION ALL SELECT * FROM retail.store_467
UNION ALL SELECT * FROM retail.store_313
UNION ALL SELECT * FROM retail.store_682;

SELECT *
FROM retail.tenants
WHERE Store = 313
ORDER BY SortKey;

For each store we canonicalized the local and federated frames, ran the same held-out rows through TabPFN twice, and checked both isolation and invariance:

assert local_context.equals(federated_context)
assert set(federated_context.Store) == {store}

p_local = predict_with_tabpfn(local_context, test)
p_federated = predict_with_tabpfn(federated_context, test)
assert np.max(np.abs(p_local - p_federated)) == 0.0

All five stores passed. This was a correctness test rather than a latency benchmark; warm context fetches took 1.7–2.5 seconds.

C. Reproducibility: return to the original snapshot

The test consisted of three reads and one mutation:

# 1. Predict from the original, immutable context.
S1 = table.metadata.current_snapshot_id
context_s1 = dremio.query(f"""
    SELECT * FROM retail.store_313
    AT SNAPSHOT '{S1}' ORDER BY SortKey
""")
p1 = predict_with_tabpfn(context_s1, test)

# 2. Move the live table forward and predict from its new state.
table.append(four_synthetic_rows)
p2 = predict_with_tabpfn(
    dremio.query("SELECT * FROM retail.store_313 ORDER BY SortKey"),
    test,
)

# 3. Address S1 again through the same serving path.
context_s1_reproduced = dremio.query(f"""
    SELECT * FROM retail.store_313
    AT SNAPSHOT '{S1}' ORDER BY SortKey
""")
p1_reproduced = predict_with_tabpfn(context_s1_reproduced, test)

assert not np.array_equal(p1, p2)
assert context_s1.equals(context_s1_reproduced)
assert np.array_equal(p1, p1_reproduced)

The four appended rows were deliberately extreme, making the test sensitive to context change rather than implying that every append causes dramatic drift. The current-state prediction moved by as much as 24,309.1, while the snapshot-addressed reproduction differed from the original by exactly 0.0.

entry.title: When to Scale Resources vs. When to Optimize Code in SAP Commerce Cloud
entry.content:
One question that may come up when working with SAP Commerce Cloud is: “Our storefront is slow — should we add more resources or investigate the code?”

The answer isn't always straightforward. Scaling up infrastructure might help in some situations, while in others, it may only mask underlying inefficiencies. On the other hand, focusing on code optimization too early can lead to unnecessary effort if the main issue is simply a lack of capacity.

In this post, I'll share some practical considerations that can help when investigating performance issues and deciding where to focus first.


Understanding the Two Levers

Scaling Resources means increasing the compute capacity available to your SAP Commerce Cloud environment. In the context of SAP Commerce Cloud, this typically involves:

  • Increasing the number of service replicas (horizontal scaling)
  • Increasing Service resources for higher CPU/memory (vertical scaling)
  • Scaling backgroundprocessing nodes independently from storefront nodes

Optimizing Code means improving the efficiency of your application logic, queries, or integrations so that the same workload consumes fewer resources. This includes:

  • Refactoring inefficient FlexibleSearch or SQL queries
  • Reducing unnecessary service calls or cache misses
  • Improving ImpEx import performance
  • Streamlining custom extensions and event listeners
  • Leveraging SAP Commerce Cloud's built-in caching layers (RegionCache, EhCache)

The Decision Framework

You can use the following signals to help guide your decision:


Signal:   


CPU/memory consistently at 80–100% under normal load

  Scale Resources: 


✅

Optimize Code:


Consider first

Slow response times despite low resource utilization

❌

✅

Performance degrades only during peak traffic

✅

Evaluate both

Specific API endpoints or pages are slow

❌

✅

Database query times are high

❌

✅

Cache hit ratio is low

❌

✅

Scaling already done but no improvement observed

❌

✅

New feature release caused regression

❌

✅

Business growth driving sustained higher baseline traffic

✅

✅

When to Scale Resources First

Scaling is the right first move when:

  1. You have a proven, optimized baseline — your code is already efficient, and growth is the driver.
  2. You face a time-critical situation — a major campaign or product launch is imminent and there is no time for a code cycle.
  3. Infrastructure metrics confirm saturation — monitoring tools (e.g., Dynatrace, integrated with SAP Commerce Cloud) show consistent CPU/memory exhaustion across all nodes.
  4. Horizontal scaling is cost-effective — adding nodes is cheaper than the engineering effort required to optimize at that moment.

Note: Scaling without understanding the root cause is a temporary fix. Always schedule a post-incident optimization review.

When to Optimize Code First

Code optimization should be your first move when:

  1. Resource utilization is low but latency is high — this is a classic sign of blocking operations, N+1 query problems, or synchronous calls that should be asynchronous.
  2. A specific component is the bottleneck — profiling tools reveal that one service, query, or extension is responsible for the majority of response time.
  3. Cache effectiveness is poor — SAP Commerce Cloud's caching architecture is powerful; if cache hit rates are low, tuning cache regions can yield dramatic improvements without any infrastructure cost.
  4. You are hitting database limits — adding service replicas will not help if the bottleneck is in the database layer. FlexibleSearch query optimization, proper indexing in the underlying DB, and reducing query frequency are the right tools here.
  5. Costs are a concern — optimized code reduces the infrastructure footprint needed, directly impacting cloud spend.
A Practical Diagnostic Workflow

Before making any decision, you can follow this sequence:

  1. Reproduce the issue in a non-production environment (Staging)
  2. Enable performance profiling (Dynatrace APM or SAP Commerce Cloud built-in monitoring)
  3. Identify the top 3 slowest transactions or endpoints
  4. Check resource utilization metrics (CPU, Heap, GC pressure, DB connections)
  5. Review FlexibleSearch query execution plans
  6. Check cache hit/miss ratios per cache region
  7. Decide: Is the bottleneck compute-bound or logic-bound?

→ Compute-bound → Scale
→ Logic-bound → Optimize
→ Both → Optimize first, then right-size

Real-World Scenario Examples

Scenario A — Black Friday Preparation A retailer notices that during load tests simulating Black Friday traffic, all nodes reach 90% CPU. The application has been running stably for 2 years with no major code changes. The traffic volume is genuinely 3x the normal baseline. → Decision: Scale horizontally. This is a capacity problem, not a code problem.

Scenario B — New Promotion Engine Deployment After deploying a new custom promotion rule engine, the cart calculation endpoint degrades from 200ms to 4 seconds. CPU utilization is at 30%. → Decision: Optimize code. The low CPU with high latency points to an inefficient algorithm or blocking call in the new code.

Scenario C — Gradual Degradation Over 6 Months Performance has slowly worsened over 6 months with no major releases. Resource utilization is moderate but trending upward. → Decision: Investigate first. Check for data volume growth impacting FlexibleSearch queries, growing session counts, or accumulated technical debt in background jobs. Likely a combination of optimization and right-sizing.

Key Takeaways

 

  • Scaling buys time; optimization solves problems. Use scaling strategically, not as a default response to performance issues.
  • Always profile before deciding. Gut feeling is not a substitute for data from monitoring tools.
  • SAP Commerce Cloud's architecture supports both levers — the platform is designed for cloud-native horizontal scaling AND provides rich optimization capabilities at the application layer.
  • Cost and time are real constraints — factor them into your decision, but never let them lead you to permanently mask a code problem with infrastructure spend.
  • Iterate — performance engineering is not a one-time activity. Build a culture of continuous profiling and optimization.

entry.title: Second Half 2026 Release: What’s New in SAP SuccessFactors HCM?
entry.content:
The SAP SuccessFactors 2H 2026 release marks an important milestone. It is the first major wave of innovation since SAP announced its vision for Autonomous HCM, where AI orchestrates end-to-end processes, drives context-aware decisions, and optimizes workforce operations at scale. In this release, we are delivering hundreds of new capabilities and enhancements across the suite that will bring this vision to life.

Here’s a snapshot of some of the key innovations, aligned to stages of the employee lifecycle:

 

Plan & Hire

 

Recruiting

  • Internal hires can now route automatically from SmartRecruiters for SAP SuccessFactors to SAP SuccessFactors Onboarding and SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central, with sync status visible in real time, keeping recruiting and core HR data aligned. Additionally, business rules now connect SmartRecruiters solutions data to configurable automation, removing manual steps across the hiring workflow.
  • Winston Match results are now fully reportable in Report Builder, including overall match bands and dimension-level detail across jobs and applications. Recruiters can see exactly how AI-driven candidate rankings affect pipeline progression, connect scoring to hiring outcomes, and review or explain AI-assisted decisions with confidence, making it easier to identify the candidates most likely to succeed. Winston Screen builds on this by applying repeatable, configurable screening questions consistently across roles, helping recruiters narrow large applicant pools more efficiently, with results reportable in Report Builder alongside the full pipeline.

Winston Screen

 

  • A new agentic scheduling capability, available through Winston Companion, enables interviews to be booked with a single prompt, replacing fragmented manual coordination. And during interviews, the new Interview Summary Agent automatically captures and posts a structured interview summary to the candidate profile. This agent works directly with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and Gong.

Agentic scheduling

 

Onboarding

  • The Onboarding Assistant helps HR teams deliver personalized new hire experiences at scale through agentic capabilities that provide intelligent prioritization, simplified task creation, and automated custom form conversion. The assistant delivers AI-orchestrated task tracking that coordinates and tracks onboarding actions, highlights clear next best steps, and surfaces bottlenecks or risks before they delay onboarding progress. To further support day-one readiness, HR teams can also use the assistant to easily create unique onboarding tasks and localized, custom multilingual forms.

Onboarding Assistant

 

Manage & Pay

 

Core HR

  • The HR Operations Assistant allows organizations to manage workforce data and employee changes more intelligently. The assistant proactively identifies and resolves data issues, streamlines employment and organizational changes, accelerates workflows, optimizes position management, and helps safeguard payroll-related transactions. entry.title: EWM Outbound: The Correct Sequence for Correcting a Delivery Item After Warehouse Task Confirmation
entry.content:
Introduction
One of the most common process mistakes in SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) outbound operations happens when a warehouse coordinator or logistics analyst needs to correct a delivery item,  a quantity change, a batch reassignment, or a batch split sub-item removal after the warehouse task has already been confirmed and the stock is packed into a Handling Unit (HU).

The instinct is to go directly to the ERP delivery (VL02N) and make the correction. It seems logical: the issue is in the delivery document, so fix the delivery document. However, this approach, while intuitive, breaks the reference link between the EWM HU and the ERP delivery item, causing a silent but severe data inconsistency that only surfaces when the system tries to proceed to the next step in the outbound process.

This post documents the problem pattern, explains why it happens, and provides the correct step-by-step sequence to follow whenever a delivery item correction is needed after picking has been confirmed.

The Problem — What Goes Wrong

Symptoms

When the wrong sequence is followed, the following symptoms appear in EWM:

  • Warehouse request is empty — no items available to generate new warehouse tasks
  • Physical stock in the HU shows Item = 0 — the HU contains stock but references a delivery item that no longer exists
  • Subsequent warehouse task cannot be created — the outbound flow to staging or GI zone is blocked
  • Goods Issue cannot be posted — the entire outbound billing chain is halted

The Root Cause

In SAP EWM, when a warehouse task is confirmed, the system creates a direct link between the physical stock in the Handling Unit and the delivery item in the EWM Outbound Delivery Order (ODO). This link is stored at the HU item level with a reference to the specific delivery item number.

When the delivery item is then modified or deleted in ERP — for example, by removing a Batch Split (BSP) sub-item or zeroing out the main item quantity — EWM is not aware of this change until a full redistribution of the delivery occurs. In the meantime, the HU item still holds the old reference. If that delivery item no longer exists, the reference becomes orphaned, and the field Item in the HU physical stock view shows 0 (zero), meaning: "this stock is assigned to this delivery, but to an item that no longer exists."

The result:

HU has stock → delivery item reference = 0 (orphaned)
Warehouse request → empty (no valid items to pick)
Next step (YEST / GI zone) → cannot be triggered
Goods Issue → blocked

How to Identify the Issue

Before attempting any correction, confirm the inconsistency:

Step 1 — Check the Warehouse Request

  • Run the warehouse task creation transaction for the affected ODO
  • If the "Solic. depósito" (Warehouse Request) tab is empty → issue confirmed

Step 2 — Check Physical Stock (/SCWM/ADHU)

  1. Run /SCWM/ADHU
  2. Search by Warehouse Number and Document (ODO number)
  3. Open the Physical Stock (Estoque físico) tab
  4. Look for entries where Item = 0 → orphaned HU item confirmed

Step 3 — Trace the Sequence (/SCWM/ACTLOG)

  1. Run /SCWM/ACTLOG
  2. Filter by Warehouse Number and ODO number
  3. Look for a delivery modification that occurred after a warehouse task confirmation
  4. This confirms the wrong sequence was followed

The Wrong Sequence ❌

1. WT confirmed (picking done, stock in HU)     ✓
2. Delivery modified in ERP (VL02N)             ← WRONG — HU not unpacked first
3. Item deleted / quantity zeroed out           ← HU now references non-existing item
4. Item = 0 appears in HU physical stock        ← Inconsistency created
5. Subsequent WT creation fails                 ← Process blocked

The Correct Sequence ✅

Whenever a delivery item needs to be corrected after a warehouse task has been confirmed and stock is packed in an HU, always follow this sequence:

Step 1 — Cancel / Reverse the Warehouse Task Confirmation

  • Navigate to the confirmed warehouse task in EWM
  • Reverse/cancel the confirmation to return stock to its source bin
  • The HU assignment is released

Step 2 — Unpack / Deassign the HU Item

  1. Run /SCWM/ADHU
  2. Locate the HU containing the stock for the affected item
  3. Remove (deassign) the item from the HU
  4. Confirm the physical stock no longer shows the delivery item reference

Step 3 — Perform the Delivery Correction in ERP

  • Run VL02N in ERP
  • Apply the necessary correction (delete BSP sub-item, change batch, adjust quantity, etc.)
  • Save the delivery

Step 4 — Re-distribute the Delivery to EWM

  • Re-save the delivery or use VL06O to push the updated delivery to EWM
  • Confirm the ODO in EWM reflects the corrected items

Step 5 — Re-generate and Execute the Warehouse Task

  • Create a new warehouse task for the corrected items
  • Confirm the task via /SCWM/RFUI or the appropriate RF transaction
  • Pack stock into the HU again
  • Continue the outbound flow normally

Visual Summary

✅ CORRECT SEQUENCE

WT Confirmed → Stock in HU
        ↓
[1] Reverse WT confirmation
        ↓
[2] Unpack HU item (/SCWM/ADHU)
        ↓
[3] Modify delivery in ERP (VL02N)
        ↓
[4] Re-distribute to EWM (VL06O)
        ↓
[5] Re-generate WT → confirm → pack → continue flow

Why This Matters — Business Impact

Skipping steps 1 and 2 before modifying the delivery may seem like a time-saving shortcut, but the consequences are severe:

Impact Area Consequence
Warehouse OperationsPicking tasks cannot be created — pickers are blocked
Outbound LogisticsGoods Issue cannot be posted
Customer BillingInvoice generation delayed or blocked
Data IntegrityOrphaned HU items require manual correction by support team
System RecoveryEach affected ODO requires individual manual data fix

In large warehouse environments with high-volume outbound processing, a single incorrect sequence applied to multiple deliveries can result in significant operational disruption and financial exposure.

Prevention — Process and Authorization Controls

Process Training

Warehouse supervisors and logistics coordinators should be trained on this sequence. A simple rule to communicate to the team:

"Never modify a delivery in ERP if the stock has already been confirmed and packed in EWM. Always unpack and reverse first."

Authorization Control (Recommended)

Consider restricting the user role authorization in ERP to prevent deletion or modification of delivery items that have active HU assignments in EWM. This removes the possibility of the wrong sequence being followed unintentionally.

Proactive Monitoring

Implement a daily check in /SCWM/MON for ODOs that:

  • Have HUs assigned
  • Have no open warehouse tasks
  • Have not yet posted Goods Issue

Catching these early (before the shipping window) avoids escalation to a business-down situation. Moreover, this proactive monitoring should be performed only when the behavior is already noticed but not fixed or identified how many deliveries could be affected by this behavior. 

Conclusion

The EWM outbound process enforces a tight coupling between delivery items in ERP and physical stock in Handling Units. This design ensures data consistency but requires discipline when corrections are needed mid-process. The correct sequence — reverse → unpack → correct → redistribute → re-execute — must always be followed when modifying a delivery item after warehouse task confirmation.

Understanding this sequence is fundamental for anyone operating or supporting EWM outbound processing, and implementing the appropriate process controls prevents it from becoming a recurring incident.

 Author: Jacson Folmer Dias — EWM Consultant | SAP Global Delivery Hub Americas LAC

entry.title: Building an AI Agent Inside SAP CAP — A Developer POC
entry.content:
We have a Fiori app that lists all supplier quotations — extracted from PDFs, stored in CAP, ready to review. The listing part works great. But comparing them? That's where it gets painful. You open one quotation, note the price, go back, open another, try to remember the first one. Do that five times and you're already reaching for Excel.

That's what triggered the idea — the data is all there, the app already has everything, we just needed a smarter way to interact with it.

The interesting thing about @cap-js/agents is that this kind of agent can be built completely standalone as an independent service, or embedded directly inside an existing app. We went with inside the Fiori app — because that's exactly where the quotation data already lives. No duplication, no new backend, no separate deployment.

Two annotations on the CDS service and CAP registers a fully A2A-compliant agent endpoint:

@AGent
@protocol: 'agent'
service QuotationAgentService { ... }

 

The agent gets your OData entities as tools and queries them on demand. But here's the part that made it actually useful — the agent doesn't just return data, it decides how to present it based on the context of the question. Ask "compare total prices across suppliers" and it picks a bar chart because you're comparing across many items with long names. Ask "show quotation status breakdown" and it picks a donut chart because you're looking at proportions of a whole. Ask "how many quotations were submitted over time" and it picks a line chart because that's a trend. The right chart for the right question — automatically.

All of it rendered as SAPUI5 Integration Cards inline in the chat, inside the same Fiori app.

Connected it to Gemini 2.5 Flash via SAP AI Core and built the chat dialog in TypeScript. The hardest part honestly was the prompt — getting the LLM to always pick the right chart type and never skip it took more iterations than the actual code.

entry.title: SAP PP/ABAP: Recursive BOM Explosion for Cross-Plant Special Procurement Items
entry.content:
Requirement

I have a requirement to develop a program that can explode a BOM (Bill of Material) containing items with a Special Procurement Key at the item level.

Currently, these items are not being exploded further because of cross-plant references, either through CS11 or the standard BOM explosion BAPI.

My Approach / Proposed Solution

I am planning to develop a custom program using a recursive approach.

1. I have created a method that performs BOM explosion for a single BOM input. The method explodes the BOM and stores all the child items in a global internal table within the class.

2. During the explosion, whenever an item with a Special Procurement Key is encountered, the program retrieves the relevant plant, alternative BOM, and BOM usage details from the MAST and T406 tables.

3. Using these details, the program triggers the BOM explosion for the corresponding BOM in the other plant.

4. This process continues recursively until no further items with a Special Procurement Key are found at any level of the BOM hierarchy.

5. Finally, all the exploded components are stored in the global internal table.

What do you think about this approach?

Is this approach technically feasible in SAP ABAP? Are there any standard SAP function modules, BAPIs, or better alternatives to handle cross-plant BOM explosion scenarios?

I would appreciate your suggestions and recommendations on potential challenges, performance optimization, or best practices for implementing this solution.

entry.title: SAP Key Management Service: Taking Control of Your Encryption Keys in the Cloud
entry.content:
SAP Key Management Service: Taking Control of Your Encryption Keys in the Cloud

How SAP KMS empowers customers to manage their own cryptographic keys across SAP cloud services and products

Introduction

In an era where data sovereignty and regulatory compliance are paramount, organizations moving to the cloud face a critical question: who controls the encryption keys that protect their most sensitive data? SAP has answered this question with the SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) — a service designed to put customers firmly in control of their data across SAP cloud services and products.

By managing their own encryption keys, customers decide exactly who can access their information. With SAP KMS, data remains inaccessible to any external party — including SAP. This represents a fundamental shift in how data sovereignty is maintained in SAP cloud environments.

This blog post provides an in-depth look at SAP KMS, its capabilities, the key management models it supports, and how it integrates with SAP’s cloud portfolio to deliver enterprise-grade data protection.

 

Why Key Management Matters in the Cloud

For enhanced security and data protection, customers require control over their cryptographic keys, empowering them to take a proactive approach to securing their data hosted on SAP cloud services.

The need for customer-controlled key management is driven by several factors:

  • Regulatory Compliance: Regulations such as GDPR, CCPA, and industry-specific mandates often require organizations to demonstrate control over their encryption mechanisms and keys.
  • Data Sovereignty: Organizations need assurance that their data cannot be accessed by unauthorized parties, including cloud service providers.
  • Risk Mitigation: Controlling encryption keys allows organizations to revoke access instantly, rendering data unreadable in the event of a breach or a change in business relationships.
  • Zero-Trust Architecture: Modern security frameworks demand that no entity — internal or external — is implicitly trusted. Customer-controlled key management aligns with this principle.

 

What Is SAP Key Management Service?

SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) is a cloud-based service that provides customers with a centralized and secure way to manage the cryptographic keys used to encrypt data across SAP cloud services.

The service enables customers to securely manage and control the encryption keys used to protect their business data, and helps ensure that encryption and decryption can occur only with their approval.

 

Core Capabilities

SAP KMS provides a comprehensive set of key management capabilities:

Capability

Description

Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)

Import existing keys from external key management systems into SAP KMS FIPS 140-2 Level 3-compliant keystore

Hold Your Own Key (HYOK)

Register a key from an external keystore to keep the key material in the customer keystore only

Key rotation

Rotate keys on demand and re-encrypt top-level keys

Global or regional deployment

Deploy one or multiple SAP KMS tenants based on customer need

4+ eyes principle

Use workflows to secure all key actions executed by key administrators

Key wrapping

Wrap and unwrap data encryption keys for secure distribution across services

Flexible assignment

Flexibly assign SAP cloud solutions to customer keys

Access control

Role-based access, authentication, and authorization for key management operations

 

Customer-Managed Key Scenarios

SAP KMS supports multiple key management models to accommodate different security requirements and compliance postures. Each model offers a different balance of control, convenience, and operational responsibility.

Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)

BYOK allows customers to generate a key externally and import it into the SAP KMS tenant. This model is suited for organizations that want to generate keys using their own certified hardware security modules (HSMs) while still leveraging SAP’s managed key infrastructure for daily operations.

Hold Your Own Key (HYOK)

HYOK represents the highest level of customer control. The encryption key never leaves the customer’s external keystore. SAP KMS is connected to the customer’s external key management system and uses the permitted key for cryptographic operations without ever storing or caching it.

  • The key remains under the customer’s sole control at all times
  • The customer can revoke access instantly by disabling the key in their external keystore

 

Key Scenario Comparison

Aspect

BYOK

HYOK

Key location

Generated externally, imported to SAP

Customer’s external keystore

Customer control

After import of the key, lifecycle within SAP KMS

Complete — key never leaves customer

SAP access to key

No direct access

No access — remote calls only

Revocation speed

Immediate via SAP KMS tenant

Immediate via external keystore

Best for

HSM-centric, flexible organizations

Maximum control & compliance

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Integration with SAP Cloud Services

SAP KMS integrates natively with a growing portfolio of SAP cloud services, enabling customer-managed encryption across the SAP landscape:

  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (coming soon)
  • SAP Datasphere (SAP Business Data Cloud)
  • SAP Credential Store (SAP Business Technology Platform)
  • SAP HANA Cloud (SAP Business Technology Platform)
  • More to come…

 

How SAP KMS Works: Architecture Overview

At a high level, SAP KMS operates within a layered encryption architecture:

  1. Data Encryption: SAP cloud services encrypt data at rest using Data Encryption Keys (DEKs) generated by the service itself.
  2. Key Encryption: The DEKs are encrypted (wrapped) using root encryption keys managed within the SAP service’s secure store (e.g., SAP HANA’s Instance Secure Store or Local Secure Store).
  3. Customer Master Key: SAP KMS provides the customer’s master key, which encrypts (wraps) the root encryption keys. This is the key the customer controls.
  4. Access Control: Without the customer’s master key, the root keys cannot be decrypted, and therefore the data remains inaccessible. Revoking the key immediately locks the data.

This envelope encryption approach ensures that SAP never needs direct access to customer data, while the customer maintains a “kill switch” capability to revoke access at any time.

SAP Key Management Service Architecture

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Security Foundations

SAP KMS is built on robust security foundations to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of key management operations:

  • FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Compliance: The underlying keystore infrastructure meets stringent federal security standards
  • Cloud-Agnostic Architecture: SAP KMS operates independently of the underlying hyperscaler, providing consistent security across multi-cloud deployments
  • Role-Based Access Control: Granular roles (Key Administrator, Key User) ensure separation of duties in key management operations
  • Comprehensive Audit Trail: Every key operation is logged for compliance and forensic purposes

 

Conclusion

SAP Key Management Service represents a significant step forward in SAP’s commitment to customer data sovereignty and cloud security. By enabling customers to manage, rotate, and revoke their own encryption keys, SAP KMS ensures that organizations maintain full control over their data — even in a fully cloud-hosted environment.

Whether you choose BYOK or HYOK for maximum control with keys that never leave your keystore, SAP KMS provides the flexibility to meet your security and compliance requirements.

As SAP continues to expand the integration of KMS across its cloud portfolio, organizations can confidently accelerate their cloud transformation knowing that their most sensitive data remains firmly under their control.

If you want to learn more about the new solution, actively engage with SAP subject matter experts and your peers, and stay up to date about the topic of SAP Key Management Service, join our community at our SAP Key Management Service topic page!
