entry.title: ABAP to Full Stack: Making Sense of What’s Behind a Fiori App (OData, Class, Virtual Element)
entry.content:
Hello! I’m Andréa Molina. After more than 20 years in SAP, the new SAP world left me completely lost, so I decided to share my experience and learn together. I’m moving from classic ABAP to the SAP full stack, one real project at a time, drama included.

From overwhelmed to curious, my journey had (and still has) a lot of bumps. You can check my other posts here. I hope you find understanding and empathy here, and maybe a few laughs.

If you’re in the same boat, this series is for you. In this post: I will share my experience creating a List Report (a Fiori floorplan) built on a CDS view exposed as OData V4, with a virtual element calculated by an ABAP class. Plus a plot twist in Step 5.

A bit of background

On my journey I always try to use case studies that are real and will add value to the business. The library and ice cream examples just give me more anxiety and make no sense to me. So this time I’m turning an existing query/infoset (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori app, to understand how much effort and time it would take.

So far I have worked with the Basic template and one CDS KPI app, and I knew there were more template options to explore. This time I thought the List Report Page would work best (well, not really, but let’s move forward for now... surprise at Step 5 of this blog).

Before we move on, read this if you are asking "What on earth is List Report Page and Basic Template?"
When you create a new app from a template, you can choose among a lot of frameworks. Each framework provides a set of prebuilt files, structure and more.

You can read more about FloorPlans here: https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-136/page-types/floorplans/when-to-use-which-floorplan

The project

Transform an existing Query/InfoSet (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori application. 

Does SAP Make This Easy?

In my research and studying I couldn't find a tool that automatically converts queries into Fiori applications. If you know of a better approach, please share it in the comments. I'd genuinely love to learn. 

The Challenge

… because I have never done before this project

  • Create a CDS view that delivers the data exactly the way I want it to be displayed, with logic and not just selection from the database
  • Create an ABAP class that is called by the CDS
  • Understand how the ABAP class and the CDS work together
  • Create a KPI on top of the report list

The best way to learn: get your hands dirty! A simple learning exercise 

I am suggesting here a very simple example of CDS, class and app: create a List Report Page based on a CDS.

The result should show all the Sales Orders created in the last 30 days and flag the ones created today.

Step 0: Eclipse

The way to create backend objects for apps is using the ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse. If you are new here, check this tutorial to set up your Eclipse ADT: https://developers.sap.com/tutorials/abap-install-adt/ 

Step 1: The CDS Views

To get familiar with frontend and backend (together, they make the full stack), here is what is what.

  • Backend: where the data comes from.
  • Frontend: the screen the user interacts with. This part of the development is the backend.

What is backend: Where the data comes from. Put in very simple words.  it's the data that will populate the frontend. 

The CDS will select from I_SalesOrder, and we will use a virtual element (calculated by an ABAP class) to flag the orders created today. It will only return the last 30 days, so we don't select hundreds of records. 🥴 

Why I_SalesOrder and not VBAK?

If you grew up in ECC like I did, you might be asking: why not use VBAK?

  • Tables move, CDS adapts. Moving from ECC to S/4HANA changed a lot of tables. Take VBUK, where we used to read the order status. Its fields now live in VBAK, so every program that selected from VBUK needs to change. But a program reading the status through I_SalesOrder will keep working, because SAP updated the view and left the interface alone. That's the idea behind released CDS views: SAP can rearrange it, and your app doesn't notice.
  • Clean core. Clean core is the promise of updating the system faster and more often than before, allowing companies to use the new technologies instead of waiting years for a hard and difficult system upgrade. To do that, you need to use standard objects. If you have already migrated to S/4, you know what I am talking about needing to adapt the system considering all changes. Using CDS views instead of tables is one step in the clean core approach. 
  • It already speaks Fiori. SAP does the hard work of the joins and associations, so you just use it the way you need, and it's all ready for the day you want an Object Page.

Yes, I know. It's not our language YET, we don't know those CDS names yet, and it's so easy to use a table we know. But remember when VBAK sounded just as weird as I_SalesOrder does now? It stuck because we used it every day. This will stick too, if we choose to start.

Now we have AI to help us speed up our knowledge and search for the right object to select from.  But I always use AI as a co-worker and never as the builder and be sure you add on the prompt to use best practices and use Standard objects whenever possible

So let’s go for it! Creating the CDS on Eclipse…

CDS Code 

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED //Authorization is not required
@EndUserText.label: 'Demo for ABAP Class' //Just a text
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true //
define view entity ZC_DEMO
 as select from I_SalesOrder
{
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 10, importance: #HIGH }] //The field below will be the first (10) column on the report
     @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 10 }] //The field below will be on the app as a search field
 key SalesOrder,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 20 }]
     SalesOrderType,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 30 }]
     SalesOrganization,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 40 }]
     @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 20 }]
     CreationDate,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 50, label: 'Created Today' }]
     @ObjectModel.virtualElement: true //The field below will use an virtual Element
     @ObjectModel.virtualElementCalculatedBy: 'ABAP:ZCL_VIRT_DEMO' //This is the Class you use to calculate the field below
     cast( ' ' as abap.char(1) ) as CreatedToday
}
where CreationDate >= dats_add_days( $session.system_date, -30, 'NULL' ) //Just select the last 30 days

UI annotations: how the backend tells the frontend what to draw

The Fiori app doesn’t know anything about our fields. The annotations in the CDS are instructions that travel with the OData service, and Fiori elements reads them to build the screen.

In plain English: the CDS doesn’t only deliver the data, it also sends instructions to the screen the user interacts with: “Hey, look, here is what you show in the table and here is what you show in the filters.” 

 In our code:

  • @UI.lineItem: this field becomes a column in the report.
  • @UI.selectionField: this field becomes a filter in the filter bar at the top.

The position number sets the order: 10 comes first, then 20, and so on.

Note: I prefer using a Metadata Extension (a separate file that keeps the annotations out of the CDS view), but I really want to keep this very simple here.

Step 2: Create the Virtual Class

Note: I know we could get this logic using a CASE in the CDS, but the idea here is to show how to use the class in a very simple example that everybody understand 😉

This part here is important, so let's translate what this part of the code is saying: 

"Hey CDS, this field will use a virtual element. The value will be calculated by an ABAP class called ZCL_VIRT_DEMO. If nothing is returned, the value is blank. The field will contain a value of 1 char (ABAP CHAR1) and will be exposed as CreatedToday. Nice. See you in the class!" 

So now we need to create the virtual class. 

 

The code

CLASS zcl_virt_demo DEFINITION
 PUBLIC                      "Can be used by other objects
 FINAL                       "Cannot be inherited
 CREATE PUBLIC.
 PUBLIC SECTION.
   "This makes the class a calculator for virtual elements
   INTERFACES if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read.
ENDCLASS.
CLASS zcl_virt_demo IMPLEMENTATION.
 "STEP 1 - Runs FIRST, before the database read.
 "Which real fields do you need to calculate your virtual field?"
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~get_calculation_info.
   "Only if the app really asked for CreatedToday (names come in UPPERCASE)
   IF line_exists( it_requested_calc_elements[ table_line = 'CREATEDTODAY' ] ).
     "Tell SADL to also read CreationDate from the database
     APPEND 'CREATIONDATE' TO et_requested_orig_elements.
   ENDIF.
 ENDMETHOD.
 "STEP 2 - Runs AFTER the database read, once per package of rows.
 "Here we fill the virtual field.
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~calculate.
   "Table typed with the CDS view, so we can access fields by name
   DATA lt_orders TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF zc_demo WITH DEFAULT KEY.
   "Copy the generic data into our typed table
   lt_orders = CORRESPONDING #( it_original_data ).
   "Read the date once, outside the loop (no need to ask on every row)
   DATA(lv_today) = cl_abap_context_info=>get_system_date( ).
   LOOP AT lt_orders ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<order>).
     "Created today? Mark with 'X'
     IF <order>-creationdate = lv_today.
       <order>-createdtoday = 'X'.
     ENDIF.
   ENDLOOP.
   "Give the result back to SADL (same rows, same order)
   ct_calculated_data = CORRESPONDING #( lt_orders ).
 ENDMETHOD.
ENDCLASS.

How to debug it

Go to SE24 and search for the class you created. 

Double-click the method you want to debug and create an EXTERNAL breakpoint. 

Important

You can preview the data in Eclipse, right? Yes, but there the class will not be called, and the virtual element comes back blank. Don’t do what I did: I thought my class wasn’t working and spent a long time trying to understand why! Let me save you the trouble: to see the class running, you need to create the service definition, the service binding and the app. 

Step 3: Service Definition and Service Binding

Service Definition - You tell the OData service (the object that selects the data) what you want to be displayed in the result. 

The Code

@EndUserText.label: 'Service Definition for ZC_DEMO'
define service ZUI_DEMO {
 expose ZC_DEMO;
}

Service Binding - You expose the service definition as an OData V4 UI service, so the app can consume your CDS data. 

Activate

When it does not activate

Depending on the architecture of your system, you might not be able to publish your service in Eclipse. If this is your case and you are using V4, you need to go to tcode /n/IWFND/V4_ADMIN. 

Search for your Service Binding, select it and publish it. 

Go back to Eclipse and you will see that the binding is now published.

Step 4: Creating a List Report Page

Just leave the project attributes as they are and finish the project.

You will get a message like the one below:

When it finishes, you will get this message:

  • Open Folder means you will only get this project in BAS.
  • Add Project to Workspace means it will be added to your other projects in BAS. I always use this option. 

Then you can preview the application by right clicking on webapp

The terminal will run and another tab will open with your app! Voilá!

Step 5 - Adding a UI5 element on top of the report

 Until here things went smoothly, but I want to add a Radial Micro Chart on top of the report. So my first instinct was to look for the controller and the view, but there was no MVC… WHAT??????? 

But first, what is MVC?

If you don't know what MVC means and you are an ABAPer, please read this blog post:  Getting cozy with familiar ABAP terms on your new BTP neighborhood 

It was a surprise to me, and then I thought: "Wait... does every template have completely different code and a completely different way of developing?" Gosh! 😅 (Actually, I said a bad word, but let's keep this blog civilized.)

But, as I mentioned in my previous blog Overwhelmed by SAP's new everything? Read this before you give up! I moved from being overwhelmed to being curious, and this time I was curious about how I would add the logic in the backend and not in the frontend.

So I asked Claude and, after a long discussion and a lot of changes, we decided that the best option was to create a Basic app because it was more familiar to me (my first 2 apps were created using Basic Template; be aware that to get to those 2 apps I created like 10 hahahaha).

The main point was that it was very simple to achieve parts of this using the List Report Page, but I couldn't make my UI5 element show up in the app using a custom UI5 extension (a controller file I added to the app), which probably says more about me than about the template. If you know the trick, please tell me. And with the Basic Template, I was trying to reinvent the wheel way too hard.

Then I was like: "There is NO WAY no one wanted to do this before and it is this hard!!"

Trust AI but learn your stuff

I started investigating it. I have taken lots and lots of SAP courses over the course of my career, and many were focused on UX, so I knew about the floorplans. Let's be honest here: it's so easy to think that AI knows more than you do! I think this is going to be the learning curve with this tool: understanding that your expertise matters more than you think.

So I learned that there is something called the Analytical List Page (ALP). The ALP is exactly the combination I was after: KPIs on top, report below. EXACTLY what I need. Claude never suggested it to me until I suggested it to Claude, and then it said that it was obvious that ALP was the best option 😅

What did I learn from this project? 

The nicest thing about being new at something is that once you overcome the first aversion to the new, you learn a lot very fast and mostly by making mistakes. With this project I tried a custom UI5 extension, two new floorplans, an ABAP class in a CDS, an analytical data definition and more.

Now I know when to use an Analytical List Page and when to use a List Report Page. List Report when the goal is to list and filter. ALP when you want KPIs and charts on top, working together with the list below. 

I tried to summarize it all here so you could learn from my experience. Let me know if it worked! 😉

——————

While this post might be basic to some, I added here everything that was getting me overwhelmed for years and all my questions related to those things. My goal with these posts is to demystify the new SAP development world together with you.

I'll continue sharing simple posts based on real discoveries, real questions and real experiences, sharing my journey, my learnings and my bumps along the way so you don't need to go through some of them yourself.

If you're in the same boat, stay tuned. There will be many more posts about this journey.

If you're further along than this, pretty please help us in the comments.

To be continued

I’m on holiday now, in Brazil to be more exact , so there’s no ALP update yet (yes, I’m still writing here, apparently I can’t help it 😅). But I will write about the Analytical List Page as soon as I’m back and get it sorted. And I promise to tell you honestly what worked and what didn’t. 

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: Blog 10 - SAP ESM for HR - GoLive Cutover and the First 30 Days: Making It Stick
entry.content:
The Final Mile

You have designed the organisation. You have built the service catalog. You have configured the channels, the routing rules, the SLAs, and the SuccessFactors integration. You have validated everything in UAT. The go/no-go criteria are green.

Now comes the part that determines whether months of careful work translate into a successful operation, or a painful first week that erodes stakeholder confidence before the system has had a chance to prove itself.

The go-live cutover is not the end of the implementation. It is the beginning of the HR operation. And the first 30 days after cutover set the trajectory for everything that follows.

This post covers both: the mechanics of a structured cutover, and the operational discipline of the hypercare period that follows.

What a Cutover Plan Actually Is

A cutover plan is not a project plan. It is a precise, sequenced checklist of every technical and operational action that must be completed in a specific order, within a specific time window, to transition from a configured and tested system to a live production environment.

The difference between a cutover plan and a to-do list is specificity. Every item has an owner, a start time, an end time, a dependency, and a validation step. If any item fails, the plan tells you what to do: who to escalate to, whether to pause and investigate, and what the rollback trigger is.

A well-built cutover plan for SAP ESM for HR typically spans 72 hours and is structured in three phases.

Phase 1 — Pre-Cutover (T-72 to T-24 Hours)

This phase is about preparation and final validation. Nothing changes in the production environment yet. The goal is to confirm that everything is ready to switch.

Key activities in this phase:

Configuration freeze

All configuration changes to the UAT and production environments are frozen. No new routing rules, no SLA adjustments, no catalog changes. What was tested in UAT is what goes live. Any change after the freeze requires formal change control approval.

Production environment readiness checks

Validate that the production ESM tenant is fully provisioned, that all SuccessFactors integration connections are active, that IAS and BTP configurations are in place, and that the email channel is pointing to the live HR mailbox (not the test mailbox).

Data readiness

Confirm that all HR agent user accounts are provisioned in production, IAS user groups are populated, and SuccessFactors permission roles are correctly assigned. Validate with a sample of five to ten employees across different countries that SSO works end-to-end in the production environment.

Communication preparation

Prepare all go-live communications: the employee announcement email, the HR agent briefing, the manager notification. Do not send yet, these go out in Phase 2.

Rollback plan confirmation

Define the exact trigger for a rollback decision: which P1 failure, within which timeframe, would cause you to revert to the previous HR service process. Confirm that the rollback procedure is documented, tested, and understood by the hypercare team.

Hypercare team briefing

The hypercare team, typically a small group of experienced consultants and HR SSC leads available full-time for the first two weeks, should be briefed, available, and clear on their escalation path before Phase 2 begins.

Phase 2 — The Cutover Window (T-24 to T-0 Hours)

This is the live switch. The production system goes live and the old process is retired.

Key activities in this phase:

Final production validation (T-24)

Run a final smoke test in production: create one case per configured channel, verify routing to each Agent Group, confirm SLA timers initialise correctly, validate SSO for one employee and one HR agent. This is not a full UAT rerun: it is a 30-minute sanity check that the production environment is behaving as expected.

Old channel retirement

If employees were previously emailing HR directly (individual inboxes, shared distribution lists), those inboxes must be redirected or decommissioned at go-live. Set up auto-replies on any retired HR mailboxes directing employees to the new HR portal or the new central HR mailbox. Leaving old channels open is the single fastest way to undermine self-service adoption.

Employee communications (T-4 hours)

Send the employee go-live announcement. The message should be short, clear, and action-oriented: here is your new HR portal link, here is what you do when you have an HR question from today, here is what happens if you email the old address. Avoid lengthy explanations of the system architecture. Employees do not need to understand how ESM works, they need to know where to go.

HR agent activation (T-1 hour)

Brief HR agents one final time. Confirm they can log in, see their queue, and access the knowledge base. Identify the hypercare contact for day one, the person they call if something is not working.

Go/no-go confirmation (T-0)

The project sponsor, HR SSC lead, and IT lead confirm go-live. Document the decision with a timestamp. The system is now live.

Phase 3 — Day One (T+0 to T+24 Hours)

The first day of live operations is the most intensive day of the entire programme. Plan for it accordingly.

What to monitor on day one:

Metric

What you are watching for

Case volume by channel

Is the self-service portal being used? Is email volume higher than expected?

Routing accuracy

Are any cases landing in the wrong queue?

SLA timer initialisation

Are all cases picking up the correct SLA?

Integration errors

Are any SuccessFactors lookups failing?

SSO failures

Are any users unable to log in?

HR agent queue depth

Is any team's queue growing faster than agents can handle?

Joule deflection rate

Are employee questions being answered without creating cases?

The hypercare team should have a live monitoring view open throughout day one. Set a check-in cadence, every two hours is appropriate, with a defined escalation path for any issue that cannot be resolved within 30 minutes.

What to communicate on day one:

If any issue affects a significant number of users, communicate proactively. Do not wait for the volume of complaints to force a response. A short message: "We are aware of an issue with X and are working to resolve it by Y", is far better than silence.

The 30-Day Hypercare Period

The hypercare period is not just about fixing problems. It is about stabilising the operation, tuning the configuration based on real usage data, and building the habits and disciplines that will sustain the system long term.

What to do in the first 30 days:

Week 1 — Stabilise

Focus entirely on resolving P1 and P2 issues. Track every defect, every workaround, every agent question. Daily hypercare check-ins. The goal is a fully stable system by the end of Week 1.

Week 2 — Tune

Review the first week's case data. Are routing rules working as designed? Are SLA targets realistic based on actual case complexity and volume? Is the knowledge base deflecting queries, or are employees finding it and not finding answers? Make targeted adjustments, but log every change. You need to know what you changed, when, and why.

Week 3 — Optimise the knowledge base

The first two weeks of live data will tell you which HR queries are generating the most cases. These are your highest-priority knowledge base gaps. Write or improve the articles for the top ten query types. This is the fastest way to drive deflection rate improvement.

Week 4 — First performance review

Run the first formal performance review with the HR SSC leadership. Present case volume, channel mix, routing accuracy, SLA adherence, and deflection rate. Compare actuals against the targets you set during design. Identify the three most important improvement actions for Month 2.

The Metrics That Tell You If It Is Working

By the end of 30 days, you should be tracking five key metrics regularly. By 90 days, you should have enough data to assess whether the implementation is delivering the outcomes it was designed for.

  • Self-service adoption rate

The percentage of all HR contacts initiated through the self-service portal. Target: >60%. If this is below 40% at 30 days, the employee communication and adoption plan needs attention, the system is working, but employees are not using it.

  • Tier 0 deflection rate

The percentage of employee visits to the self-service portal that are resolved without a case being created, answered by the knowledge base, or by Joule. Target: 30–40%. If this is below 15%, the knowledge base coverage is insufficient and needs immediate attention.

  • Joule deflection rate

If Joule is active: the percentage of Joule conversations that resolve without creating a case. Target: 15–25%. Below 10% at 30 days suggests knowledge base coverage gaps that Joule is drawing on is insufficient.

  • Tier 1 first-contact resolution rate

The percentage of cases handled by Tier 1 that are resolved without escalation to Tier 2. Target: 50–60%. Consistently below 40% suggests either that the Tier 1 scope is misconfigured (taking on cases that should go directly to Tier 2) or that Tier 1 agents need additional training or knowledge base support.

  • SLA adherence rate

The percentage of cases resolved within their configured SLA. Target: ≥95%. Consistently below 90% in the first 30 days is a signal to review either SLA targets (were they realistic?) or team capacity (are agents under-resourced?).

Continuous Improvement: What Happens After Hypercare

Hypercare ends, but the improvement cycle does not. The most successful SAP ESM implementations treat the system as a living platform, not a completed project.

Knowledge base maintenance

Assign ownership of the knowledge base to a named HR operations role. Schedule a monthly review of the top twenty case categories: are articles up to date? Are there new categories generating cases that need articles? A stale knowledge base is the fastest way to erode deflection rates over time.

Service catalog evolution

As you collect data on actual case volumes and categories, you will find that your Wave 1 catalog was a good starting point but not a perfect one. Plan a catalog review at Month 3 and Month 6, add L3/L4 categories where volume and routing complexity justify it, retires categories that generate no cases.

Routing refinement

Review routing accuracy monthly for the first six months. Misrouted cases are easy to spot in the data — cases that are reassigned shortly after creation are a routing signal. Use this data to tune rules progressively.

Wave 2 planning

If your go-live was a pilot (2–3 countries, as recommended), the first 90 days of live operation give you the most valuable input for Wave 2 scoping: what to replicate exactly, what to adjust, and what to add. Start Wave 2 planning conversations at Day 60, not after hypercare ends.

Closing the Series: Ten Posts, One Journey

This is the tenth and final post in "Implementing SAP ESM for HR — A Practitioner's Guide from Zero to Go-Live."

When I started this series, the goal was simple: to give customers and partners who are beginning their SAP ESM for HR journey a structured, practitioner-grounded guide that takes them from zero knowledge to a confident go-live. Not a marketing document. Not a product brochure. A real guide, written by someone who has been through these implementations and wants to share what actually matters.

Here is what we covered:

Blog

Topic

1

What SAP ESM for HR is and why it exists

2

The architecture you must understand before you configure anything

3

Designing your HR Shared Service Organisation

4

Building your HR service catalog

5

Omnichannel strategy and channel design

6

Case routing and SLA design

7

The SAP SuccessFactors integration

8

Roles, permissions, and identity

9

UAT and the go/no-go decision

10

Go-live cutover and the first 30 days

If you are implementing SAP ESM for HR and have questions that this series has not answered, post them in the SAP Community. I will do my best to respond.

Good luck with your implementation. The work is not trivial, but the outcome, an HR service operation that genuinely works for employees and HR teams alike, is worth every hour of it.

entry.title: Re: My Purchase requisition New Fiori App
entry.content:
Hi Sanan,

In your screenshot NB has no input field in the item line, so the app doesn't let you change it there. I wanted to know where that NB comes from, so I followed it in the code of the self-service purchase requisition in an S/4HANA 2023 system. NB is the last option, not the first. When a new requisition starts, the header gets its document type in this order:

  1. The default saved for the user in table USER_DEF_SETTING (field PURCHASINGDOCUMENTTYPE).
  2. The attribute BSART of the user in the organizational plan.
  3. The user's own default values (stored in ESDUS).
  4. The BAdI MMPUR_REQ_DEFAULT_DATA, which has a DOCUMENTTYPE field in CS_ITEM.
  5. Only when all of these are empty, 'NB', written directly in the code (CL_MMPUR_SSP_PR_BOPF_API).

What surprised me: the item BAdI that people usually try first, MM_PUR_S4_SSPPR_MOD_DRAFT_ITEM, lets you change 60 fields of the item, and the document type is not one of them. So I would set ZNB as a default in 1, 2 or 3 before looking for an exit.

One more check. Whatever type the header gets, the app checks authorization object M_BANF_BSA with activity 01 for it. Without it for ZNB, the message is "No Authorisation to create Purchase Requisition for Document Type ZNB" (MMPUR_REQ_COMMON 017).

I read the code, I didn't create a requisition with ZNB in the app. Your tags say Private Edition, which runs the same code line as on-premise, but your release may be different from mine. If you get a message after you change the default, could you share the exact text?

entry.title: Consuming SAP Integration Suite OData Provisioning from SAP Business Application Studio Across BTP
entry.content:
SAP OData Provisioning with BAS / SAP Fiori Tools Across BTP Subaccounts

Step 1: Configure the Backend Connection for OData Provisioning

In the SAP Integration Suite subaccount, create an HTTP destination pointing to the SAP Business Suite backend.

A simplified destination configuration is:

Name: ECC_ODP_BACKEND

Type: HTTP

ProxyType: OnPremise

Authentication: PrincipalPropagation

sap-client: 100

odc: true

Backend URL: SAP Backend Example

The important OData Provisioning property is:

odc = true

This destination provides the connection from OData Provisioning to the on-premise SAP backend.

Step 2: Register the OData Service

In SAP Integration Suite, navigate to:

Configure

→ OData Services

→ Register

Select the backend destination created in Step 1.

Then register the required OData service.

For example:

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

After registration, the service is published through OData Provisioning rather than being consumed directly from the on-premise SAP Gateway endpoint.

Step 3: Create OData Provisioning Runtime Access

For runtime access, create the appropriate OData Provisioning runtime service instance and service key.

The generated credentials conceptually contain the following information:

API URL:

ODP Runtime Host.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Client ID:

sb-dummy-client-id

Client Secret:

dummy-client-secret

Grant Type:

client_credentials

Token URL:

Authentication Host.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token

The configuration discussed here uses:

Service: xfs-runtime

Plan: odpruntime

The service-key credentials provide the information needed to authenticate against the OData Provisioning runtime.

Step 4: Test OAuth Independently from BAS

Before configuring SAP Fiori Tools, first verify the ODP runtime independently from the BAS terminal.

Obtain an OAuth access token using the Client ID and Client Secret.

Example command:

curl -s \

-X POST \

-u 'sb-dummy-client-id:dummy-client-secret' \

-H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \

-d 'grant_type=client_credentials' \

'ODP OAuth Token Endpoint'

After receiving the token, save it locally:

export TOKEN='<access-token>'

This test is useful because it validates OAuth authentication separately from the SAP Fiori Tools configuration.

Step 5: Use the Correct ODP Runtime Endpoint

This was one of the key findings during troubleshooting.

Initially, the Integration Suite application URL was tested using a URL similar to:

https://<tenant>.integrationsuite.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/xfsrt/odp/...

An unauthenticated curl request returned:

HTTP 200

However, the returned content was:

Content-Type: text/html

The response contained an interactive XSUAA login flow rather than an OData response.

Therefore, an important troubleshooting rule is:

HTTP 200 does not automatically mean that the OData request succeeded.

The correct test in this setup is against the ODP runtime host supplied by the runtime credentials.

Example:

ODP Runtime Endpoint

Step 6: Validate an Individual OData Service

The working ODP service URL follows this structure:

https://services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

To retrieve the service metadata, execute:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/xml" \

"ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV Metadata"

A successful result should return:

HTTP 200 OK

and:

Content-Type: application/xml

The metadata should begin with an XML element similar to:

<edmx:Edmx ...>

At this stage, the test independently validates:

  • BAS network connectivity: OK
  • OAuth token acquisition: OK
  • ODP runtime authentication: OK
  • Registered OData service: OK
  • OData metadata retrieval: OK

Step 7: Validate the OData Provisioning Service Catalog

Another important finding is that OData Provisioning exposes its own CATALOGSERVICE.

The catalog metadata can be tested using:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/xml" \

"https://services.odp.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/$metadata"

The catalog contains entities such as:

  • ServiceCollection
  • CatalogCollection
  • Annotations
  • Vocabularies
  • TagCollection
  • EntitySetCollection

To retrieve the registered OData services:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/json" \

'ODP Service Collection'

For a registered service such as ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV, the response contains information conceptually similar to:

Description: Project Request

Title: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

TechnicalServiceName: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

TechnicalServiceVersion: 1

Service URL: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

Metadata URL: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV Metadata

This proves independently that the ODP catalog itself is working correctly.

Step 8: Configure the BAS / Build Code Subaccount Destination

In the BAS / Build Code subaccount, create the following destination.

Name: SAP_Gateway

Type: HTTP

URL: ODP Runtime Host

ProxyType: Internet

Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials

Client ID: sb-dummy-client-id

Client Secret: dummy-client-secret

Token Service URL: ODP OAuth Token Endpoint

Add the following additional properties:

WebIDEEnabled: true

WebIDEUsage: odata_gen

HTML5.DynamicDestination: true

HTML5.Timeout: 60000

Important

Do not add $metadata to the destination URL.

The destination should point to the ODP runtime host.

Understanding WebIDEUsage

Understanding WebIDEUsage became one of the most important parts of the troubleshooting.

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

With:

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

SAP Fiori Tools treats the destination as a generic/partial OData destination in the tested setup.

In the Fiori Application Generator, select:

Connect to a System

→ SAP_Gateway

BAS then presents a Service Path field.

Enter the required ODP service path.

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

This works in the tested environment.

The configuration is therefore effectively:

ODP Runtime Host

  •  

OData Service Path

=

Complete OData Service URL

For example:

ODP Runtime Host:

services.odp.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com

Service Path:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

Why odata_abap Fails with OData Provisioning

Initially, the expectation was that:

WebIDEUsage = odata_abap

would allow BAS / SAP Fiori Tools to display and browse the ODP catalog automatically.

Instead, BAS returned:

Internal server error

Request failed with status code 500

Running:

Fiori: Open Environment Check

revealed the actual problem.

For OData V2 catalog discovery, Fiori Tools constructed:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

For OData V4, it attempted:

/sap/opu/odata4/iwfnd/config/default/iwfnd/catalog/0002

These are ABAP Gateway catalog routes.

However, the working OData Provisioning catalog in this environment is:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Therefore, there is a catalog-path mismatch.

OData Provisioning

Catalog Path:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Result: OK

BAS with odata_abap

Catalog Path attempted by Fiori Tools:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Result: FAIL

This means the observed issue was not caused by OAuth authentication.

It was not caused by Cloud Connector connectivity.

It was not caused by ODP service registration.

It was not caused by the ODP runtime itself.

The problem was the difference between the catalog URL exposed by OData Provisioning and the standard ABAP Gateway catalog URL expected by the odata_abap discovery flow.

What About odata_hcp_odp?

Older SAP Web IDE documentation contains another WebIDEUsage value:

WebIDEUsage = odata_hcp_odp

Historically, the distinction was:

odata_abap

for OData services hosted on SAP Gateway systems.

Whereas:

odata_hcp_odp

was associated with OData Provisioning systems on SAP Cloud Platform.

This initially appeared to match the required architecture.

However, in the tested current BAS/Fiori Tools environment, after configuring:

WebIDEUsage = odata_hcp_odp

the destination was not displayed in the Fiori Application Generator.

The observed behavior was therefore:

odata_gen

Destination visible

→ Service Path field available

→ ODP service path can be entered

→ Works

odata_abap

Destination visible

→ Standard ABAP catalog attempted

→ Catalog discovery fails

odata_hcp_odp

Destination not displayed in the tested Fiori Application Generator

Current Working Approach

For the tested BAS/Fiori Tools environment, the reliable configuration was:

URL: services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials

WebIDEUsage: odata_gen

WebIDEEnabled: true

HTML5.DynamicDestination: true

HTML5.Timeout: 60000

Developers then select:

Connect to a System

↓

SAP_Gateway

↓

Service Path

and enter:

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

Catalog Browsing Limitation

The ODP catalog itself is operational.

The registered services can be retrieved from:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/ServiceCollection

However, in the tested BAS/Fiori Tools environment, the native Connect to a System → catalog selection flow could not consume the ODP catalog in the same way.

The important distinction is:

OData Provisioning Flow

ODP

↓

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

↓

Direct OAuth request works

↓

ServiceCollection

↓

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

BAS odata_abap Flow

BAS / Fiori Tools

↓

WebIDEUsage = odata_abap

↓

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

↓

Fails because a different catalog path is being requested

If the catalog-selection UX is mandatory, support for an ODP-specific discovery mechanism should be validated for the target SAP Fiori Tools environment.

Principal Propagation and End-User Identity

There is another important distinction between design-time authentication and runtime end-user identity propagation.

OAuth2ClientCredentials is useful in this scenario for:

  • Design-time connectivity
  • Verifying the ODP runtime
  • Retrieving the ODP catalog
  • Retrieving OData metadata
  • Testing the OData service from BAS

However, Client Credentials represents the OAuth client, not the interactive Fiori end user.

If the runtime requirement is:

User A logs into Fiori

↓

Request reaches ABAP

↓

sy-uname = USER_A

and:

User B logs into Fiori

↓

Request reaches ABAP

↓

sy-uname = USER_B

then the runtime architecture must preserve the user context rather than relying solely on the Client Credentials token.

In the described landscape, the downstream configuration was:

OData Provisioning

↓

Principal Propagation Destination

↓

SAP Cloud Connector

↓

ABAP Backend

When accessed using the required interactive user context, the mapped SAP user was received in the ABAP backend through:

sy-uname

Therefore, BAS design-time authentication and runtime end-user principal propagation should be treated as separate concerns.

Troubleshooting Checklist

1. Check Network Connectivity

Verify that BAS can reach the ODP runtime host:

services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

If this fails, troubleshoot network connectivity before investigating the Fiori Tools configuration.

2. Check OAuth Authentication

Verify that the ODP runtime service credentials can generate an OAuth access token.

Confirm that the following are correct:

  • Client ID
  • Client Secret
  • Grant Type
  • Token Service URL

The expected grant type in this setup is:

client_credentials

3. Check the Individual ODP Service

Using the OAuth token, retrieve:

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/$metadata

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/$metadata

A successful response should return:

HTTP 200 OK

and XML metadata.

4. Check the ODP Catalog

Using the same OAuth token, verify:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/$metadata

Then verify:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/ServiceCollection?$format=json

If both requests succeed, the ODP catalog itself is operational.

5. Run BAS Environment Check

In BAS, run:

Fiori: Open Environment Check

This was particularly useful because it exposed the catalog URL that Fiori Tools was actually requesting.

In this case, it showed:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

rather than the working ODP catalog path:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

6. Always Inspect the Response Content Type

A common troubleshooting mistake is assuming:

HTTP 200 = OData request succeeded

That is not necessarily true.

For $metadata, expect an XML response such as:

Content-Type: application/xml

The response should contain metadata beginning with something similar to:

<edmx:Edmx>

If the response instead contains:

Content-Type: text/html

the request may have returned an authentication or login page rather than OData metadata.

Final Validation Result

The tested setup produced the following results:

✅ BAS → ODP network connectivity: WORKING

✅ ODP OAuth runtime access: WORKING

✅ ODP service metadata: WORKING

✅ ODP CATALOGSERVICE: WORKING

✅ ODP ServiceCollection: WORKING

✅ ODP → ABAP Principal Propagation: WORKING

✅ odata_gen + Service Path: WORKING

❌ odata_abap automatic catalog browsing: NOT WORKING

⚠️ Historical odata_hcp_odp: Destination not displayed in the tested current Fiori Application Generator

Conclusion

The most important lesson from this troubleshooting exercise is to separate four different layers:

1. BAS → ODP Network Connectivity

2. BAS → ODP Authentication

3. Fiori Tools Design-Time Service Discovery

4. ODP → SAP Backend Principal Propagation

In this case, network connectivity worked.

OAuth runtime authentication worked.

Individual OData service metadata worked.

The ODP CATALOGSERVICE worked.

The ODP ServiceCollection worked.

Principal Propagation from ODP to the ABAP backend worked.

The remaining problem was specifically the design-time catalog-discovery mechanism used by Fiori Tools with odata_abap.

The working development approach in the tested environment was therefore:

SAP Integration Suite

↓

OData Provisioning

↓

xfs-runtime OAuth Credentials

↓

BAS Destination

↓

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

↓

Connect to a System

↓

SAP_Gateway

↓

Service Path

↓

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

This approach keeps the SAP Integration Suite OData Provisioning runtime separate from the underlying SAP Gateway implementation and provides the working path used in this cross-subaccount setup.

entry.title: Your activation checklist for SAP Ariba Sourcing - Five steps to get started this month
entry.content:
Welcome back to this three-part blog series on accelerating your sourcing processes. The first two blogs discussed why procurement practitioners should care about slow sourcing and how activating key capabilities in your SAP Ariba Sourcing solution can help reduce sourcing cycle time.

With this background, you should be ready to get started. This blog offers a sourcing activation checklist that highlights the five most impactful things you can do this month to decrease your sourcing cycle time.

Eliminating the expertise barrier

Many procurement professionals doubt their ability to increase procurement efficiency. They believe such an effort requires deep platform expertise or a large commitment from IT to execute a lengthy improvement project.

If you share these concerns, please know that you needn’t worry. There are simple steps you can take to reduce your sourcing cycle time, quickly and with less effort than you expect. By following the sourcing activation checklist outlined in the next five sections, you can make meaningful progress toward your goal of reducing sourcing delays.

Each of the following steps describes a self-contained action that you can execute, along with SAP resources that can help you get started. By taking one meaningful, limited-scope step this month, you can make significant progress—even without a detailed project plan. Where is the best place to begin?

 

Step 1: Understand sourcing performance

One logical place to start is to compare your average sourcing cycle time with a benchmark. SAP offers a benchmarking program you can use to assess your performance objectively. This program helps you analyze transaction data from SAP Ariba solutions and user-submitted survey data. To learn how to assess performance, read more about the benchmarking program from SAP.

Step 2: Determine which features are being used

Now that you better understand sourcing performance, check which solution capabilities have been deployed by your team. One key feature that can help is the guided sourcing capability for SAP Ariba Sourcing, which offers a streamlined, intuitive way for practitioners to create and manage sourcing projects and events. If your team has already created guided sourcing templates, you can start using them to streamline sourcing. Learn more about using the guided sourcing capability here.

Step 3: Standardize one type of sourcing event

After checking for guided sourcing templates, consider the event types your team uses for sourcing, such as RFIs, RFPs, and auctions. Choose one of these event types and use the guided sourcing capability to standardize it across your sourcing process. By standardizing one event type each month, you can quickly improve user speed and efficiency. This guided sourcing playbook can help you discover how to standardize sourcing event types. Use this guide to learn how to create project templates.

Step 4: Reduce setup time by using a template

Another way of standardizing procurement processes is by using templates. However, it’s not necessary to create a new template for each project. SAP Ariba Sourcing offers a sourcing library that contains templates and content from previous projects. To save time and effort, you can reuse these templates or copy existing content in a new template. Discover how you can use the sourcing library to reuse templates. Watch this demo to learn how to use the sourcing library to improve content creation.

Step 5: Share what you’ve learned

Activating valuable capabilities in your SAP Ariba Sourcing solution can help your procurement team work faster and more efficiently. Why not improve your outcomes by sharing this knowledge with your colleagues and managers? By forwarding this checklist to those who manage your company’s sourcing operations, you can begin aligning on next-best steps and work together to reduce sourcing cycle time.

Ready to go deeper?

To go beyond these five steps, check out this course on reducing sourcing cycle time. To access the course materials, you’ll need to log in with your S-user number or SAP Universal ID.

Further reading:

  • What is procurement?
  • What is spend management?
  • How can SAP Ariba Sourcing support spend management?
  • What is SAP Ariba Sourcing Suite? (Now called SAP Ariba Strategic Sourcing Suite)

entry.title: Your three-phase road map to faster sourcing - Go from manual work-arounds to measurable outcomes
entry.content:
Now that we’ve reviewed the causes and costs of slow sourcing (see the first blog in this series), you’re ready to take action. But what’s the best way to speed up your sourcing cycle without launching a new technical implementation?

The good news is that you can make this shift using your existing SAP Ariba Sourcing solution. What’s more, this isn’t a long-term technical project. Most procurement practitioners who adopt this process begin to see real benefits within the month.

Read on to learn the three steps you can take to shrink your procurement sourcing cycle. By following this road map, you can reduce setup time, create a structured sourcing approach, and deliver new business value.

A misconception about slow sourcing cycles

Many people assume that the best way to decrease procurement lead time is simply to work harder, looking for ways to trim time from each process or step. The truth is a little more complex.

Many companies adopt procurement workarounds that rely on email, spreadsheets, and copy-and-paste RFP text because they feel more familiar to users than learning a new solution. Yet the manual data intake, sequential approvals, and ad hoc supplier identification processes needed to support these workarounds create friction. This leads to bottlenecks in your sourcing value flow and delays at every stage of the sourcing process.

Instead of trimming sourcing processes, look for opportunities to remove the friction. The following sections offer guidance that can help you get started.

Phase 1: Where is your time leaking?

To fix the problem, you need to clearly understand where friction slows your processes. There are a couple of key steps you can take to pinpoint where tasks create bottlenecks.

Take time to assess the full sourcing journey and map your sourcing cycle from end to end. Don’t skip anything. Consider each part of the procurement process, from demand capture to contract creation.

You can assess areas such as sourcing flows, intake, creation, approvals, awards, and contracts. Evaluate each process to determine which tasks slow procurement, introduce complexity, or create opportunities for errors.

Keep in mind that common sourcing activities such as manual data intake, sequential approvals, and ad hoc supplier identification processes all create delays. Other common obstacles that can slow your sourcing cycle include:

  • Manual processes that introduce errors and inhibit progress.
  • Inefficient communication that causes delays, slowing decision-making.
  • Multiple approvals required from different company departments, elongating the procurement cycle.

If you need additional help visualizing friction sources, you may want to use tools such as the SAP Signavio Process Intelligence solution, which is integrated with SAP Ariba Sourcing. This solution can help you understand where bottlenecks occur and how hidden resistance complicates sourcing. It answers questions such as:

  • Where are approvals piling up?
  • Which categories have the longest turnaround?
  • Are templates being reused or rebuilt for each procurement process?

Phase 2: Which solution capabilities reduce sourcing delays?

Once you’ve identified the sources of friction in your sourcing processes, the next step is to determine how to use existing tools to address these issues and generate real value. Many sourcing practitioners are surprised to find that they already have the tools they need to accelerate sourcing cycles. But often those tools need to be activated, aligned, and embedded in your company’s daily process execution.

To begin activating your available sourcing capabilities, think about how you can use the high-impact, low-friction levers already available in your SAP Ariba Sourcing solution. These capabilities can help you address each friction point directly.

Guided sourcing

SAP Ariba Sourcing offers a guided sourcing capability that helps practitioners create and manage sourcing processes and RFx events from a single page. The capability’s interface structures demand capture and event creation, using templates that encode best practices. By removing the need for administrator-level setup for every event, the guided sourcing interface makes it easier for nonexpert users to get started.

The interface also offers autonomous procurement features that automate RFx event creation. Category management capabilities support comprehensive category planning, execution, and reporting. You can also use multi-round bidding to streamline long lists of suppliers to a best and final offer. This toolkit helps you adopt the guided sourcing capability based on your organizational role.

Benefit: Enables twice as many sourcing events per practitioner, with 30% to 40% faster cycle times

Sourcing libraries

Another way to streamline procurement and reduce friction is by using the sourcing library in SAP Ariba Sourcing. This library stores content, which you can use to create new procurement events and templates.

Users can reuse content from the library, copying it into negotiation documents. They also can explore the library to locate desired documents for each spend category. By reusing content and templates from the sourcing library, casual users benefit from the governance and structure created by power users, without needing to understand how to create that value themselves.

Benefit: Reduces template setup time by up to 70%

Project template guides

To create a procurement project, you need to use a template that defines your standard business processes. But administrators who want to create a project template don’t need to start from scratch.

SAP Ariba Sourcing offers project template guides that help administrators define project templates quickly and with minimal effort—reducing sourcing cycle time.

Benefit: Up to 9.4% annual sourcing savings as a percentage of addressable spend (Source: SAP Ariba, Procurement Benchmark Survey Insights, May 2024)

Guided sourcing e-learning

To support further adoption of these capabilities, the Creating Sourcing Events within SAP Ariba Guided Sourcing course explains how sourcing events are created and managed within guided sourcing. It covers the use of templates, guided workflows, and sourcing event types such as RFIs, RFPs, and auctions. The course can help sourcing practitioners understand how standardized processes and reusable content can reduce manual effort, improve consistency, and support shorter sourcing cycle times.

Benefit: 40% reduction in sourcing cycle time thanks to expedited price negotiations (Source: SAP internal benchmarking)

Phase 3: What’s the best way to measure your progress?

The old saying “what’s measured gets managed” also applies to accelerating your procurement cycle. You can use advanced SAP Ariba Sourcing capabilities to measure your progress and quantify improvements so you can further optimize your team’s performance.

The solution offers robust features that help you make your enhanced procurement speed more visible to procurement practitioners, administrators, and management. For example, you can use SAP Ariba Sourcing to generate monthly or quarterly KPI reviews that highlight procurement process improvements such as:

  • Sourcing cycle time
  • The percentage of procurement events awarded
  • The number of sourcing events created per project owner

Using these KPIs, you can gain insights into sourcing performance, supplier engagement, and cycle times.

SAP Ariba Sourcing also offers process optimization features that help you identify bottlenecks, pinpoint approval delays, and spotlight opportunities to reduce processing time. By helping you effectively measure and optimize sourcing processes, the tools offer insight that helps reduce delays, enhance supplier collaboration, improve cost management, and increase supply chain efficiency.

Start this month, not next quarter

As this three-step road map shows, accelerating your sourcing processes isn’t a massive, time-consuming project. You don’t need a large-scale rollout, deep product expertise, or IT involvement to reduce your procurement cycle time.

You can follow these steps on your own, starting this week and using capabilities that already exist in your SAP Ariba Sourcing solution. Best of all, you can begin to see results—not in years, but in the next month or less.

Discover what’s next by reading the third blog in this series, “Your activation checklist for SAP Ariba Sourcing: Five steps to get started this month.”

Learn how to use SAP Ariba Sourcing to create safe, efficient, and cost-effective sourcing events.

Further reading:

  • What is strategic sourcing?
  • How to source successfully across borders

entry.title: [SPORTS] SAP Learning Curriculum for Sports and Entertainment Industry
entry.content:
SAP Learning Curriculum for Sports and Entertainment

The Sports and Entertainment industry combines the challenge of achieving sporting success with the need to engage audiences, manage increasingly complex operations, and create sustainable business value.

SAP solutions for sports teams, leagues, federations, and venues support areas such as sports management, performance analysis, fan engagement, ticket sales, and operational efficiency. This learning curriculum provides a structured starting point for developing relevant industry, SAP Sports One, and SAP Analytics Cloud knowledge.

You can also explore the complete offering on the SAP Learning page for Sports and Entertainment.

Sports and Entertainment Learning Curriculum

Industry Foundation

ISE010 – Introducing the Sports & Entertainment Industry

A foundational introduction to the Sports and Entertainment industry, its terminology, business processes, differentiators, challenges, value chain, and SAP solution landscape.

SAP Sports One

ICS101 – Exploring SAP Sports One - Training Management

A comprehensive introduction to Training Management with SAP Sports One, covering the training management process throughout a season, planning, documentation, target setting, and analysis.

ICS120 – Exploring SAP Sports One – Team Management and Administration

An introduction to team operations and administration with SAP Sports One, including system administration, user management, season preparation, calendars, media, person management, and season change.

ICS130 – Exploring SAP Sports One - Medical & Return to Play

An introduction to athlete health management, medical incidents, physical well-being, and the Return-to-Play process in SAP Sports One.

Sports Analytics

ICS150 – Exploring SAP Analytics Cloud for Sport Industry

An introduction to using SAP Analytics Cloud in a sports-industry context, including system setup, basic stories, and SAP Sports One reference content.

ICS151 – Answering Frequently Asked Questions for SAP Analytics Cloud for the Sports Industry

A focused follow-up course covering selected SAP Analytics Cloud functionality at beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels.

Detailed Course Descriptions

ISE010 – Introducing the Sports & Entertainment Industry

Foundation course for understanding the Sports and Entertainment industry and SAP’s role within it.

Access ISE010 on SAP Learning

The course establishes a common understanding of the Sports and Entertainment industry before learners move into solution-specific topics.

After completing the course, learners should be able to:

  • Understand industry-specific business processes, differentiators, and challenges
  • Use terminology specific to the Sports and Entertainment industry
  • Articulate the end-to-end SAP solution story for the industry 

Course structure

The course contains two units:

  1. Getting to Know the Sports and Entertainment Industry
  2. Explaining the Key Capabilities of SAP Solutions and SAP Business AI for Sports and Entertainment Across its Value Chain

Designed for

The course is relevant to:

  • Architects
  • Business users
  • Consultants
  • Customer engagement roles
  • Presales professionals
  • Sales professionals

Recommended position in the curriculum

Start your Sports and Entertainment learning journey with ISE010.

The course provides the industry knowledge and terminology needed before progressing into SAP Sports One and SAP Analytics Cloud.

Level: Beginner
Duration: 3 hr 10 min
Units: 2
Prerequisites: None
Achievement: Leads to Achievement

ICS101 – Exploring SAP Sports One - Training Management

Comprehensive introduction to Training Management with SAP Sports One.

Access ICS101 on SAP Learning

Sports organizations rely on effective training processes to plan activities, document progress, evaluate results, and work toward sporting objectives.

This course explains the overall vision for Training Management and illustrates how key training management processes can be performed with SAP Sports One.

Learning objectives

The course helps learners:

  • Illustrate the overarching vision for Training Management
  • Explain the Training Management process during a season
  • Describe Training Management processes in SAP Sports One
  • Integrate Training Management best practices
  • Perform analyses for Training Management

Course structure

The course covers:

  1. Introducing the overarching vision for Training Management
  2. Considering the basics of Training Management
  3. Agreeing on targets at the start of a season
  4. Macro planning
  5. Micro planning
  6. Documenting training in SAP Sports One
  7. Validating targets at the end of a season

Designed for

The course is relevant to:

  • SAP Sports One consultants
  • Business users
  • Data analysts
  • Architects

Recommended position in the curriculum

Take ICS101 after completing ISE010. It is the first solution-focused course in the recommended curriculum and provides the broadest SAP Sports One learning experience in this sequence.

Level: Beginner
Duration: 8 hr 3 min
Units: 7
Achievement: Leads to Achievement

ICS120 – Exploring SAP Sports One – Team Management and Administration

Introduction to team operations, system administration, and season management with SAP Sports One.

Access ICS120 on SAP Learning

This course builds on the initial SAP Sports One foundation by focusing on Team Management and Administration.

After completing the course, learners should be able to handle system and user administration and manage team operations in SAP Sports One, including season change and communication.

Course structure

The course covers:

  1. Introducing the overarching vision for Team Management
  2. Handling system administration and data security
  3. Managing SAP Sports One users and user onboarding and offboarding
  4. Preparing a season
  5. Managing calendars in SAP Sports One
  6. Working with the SAP Sports One Media Library
  7. Managing persons in SAP Sports One
  8. Planning a season change

Designed for

The course is relevant to:

  • Architects
  • Business users
  • Consultants 

Recommended position in the curriculum

Continue with ICS120 after completing the Training Management course. This expands your SAP Sports One knowledge from training processes into team operations and administration.

Level: Beginner
Duration: 3 hr 10 min
Units: 8
Prerequisites: None
Achievement: Leads to Achievement 

ICS130 – Exploring SAP Sports One - Medical & Return to Play

Introduction to athlete health management and Return-to-Play processes with SAP Sports One.

Access ICS130 on SAP Learning

Effective health management is essential for athletes and sports organizations. This course demonstrates how SAP Sports One can be used to document medical incidents, manage the Return-to-Play process, and track athletes’ medical status. 

Learning objectives

The course helps learners:

  • Understand the importance of effective health management
  • Capture medical incidents and relevant information in SAP Sports One

entry.title: CDS View Performance Best Practice – UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN
entry.content:
UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN -  CDS (SQL) performance anti-pattern

This blog post focuses on the CDS view performance anti-pattern called "UNION in LEFT OUTER JOIN" and it's part of the CDS View Performance Best Practices series. You can find an introduction to CDS View performance recommendations, aspects you need to consider in terms of performance, and a list of all available CDS anti-patterns in the following blog post: 
CDS View Performance Best Practices 

 

Why this pattern deserves attention

A UNION in the right-hand input of a LEFT OUTER JOIN is logically valid. The risk is performance: on large data volumes and complex data models, both UNION branches may be processed before a selective filter from the left side of the join can reduce them. In simple and highly selective cases, the optimizer may apply semi-join reduction. In more complex plans, that optimization is not guaranteed because plan selection is cost based.

 

The business example

A retail company tracks customer orders for multiple sales regions. Each order is fulfilled through one of two independent delivery systems: a central warehouse or a regional warehouse. Fulfillment is exclusive in this model: an order is only assigned to one delivery system. Some orders are still open and therefore have no delivery record. The data below is intentionally minimal so that result of every row can be easily followed through each query variant by hand.

Data model

The following three tables are created and populated by the complete runnable SQL at the end of this post. All rows are shown so every query result can be verified by hand.

Table: ORDERS

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

ORD100

ORD200

ORD500

 ORD400 is still open and has no delivery in either system and therefore is not part of the following tables.

Table: CENTRAL_DELIVERIES

ORDER_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD100

2026-09-10

ORD300

2026-09-15

ORD900

2026-08-20

 ORD900 is an older, delivered order that is not part of the current ORDERS selection.

Table: REGIONAL_DELIVERIES

ORDER_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD200

ORD500

ORD950
