 ORD950 is another older, delivered order that is not part of the current ORDERS selection.

 

The original, correct query

The query goal is to list every order together with its delivery date from Region 2 (region_id = 2), regardless of which delivery system handled it. Open orders must still appear with a NULL delivery date — the LEFT OUTER JOIN is the mechanism that guarantees this.

with deliveries as (
    select order_id, delivery_date
      from central_deliveries
    union all
    select order_id, delivery_date
      from regional_deliveries
)
select o.order_id,
       o.region_id,
       d.delivery_date
  from orders o
  left outer join deliveries d
    on o.order_id = d.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2;

Please note that the query uses a common table expression (CTE). The with_clause creates a temporary result set based on its subquery. The native SQL approach uses the WITH clause for simplicity, avoiding multiple view definitions and lengthy code snippets while showing the essence of the anti-pattern in a single executable statement.

Technically, this has the same effect as when a CDS view uses an association (technically a LEFT OUTER JOIN) to another CDS view that contains a UNION.

 The main query selects from the table ORDERS and uses the temporary view (CTE) DELIVERIES in a LEFT OUTER JOIN. The CTE  DELIVERIES contains a UNION ALL of the two delivery tables CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES.

Correct and expected result of the query:

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD300

2

2026-09-15

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD500

2

2026-09-18

 

Let’s look at the execution plan for the query.

The plan places the UNION ALL below the LEFT OUTER JOIN, this means the UNION ALL is executed before the LEFT OUTER JOIN. The filtered ORDERS table is the left input, while CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES are combined as the right input.

The UNION ALL combines the rows from both delivery tables so that an order can match a delivery stored in either table. The LEFT OUTER JOIN then keeps every selected Region 2 order, including ORD400, for which neither table contains a delivery record.

The plan does not show the selected order IDs being used to reduce the scans of CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Rows that cannot match a selected order are therefore processed.

Can the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN be pushed into the individual UNION ALL branches to reduce the data earlier?

 

The tempting but incorrect rewrite

At first glance, it may seem attractive to push the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN into each UNION ALL branch:

with deliveries_wrong_opt as (
    select o.order_id, o.region_id,
           cd.delivery_date
      from orders o
      left outer join central_deliveries cd
        on o.order_id = cd.order_id
     where o.region_id = 2
    union all
    select o.order_id, o.region_id,
           rd.delivery_date
      from orders o
      left outer join regional_deliveries rd
        on o.order_id = rd.order_id
     where o.region_id = 2
)
select * from deliveries_wrong_opt;

Why it fails: Each LEFT OUTER JOIN independently preserves every selected order. ORD300 has a matching row in CENTRAL_DELIVERIES, but not in REGIONAL_DELIVERIES therefore the regional branch produces a NULL-extended row for it. ORD500 has the symmetric problem. ORD400 has no match in either delivery table, so both branches produce a NULL-extended row for it.

The UNION ALL then combines the independently produced branch results. Consequently, the rewritten query returns six rows instead of the expected three. The additional rows are not caused by UNION ALL itself; they arise because each LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched orders independently.

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD300

2

2026-09-15

ORD300

2

NULL

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD500

2

NULL

ORD500

2

2026-09-18

The execution plan shows both the performance appeal and the structural problem of this rewrite:

The UNION ALL is now above two separate LEFT OUTER JOIN operators. Each branch reads the filtered Region 2 rows from ORDERS and joins them independently with one delivery table: the first branch with CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and the second with REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Because only the selected orders participate in each join, fewer rows may be passed from the join branches into the UNION ALL.

The earlier reduction therefore looks attractive from a performance perspective, but it changes the result. Because both joins are LEFT OUTER JOINs, each branch preserves all three Region 2 orders before the branch results are combined. A match in one branch does not prevent the other branch from producing a NULL-extended row for the same order. For this data set, the UNION ALL consequently receives three rows from each branch and returns the six rows shown above.

If the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches, can the delivery tables still be reduced earlier without changing the result?

 

A semantics-preserving manual reduction

The LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot safely be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches. Therefore, we describe an approach where the selected order IDs can be used to reduce each delivery table before the tables are combined.

The query first creates selected_order_keys, containing the order IDs for Region 2. Each delivery table is then joined with these IDs, so only deliveries for the selected orders enter the UNION ALL. The LEFT OUTER JOIN remains in the main query and therefore still returns open orders, such as ORD400, exactly once.

with selected_order_keys as (
    select distinct order_id
      from orders
     where region_id = 2
),
reduced_deliveries as (
    select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
      from central_deliveries d
      inner join selected_order_keys k
        on k.order_id = d.order_id
    union all
    select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
      from regional_deliveries d
      inner join selected_order_keys k
        on k.order_id = d.order_id
)
select o.order_id,
       o.region_id,
       d.delivery_date
  from orders o
  left outer join reduced_deliveries d
    on d.order_id = o.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2;

The DISTINCT ensures that each order ID occurs only once in selected_order_keys. Otherwise, duplicate IDs could multiply matching rows in the delivery tables.

This query produces the correct and expected result:

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD300

2

2026-09-15

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD500

2

2026-09-18

The result remains the same as for the original query, but unrelated delivery rows are removed before the UNION ALL. The execution plan below shows how SAP HANA implements this reduction.

The filtered Region 2 order IDs are produced once by the DISTINCT operator and reused as a shared subplan. Each delivery table is then reduced through a HASH JOIN (SEMI): only delivery rows whose ORDER_ID occurs in selected_order_keys are passed to the UNION ALL. The resulting delivery rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER).

The semi-joins reduce the delivery branches without producing NULL-extended order rows. Preserving unmatched orders remains the responsibility of the single LEFT OUTER JOIN above the UNION ALL. The plan therefore combines early reduction with the same result semantics as the original query.

The manual rewrite makes the reduction explicit by deriving the relevant order IDs and using them to restrict both delivery branches.

But is this manual rewrite always necessary, or can SAP HANA derive the same semi-join reduction automatically?

 

How SAP HANA can apply semi-join reduction automatically

The fact that the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down does not automatically imply poor performance. SAP HANA can introduce semi-join reduction as an optimizer transformation without changing the SQL statement. Whether it does so is cost based and depends on estimated cardinalities, internal cost evaluation rules, selectivity, table sizes, statistics, and the complexity of the execution plan resulting from the surrounding data model.

In the small teaching example used so far, the delivery tables contain only a few rows. Reducing them first offers little or no cost advantage, so SAP HANA may reasonably retain the original plan.

With larger data volumes, reducing rows before the UNION ALL can provide enough benefit for the optimizer to choose semi-join reduction automatically. The following example demonstrates this with large SAP tables.

Example with large SAP tables

Table

Description

Approximate number of rows

TADIR

Directory of ABAP Repository objects. It provides the object type, object name, and package assignment.

7 million

DD03L

Contains field information for ABAP Dictionary tables and structures.

15 million

DD03ND

Contains field information for structured Dictionary objects, including objects related to CDS data definitions.

2.5 million

Purpose of the query

The query selects the names and types of table definitions (TABL) and CDS data definitions (DDLS) assigned to package FINS_CODING_BLOCK in TADIR. It combines field information from DD03L and DD03ND with UNION ALL and left-joins the result to the selected repository objects.

The LEFT OUTER JOIN ensures that repository objects without matching field information are still returned. Objects with multiple fields produce one result row per field.

with fields as (
    select d.tabname as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03l d

    union all

    select d.strucobjn as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03nd d
)
select t.object,
       t.obj_name,
       f.fieldname
  from tadir t
  left outer join fields f
    on f.objectname = t.obj_name
 where t.devclass = 'FINS_CODING_BLOCK'
   and t.object in ('TABL', 'DDLS');

Execution with automatic semi-join reduction

For runtime measurements we will use Plan Visualizer (PlanViz) instead of the explain plan. If we create the execution plan for the query using PlanViz we can find the following time measurements on the Overview tab in the execution summary section:

Execution Time (Elapsed): 4.524 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 3.771 ms

The Plan Graph view of the PlanViz looks like this:

The filtered TADIR input is evaluated once and reused as a shared subplan. The filter returns 48 rows, compared with an estimate (by the optimizer) of 12 rows (number in parentheses). The operator times shown in this Plan Graph are CPU times, not elapsed times.

SAP HANA uses this selective result to apply a TABLE SCAN SEMI JOIN to both branches below the UNION ALL. The semi-join on DD03L passes 222 rows to the UNION ALL, while the semi-join on DD03ND passes 196 rows. Only rows with an object name that occurs in the filtered TADIR result are passed to the UNION ALL.

The UNION ALL combines the two branch results into 418 rows. These rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER), while the filtered TADIR result remains the left-hand input. The outer join therefore continues to preserve selected repository objects without matching field information.

The plan demonstrates automatic semi-join reduction: SAP HANA uses the selective left-side input to reduce both large field tables before their rows are combined, without moving the LEFT OUTER JOIN into the UNION ALL branches. The measured CPU time for this run is approximately 3.8 ms.

The plan shows that SAP HANA reduces both field tables before the UNION ALL. But how much work does this transformation avoid? To make the difference visible, we can execute the same statement once more with semi-join reduction disabled and compare the two PlanViz results.

Execution with automatic semi-join reduction disabled

To isolate the effect of semi-join reduction, the same statement was executed again with the hint NO_HEX_TABLE_SCAN_SEMI_JOIN that prevents the table-scan semi-join reduction in the individual UNION ALL branches. The hint is used only for demonstration; disabling the optimization is not recommended.

with fields as (
    select d.tabname as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03l d

    union all

    select d.strucobjn as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03nd d
)
select t.object,
       t.obj_name,
       f.fieldname
  from tadir t
  left outer join fields f
    on f.objectname = t.obj_name
 where t.devclass = 'FINS_CODING_BLOCK'
   and t.object in ('TABL', 'DDLS') 
WITH HINT( NO_HEX_TABLE_SCAN_SEMI_JOIN );

The following time measurements are from the overview in the execution summary:

Execution Time (Elapsed): 472.078 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 7,291.854 ms

Compared to the previous optimized execution we can see significantly higher times.


Execution Time (Elapsed): 4.524 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 3.771 ms

The Plan Graph view looks like this:

With branch-level semi-join reduction disabled, the filtered TADIR input is still evaluated once and reused as a shared subplan. The filter returns 48 rows.

The main difference is visible below the UNION ALL. Semi-join reduction has not disappeared completely, but it now occurs above the UNION ALL. Consequently, both large field tables are scanned and combined before the result is reduced to the selected object names. The DD03L scan returns 15,747,433 rows, while the DD03ND scan returns 2,495,229 rows.

These large branch results enter the UNION ALL before a HASH JOIN (SEMI) reduces the combined field data to the object names from the filtered TADIR input. The semi-join eventually reduces the data to 418 rows, but the reduction happens only after rows from both large tables have already been read and combined.

The resulting 418 rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER). As in the optimized plan, the filtered TADIR result remains the left-hand input, so repository objects without matching field information are still preserved. The final result therefore remains unchanged. The measured CPU time for this run is approximately 7.3 s.

Comparison of the two executions

Measurement

Semi-join reduction enabled

Branch-level reduction disabled

Rows from DD03L entering UNION ALL

222

15,747,433

Rows from DD03ND entering UNION ALL

196

2,495,229

Total rows entering UNION ALL

418

18,242,662

Final result rows

418

Approximate elapsed time

4.5 ms

Approximate CPU time

Both executions return the same 418 rows, but the optimized plan reduces each field table before the UNION ALL. This avoids passing more than 18 million rows through the union and reduces CPU time from approximately 7.3 seconds to 3.8 milliseconds. But what can a developer do if SAP HANA does not apply semi-join reduction and the UNION branches become a performance bottleneck?

 

When semi-join reduction is not applied

Semi-join reduction is a cost-based optimizer decision. It may not be selected when the left-side filter is insufficiently selective, cardinality estimates are inaccurate, or join columns contain casts or calculations. The structure of the data model also matters: additional joins, aggregations, calculated fields, and nested (reusable) views can increase the complexity of the resulting execution plan and make the relationship between the selective input and the UNION branches harder for the optimizer to identify.

This is one reason why controlling CDS model complexity is important. For broader guidance, see CDS View Performance Best Practices.

Use PlanViz with representative data volumes to check where rows are reduced, how many rows enter the UNION ALL, and whether estimated row counts differ significantly from the actual values.

What can a developer do?

  • If the branches use the same source rows at the same granularity and differ only in calculated values, consider replacing the union with a single source and CASE expressions. Verify that this preserves row multiplicity and NULL handling (see anti-pattern NOT NULL preserving LEFT OUTER JOIN).
  • Consider separate, more focused views when a broadly reusable union model prevents early filtering.
  • For expensive and stable combinations, consider whether a persisted or precomputed result is appropriate.
  • Verify every redesign with PlanViz and realistic production-scale data.

The objective is not to force a particular execution plan, but to shape the data model so that SAP HANA can reduce large data sets as early as possible.

 

Conclusion

A UNION ALL on the right side of a LEFT OUTER JOIN is logically valid, but it can become expensive when large union branches are processed before the selective left-side input reduces them. Simply moving the LEFT OUTER JOIN into the individual branches is not a safe optimization and leads to a semantically different result, because each branch would preserve unmatched rows.

SAP HANA can avoid this work through semi-join reduction, restricting the union branches while keeping the LEFT OUTER JOIN above the UNION. If this optimization is not applied and the union becomes a performance bottleneck, review the CDS model for opportunities to reduce data earlier without changing row multiplicity or NULL handling. Use PlanViz with representative data volumes to identify the problem and verify any redesign.

entry.title: SAP RPT as the Decision Model for Intent-Based Development in Joule Studio 2.0
entry.content:
co-author: Sowmya B

Intent-Based Development is never a single decision. Before anything gets built, a run of questions has to be answered: what kind of asset to build, which SAP API to call, which integration pattern fits, and whether the intent is even complete enough to act on. Each of those has a clear, bounded answer, and that is where SAP RPT fits in. This experiment brings RPT into the Joule Studio IBD flow as a few-shot decision model, working alongside the LLM-driven generation Joule Studio already provides.

A Hypothesis: The Decision Chain Behind Every IBD Intent

Working through this experiment, we kept running into the same pattern. Every intent we tested in Joule Studio 2.0 seemed to need the same run of decisions before anything could be built, and they tended to arrive in the same order. Whether that sequence holds for every intent is still an open question, but it showed up consistently enough across our tests to be worth setting out.

Here is what the chain looked like:

Decision Point

The Question

Asset Type

Should this become an agent or a workflow?

SAP API

Which S/4HANA API is the right entry point for this domain and operation?

HTTP Method

Is this a read, a create, or an update? Which verb encodes that correctly?

Integration Pattern

OData, REST, or event-based? Synchronous or asynchronous?

Intent Readiness

Is the intent complete enough to act on, or are required fields missing?

Each of these has only a few possible answers, and the same questions come up in every IBD flow. This experiment is a first look at how far RPT can go in answering them.

What Joule Studio 2.0 Already Decides

Before bringing RPT into the picture, it is worth being clear about what Joule Studio 2.0 already does on its own. When a developer describes an intent, the platform makes a set of decisions on their behalf, without any explicit wiring:

Decision Area

What the Platform Handles

Intent routing

Which agent or assistant picks up the intent and when to hand off between them

Tool and action selection

Which MCP tools, SAP APIs, or backend actions to invoke based on intent context

Execution planning

Step sequence, sub-task decomposition, parallel versus serial execution

Context propagation

What session state to carry forward and what data to pass between steps

Error recovery

Whether to retry, rephrase, escalate, or gracefully degrade on a failed tool call

RPT does not replace any of this. What this experiment looks at is a specific class of decision: the design-time decisions taken while an asset is still being shaped, before it ever runs. What kind of asset to build, which SAP API it should call, which HTTP method, which integration pattern. These come down to a choice among known options and benefit from being grounded in labelled examples, which is exactly where RPT fits. It is a way to make those design-time choices more explicit, easier to inspect, and easier to tune.

RPT as a Few-Shot Decision Model

SAP RPT is a tabular foundation model. You give it a table of rows, some with known outcomes and some marked [PREDICT], and it works out the missing values from the examples in the same table. No training pipeline, no deployment step. A handful of examples in the request is enough. All the experiments here use the sap-rpt-1.6 model.

This is different from how a zero-shot model works. A zero-shot model relies entirely on what it learned during training. RPT leans on the examples you hand it, anchoring its predictions to your specific context. That matters for IBD decisions, where the same intent phrased for a different domain can point to a completely different asset type.

It also shows how an LLM and a tabular model like RPT can share the work. The LLM takes the open-ended side: reasoning, writing, synthesis. RPT takes the structured calls, where the answer is one of a known set of options and getting it right matters more than explaining it fluently. Inside a Joule Studio IBD flow, the two fit together naturally.

Decision Point One: What Kind of Asset?

The first thing we wanted to test was whether RPT could look at an intent and decide what kind of asset it should become. An intent that needs clarification, multi-step reasoning, and back-and-forth with a user points toward an agent. One that describes a clean, event-triggered integration points toward a workflow. They are fundamentally different execution models, which made this a good place to start: given a structured description of an intent, could RPT make that call from just a handful of labelled examples?

We deliberately chose two test intents at opposite ends of the spectrum. Not two similar intents with subtle differences between them, but two that clearly belonged in different worlds. The logic was that if RPT could tell these two apart from a small set of labelled examples, the approach was worth building on. If it could not manage even that, there was no point moving on to more nuanced cases.

One intent was squarely in agent territory: a procurement interaction where the system needs to understand what a user wants, work out whether an SAP action is needed, ask for any missing details, and kick off the right process. Multi-step, reasoning-dependent, user-facing. The other was the opposite: a sales order created in SAP S/4HANA triggers an extraction of order number and value, which then gets posted as a notification to Microsoft Teams. Linear, event-driven, no ambiguity about what happens next.

We also kept the labelled set deliberately small. The request carried six training examples spanning both asset types, a mix of agent and flow cases at different complexity and reasoning profiles, with the two query intents added on top. A much larger training set would have made it harder to tell whether the features were doing the work or whether RPT was just leaning on sheer volume. With only a handful of rows, the outcome rested on the features we chose: complexity, whether the intent needed reasoning, and whether it needed system interaction. Either they carried enough signal for the model to generalise, or they did not.

Each row carried the intent text plus three flags: complexity, whether reasoning was needed, and whether system interaction was needed. The ASSET_TYPE field was the prediction target, marked [PREDICT] on the two query rows and given as a labelled value on each training example.

Screenshot A: Asset Type Prediction Request and Response

Request on the left, response on the right. The request carries six labelled training examples followed by two query rows, QUERY_1 and QUERY_2, each with ASSET_TYPE marked [PREDICT]. The response returns Agent for QUERY_1 and n8n Flow for QUERY_2, both at confidence 1.0.

RPT got both right from the features alone, with no domain-specific rules or routing logic behind it. The examples carried the signal we hoped they would.

Decision Points Two and Three: Which API, and How to Call It

Knowing what kind of asset to build is a good start, but the workflow still has to know which SAP API to call and how to call it. S/4HANA exposes hundreds of APIs, and picking the wrong one, or using the wrong HTTP method, leaves you with a broken asset.

The second experiment shifted to two new targets, S4HANA_API and HTTP_METHOD, with a feature set tuned to them: the intent text, the BUSINESS_OBJECT it acts on, and an explicit OPERATION field on every row. The OPERATION field was the one that mattered most. You cannot reliably tell GET from POST by reading a free-text intent, so we encoded the operation directly: Read for the sales order retrieval intent, Create for the purchase order creation intent. The labelled examples paired each operation with its method, Read with GET, Create with POST, Update with PATCH, so RPT had the mapping to learn from.

Screenshot B: API and HTTP Method Prediction Request and Response

Request on the left, response on the right. The request carries labelled training examples followed by two query rows, each with OPERATION set ( Read for QUERY_1, Create for QUERY_2) and S4HANA_API and HTTP_METHOD marked [PREDICT] . The response returns GET and API_SALES_ORDER_SRV for QUERY_1, and POST and API_PURCHASEORDER_2 for QUERY_2, each at confidence 1.0.

Both predictions came back correct, API name and HTTP method, from the same set of features. RPT can take multiple target fields in a single request, so asset type could sit alongside these two in the same call. Here we kept the focus on the two new decisions rather than repeating the asset type test from the first experiment.

RPT as a Decision Architecture, Not a Feature

This experiment tested RPT at one stage of the IBD lifecycle, the point where the workflow works out what to build and how to connect it. But the lifecycle is longer than that. An intent passes through several stages before anything gets generated: it is structured into a product requirement, broken down into a technical specification, turned into an asset, and finally checked against the original goal. At each of those stages, the workflow runs into the same kind of split.

Some of the decisions are open-ended. What should the acceptance criteria be? How should an edge case be handled? What tone should the agent take when it asks for clarification? Work like that belongs to the LLM, and it handles it well.

Running alongside those, at every stage, are decisions where the answer is one of a known, limited set. At the intent stage, is this intent complete enough to proceed, or is something missing? At the PRD stage, which SAP system of record does it touch? At the specification stage, which API, which HTTP method, which integration pattern? At the solution stage, agent or workflow? None of these are reasoning tasks. They are classification tasks, and classification is exactly what RPT is built for.

We happened to test the specification and solution stages first, because those decisions are concrete and easy to verify. But the same structure applies further upstream. An intent readiness check at the front of the flow, looking for a missing business object, an undefined operation, or ambiguous scope, is the same kind of prediction problem. So is domain classification, or matching a business requirement to the right SAP module.

So what the experiment points to is not a feature but a pattern, one that should hold across the whole lifecycle rather than only the stages we tested here.

Treating these decisions as prediction targets rather than generation outputs changes something else as well. The choices become visible and open to inspection. You can see what drove a given prediction, question it, and correct it. As the example set grows, accuracy improves with it. And adding a new decision point is just a matter of adding another target column.

The IBD Decision Layer: How It Fits the Flow

The decision layer sits early in the IBD workflow, after a business intent has been captured and structured, and before any design or generation begins. Its job is to settle what to build, where to connect, and how to call things, so the generative steps that follow start from a clear direction.

Step 1: Business Intent  Capture what should happen. Structure the attributes: complexity, operation type, business object, reasoning requirement.

Step 2: Encode as Input Rows  Translate each intent into a structured RPT row. Mark target fields (ASSET_TYPE, S4HANA_API, HTTP_METHOD) with [PREDICT] .

Step 3: RPT Decision Inference  Submit the request. RPT returns predictions for all target fields simultaneously, with confidence scores.

Step 4: Validate the Predictions  Check API availability against the SAP API catalog. Verify method/intent consistency. Treat confidence as a weighted signal, not a gate.

Step 5: Surface to the IBD Flow  Recommend validated candidates to the developer or route directly to the next design step. Keep human approval in the loop.

Step 6: Generate and Refine  Use validated recommendations to guide asset design and code generation. Feed outcomes back to enrich the labelled example set.

The capability is already there. The API works, the predictions land, and the feature design is easy to iterate on. The next step is to build this into the Joule Studio IBD workflow properly, with a validation step sitting between RPT's output and the next design decision.

Where the Decision Model Goes Next

  • Integration pattern recommendation. Extend the target fields to recommend OData versus REST versus event-based patterns, not just API names and HTTP methods.
  • Intent readiness check. Use RPT at the front of the pipeline to catch incomplete intents before the workflow moves on, flagging a missing business object, an undefined operation, or ambiguous scope.
  • Testing at broader coverage. Run the same approach against a wider range of intents, including ambiguous and cross-domain ones, and compare against expected outcomes to get a realistic accuracy picture.

Closing Thoughts

What this experiment shows is that SAP RPT and Joule Studio 2.0 work well side by side. Joule Studio handles the generative side of intent-based development: routing, orchestration, context, and synthesis. RPT brings structured decision-making to the questions inside that flow that have a bounded set of correct answers. Each is good at something the other is not, which is what makes the pairing worth pursuing.

Across the two experiments here, RPT correctly predicted asset type in the first run, then SAP API and HTTP method in the second, each from only a small number of labelled examples. The same structure that worked for asset type worked for API selection with no changes to the architecture. That suggests this is not a one-off result but a pattern, one that should extend to other decision points in the lifecycle: integration pattern, intent readiness, domain classification.

We are still early in understanding how far this reaches. But the direction is clear enough. RPT as a decision model running alongside Joule Studio 2.0 is worth building on.

entry.content:
Keeping job architecture and workforce skills data accurate is an ongoing challenge. Role definitions drift, skill gaps go undetected, and manual maintenance slows teams down. In the second half of 2026, SAP SuccessFactors introduces two new agents in the HR Operations Assistant designed to help HR teams maintain accurate skills and job architecture data with less manual effort.

The Skills Governance Agent continuously analyzes the skills library and surfaces recommendations to help HR administrators keep skills data accurate and current. Based on how skills are inferred across the organization, the agent generates categorized proposals to add, rename, or retain each skill, with confidence scores and clear rationale for every recommendation, so administrators understand the reasoning behind each suggestion. Administrators can review inferred skills organized by trending and relevant categories, supported by inference data and source trust information. Approved proposals can be applied in bulk or skill by skill, with human oversight built in. The result is less manual curation, more accurate skill recommendations for employees, stronger matching of talent to opportunities, and more reliable skills reporting.
Skills Governance Agent

The Job Architecture Maintenance Agent helps keep job architecture accurate and current. It scans role definitions in job profile builder, compares them against employees' actual skills in the growth portfolio and open requisitions in recruiting, and flags roles that are out of date or no longer in use. Administrators and HR business partners can then review the findings and apply updates with approval. The agent can also run a full health check across all active roles, prioritizing the ones that haven't been updated in the longest time. It surfaces roles with gaps or no active assignments, grouped in batches for easy review. Job architecture becomes a continuously maintained record rather than a point-in-time document
Job Architecture Maintenance Agent

Alongside these agentic capabilities, certificate-to-role mapping is also now available. The talent intelligence hub will evaluate each employee's certificates against the requirements defined for their role in job profile builder, deriving a real-time compliance status that groups certificates as required, recommended, or additional. Critical missing certificates will be surfaced with a clear next step, so managers and HR teams can act before compliance gaps become a business risk. This capability consumes existing role-certificate mappings, including critical and recommended flags, making it immediately usable.

The talent intelligence hub also now supports bulk import of certificate data through integration center, covering validity dates, skills, and attachment settings. Administrators can upload certificate master data and employee certificate portfolios, including supporting documents, in a single file rather than entering records one by one. For organizations managing certificates at scale, this reduces a time-consuming setup task to a straightforward data load.

entry.title: SAP RAP Question: Allowing Another User to Edit Drafts
entry.content:
In RAP with draft handling (similar to the standard Manage Purchase Orders app), how can a draft that is currently owned by one user be made editable by another user? e.g. when the draft owner got ill / left the organization etc....

By default, RAP draft instances are locked and owned by the user who created them. Is there a standard RAP mechanism, configuration, or extension pattern that allows another authorized user to take over, share, or continue editing an existing draft? Alternatively, how is this requirement handled in standard SAP Fiori apps such as Manage Purchase Orders?

As per the ABAP RAP documentation, in RAP (ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model), draft handling offers two main modes: exclusive drafts and collaborative drafts.

  • Exclusive Draft Handling: Drafts are locked exclusively by the user who created them. Only the draft owner can modify, activate, or discard the draft. This means no other user can edit another user's drafts.

  • Collaborative Draft Handling: Multiple users, once authorized and invited with the "Share" draft action, can concurrently edit the same draft. 

In the latter approach, its a real pain for End users to keep inviting other users. Is there an alternative to enable Draft-handling by multiple users like the way 'Manage Purchase Order' app does?

Any guidance, best practices, or examples would be appreciated.

entry.title: How to Enable SAP Joule for SAP SuccessFactors Using SAP BTP and Cloud Identity Services
entry.content:
1. Understanding the Architecture

For a SuccessFactors implementation, the Joule landscape can be viewed in three layers.

Experience Layer

The user works primarily in SAP SuccessFactors.

Joule is embedded into the SuccessFactors user experience. Users don't need to leave SuccessFactors simply to interact with Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

Conceptually:

Employee / Manager → SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule

AI and Platform Layer

Although Joule appears inside SuccessFactors, Joule itself runs as a service on SAP BTP. [https://le...essfactors]

SAP SuccessFactors continues to own the HR business data and processes, while Joule provides the conversational and orchestration layer.

Conceptually:

SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule → SAP BTP

Identity and Authorization Layer

The third area is identity and authorization.

SAP Cloud Identity Services forms part of the Joule identity architecture, while SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions determine which SuccessFactors information and functionality a user is authorized to access. [https://le...essfactors]

This separation is important. Enabling Joule does not give the user unrestricted access to SuccessFactors.

2. Check the Prerequisites

Before configuring anything, start by validating that your landscape satisfies SAP's Joule prerequisites.

SAP's Setting Up Joule for SAP SuccessFactors Learning content lists prerequisites including:

  • SAP BTP account with the required Joule entitlement
  • Joule entitlement identified as das-application
  • SAP SuccessFactors license
  • Joule availability for the applicable data center
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants
  • SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start [https://le...essfactors]

The last prerequisite is worth noting.

Your users may access Joule directly from the SuccessFactors experience and may not use a separate SAP Build Work Zone site as their business launchpad. Nevertheless, SAP's current Learning material lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start among the prerequisites for the overall Joule setup. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, don't interpret "using SuccessFactors as the launchpad" as meaning that all SAP Start / Build Work Zone platform dependencies can simply be omitted.

Follow the dependencies presented by the Joule onboarding process for your particular landscape.

3. Check the Required Administrator Access

Before starting the implementation, make sure the configuration team has the required administrative access.

SAP's SuccessFactors Joule setup guidance identifies the following administrative roles:

  • SAP SuccessFactors Administrator
  • SAP BTP Global Account Administrator
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services Administrator [https://he...cale=en-US]

This is important because the onboarding isn't limited to SuccessFactors configuration. It crosses the SuccessFactors, BTP and identity landscapes.

At this stage, your initial checklist should therefore be:

  • SuccessFactors tenant and license are available
  • SAP BTP Global Account is identified
  • Joule entitlement is available
  • Appropriate SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants are available
  • Required administrators have access
  • Joule availability for the relevant landscape/data center has been checked
  • SAP Start / Build Work Zone requirement has been assessed according to the current Joule onboarding model

4. Verify the Joule Entitlement in SAP BTP

The next step is to verify that the SAP BTP Global Account has the required Joule entitlement.

SAP Learning specifically identifies the Joule entitlement as:

das-application

SAP recommends checking the entitlements available in the BTP Global Account. [https://le...essfactors]

If you have the appropriate SuccessFactors license but the Joule entitlement isn't available, SAP Learning advises contacting your SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Don't try to compensate for a missing Joule entitlement by manually creating unrelated BTP services. Resolve the commercial/provisioning issue first.

A successful implementation starts with the correct entitlement being delivered to the correct SAP BTP Global Account.

5. Prepare SAP Cloud Identity Services

Once the commercial and BTP prerequisites are established, the next major area is identity.

SAP Learning explicitly lists SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants as a prerequisite for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

Before starting Joule onboarding, document the participating systems and identity landscape.

At minimum, identify:

  • SAP SuccessFactors tenant
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant
  • SAP BTP Global Account
  • Relevant BTP landscape
  • Production versus non-production systems
  • User identities used across the participating systems

This might seem administrative, but it becomes extremely useful when troubleshooting authentication and user provisioning.

A common source of confusion is treating IAS and IPS as though they perform the same function. They should be considered separately.

6. Understand IAS: Identity Authentication

SAP Identity Authentication is part of SAP Cloud Identity Services.

From an implementation perspective, think about Identity Authentication as the authentication side of the architecture.

The central question is:

How is the identity of the user established across the participating SAP applications?

Your Joule implementation therefore needs to consider how SuccessFactors, Joule/BTP and SAP Cloud Identity Services participate in establishing a consistent user identity.

SAP's Learning material identifies active SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants as part of the prerequisites for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

The exact configuration should follow the Joule onboarding guidance appropriate to your tenant rather than assuming a generic IAS configuration will be sufficient.

7. Understand IPS: Identity Provisioning

Authentication isn't the whole identity story.

The second area is Identity Provisioning Service (IPS).

Conceptually:

IAS answers the authentication/identity question.

IPS deals with provisioning identities between the relevant systems.

SAP's Joule provisioning documentation explicitly includes Configure Identity Provisioning Service within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Therefore, don't document your implementation simply as "IAS configured."

Your architecture documentation should separately record:

Authentication

How users authenticate and how their identities are established across the participating applications.

Provisioning

How identities required by the Joule landscape are provisioned and synchronized.

The actual source, target and provisioning configuration should follow the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the landscape being implemented.

8. Start the Official Joule Onboarding Process

Once the prerequisites, BTP entitlement and Cloud Identity Services landscape are ready, proceed with Joule onboarding.

This is an area where it is especially important not to follow an outdated blog containing a static list of destinations, service instances or role collections.

SAP's current SuccessFactors documentation directs administrators to:

Follow the Joule Onboarding Guide to finish the setup. [https://he...cale=en-US]

SAP Learning also points to SAP's activation guidance for implementing Joule with SuccessFactors. [https://le...essfactors]

Use the official onboarding process applicable to your system.

During this phase, validate that you are working with:

  • The intended BTP Global Account
  • The intended SuccessFactors system
  • The correct SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape
  • The required Joule entitlement
  • The appropriate production or non-production environment

Avoid manually reproducing configuration from an old implementation unless that configuration is still explicitly required by the current onboarding process.

9. Understand the Role of SAP Build Work Zone / SAP Start

This particular topic can create confusion for SuccessFactors customers.

In this implementation scenario, the end user experiences Joule through SAP SuccessFactors.

That does not mean you should automatically remove SAP Build Work Zone/SAP Start from the technical architecture.

SAP's current Learning material for setting up Joule with SuccessFactors explicitly lists:

SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start

among the prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

The accurate way to describe the architecture is therefore:

SuccessFactors is the user-facing business application from which users interact with Joule. The technical services and platform dependencies required by SAP's current Joule onboarding model are provisioned separately according to SAP's onboarding guidance.

This is particularly important if you're coming from an S/4HANA Cloud background.

Don't equate the user's launchpad with every underlying platform component used to deliver Joule.

10. Complete the SuccessFactors-Side Joule Setup

After completing the required Joule onboarding activities, move to the SuccessFactors-side configuration.

The critical concept here is that provisioning Joule doesn't automatically give every SuccessFactors user access to it.

You still need to control which users have permission to use Joule.

SAP's SuccessFactors documentation explicitly identifies an Access to Joule permission. [https://he...cale=en-US]

In SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions, the documented permission is located under:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Assign this permission through the appropriate SuccessFactors RBP roles according to the users who should have access to Joule.

This gives you a clear separation:

Technical onboarding enables the Joule service.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions control which SuccessFactors users can access Joule.

11. Existing SuccessFactors Authorizations Still Apply

Granting Access to Joule should not be confused with granting unrestricted access to SuccessFactors functionality.

SAP states that the business data and actions accessed through Joule continue to be governed by existing SuccessFactors authorizations. [https://le...essfactors]

This means two conditions need to be considered.

Condition 1: Joule access

Is the user authorized to access Joule?

Condition 2: Business authorization

Is the same user authorized in SuccessFactors to access the requested HR information or execute the requested business operation?

Both are important.

For example, enabling Joule for an employee should not be considered a mechanism for bypassing Role-Based Permissions protecting manager or HR information.

This is one of the most important design principles to explain to your security and HR authorization teams.

12. Configure Employee Central Quick Actions Where Applicable

If you're using SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central, there is another configuration area to review.

SAP recommends enabling Employee Central Quick Actions and configuring the corresponding templates for Employee Central customers using Joule. [https://he...cale=en-US]

The reason this is relevant is that Joule isn't purely a question-and-answer interface.

SAP's architecture description discusses Joule supporting conversational interaction involving navigation and transactional interactions in the business application. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, for Employee Central implementations, review the Quick Actions needed for the supported Joule use cases you intend to make available.

Don't assume that every Employee Central action automatically becomes available through Joule.

Always validate the particular use case against the current SuccessFactors Joule documentation.

13. Validate Joule in SAP SuccessFactors

Once the onboarding, identity configuration and SuccessFactors authorization settings are complete, validate the solution from the SuccessFactors experience.

Use a test user that has:

  • Access to Joule
  • Correct identity configuration
  • Appropriate SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Access to the underlying SuccessFactors functionality being tested

The first validation is simple:

Can the user access Joule from the SuccessFactors user experience?

If yes, don't stop there.

The next validation is:

Can Joule access only the SuccessFactors information and operations that this user is authorized to use?

SAP states that existing SuccessFactors authorizations govern the data and actions available through Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

That means functional and security validation should be performed together.

14. Test Different Authorization Scenarios

A good implementation should test more than one type of user.

Employee User

Use an employee account with normal Employee Self-Service permissions.

Validate the supported Joule scenarios applicable to employees.

Manager User

Use a manager account with appropriate manager permissions.

Validate supported manager scenarios where applicable.

Restricted User

Use an account intentionally lacking access to selected SuccessFactors information or functionality.

Validate that giving the user access to Joule doesn't extend the user's access beyond the underlying SuccessFactors authorization.

The purpose is not merely to prove that Joule opens successfully.

The purpose is to prove:

Joule availability + correct identity + correct SuccessFactors authorization + supported use case

work together.

15. Understand Which SuccessFactors Use Cases Are Supported

Another important implementation step is determining what you actually want users to do with Joule.

Not every SuccessFactors capability should be assumed to have a corresponding Joule capability.

SAP maintains documentation for the supported Joule capabilities and use cases within SuccessFactors. [https://he...essfactors]

For example, SAP's SuccessFactors Onboarding documentation lists scenarios such as:

  • Completing required onboarding tasks
  • Assigning a buddy
  • Viewing pending offboarding tasks
  • Directing new hires to their Onboarding Checklist and Onboarding Guide [https://he...cale=en-US]

This demonstrates why the business configuration underneath Joule remains important.

Having the Joule window available doesn't automatically make every HR operation available conversationally.

For any implementation, create a list of the specific SuccessFactors Joule use cases that your organization plans to enable and validate each against current SAP documentation.

16. End-to-End Implementation Sequence

Putting everything together, the recommended implementation flow is:

Step 1: Verify SuccessFactors prerequisites

Confirm the SuccessFactors licensing and applicable Joule prerequisites.

Step 2: Verify Joule availability

Check whether Joule is available for the applicable SuccessFactors landscape/data center according to the current SAP guidance. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 3: Verify the BTP Global Account

Confirm that you're working with the intended SAP BTP Global Account.

Step 4: Verify Joule entitlement

Check that the Joule das-application entitlement is available in the BTP landscape. [https://le...essfactors]

If the entitlement is missing for an appropriately licensed scenario, follow SAP's guidance and contact the SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 5: Establish the SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape

Identify the SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant participating in the implementation. SAP lists active Cloud Identity Services tenants among the SuccessFactors Joule prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 6: Address authentication

Follow the Joule onboarding guidance for the required Identity Authentication configuration.

Step 7: Address identity provisioning

Configure the required Identity Provisioning integration according to the current onboarding flow. SAP's Joule provisioning documentation includes Identity Provisioning configuration within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 8: Complete Joule onboarding

Follow the official Joule Onboarding Guide, as directed by SAP's SuccessFactors documentation. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 9: Handle SAP Start / Build Work Zone dependencies

Implement the applicable platform dependency according to the Joule onboarding model. SAP's current Learning content lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start as a prerequisite. [https://le...essfactors]

This doesn't mean users must use a separate Work Zone site as their SuccessFactors launchpad.

Step 10: Configure SuccessFactors Joule access

Grant the relevant SuccessFactors users:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 11: Review SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions

Ensure users have the underlying SuccessFactors authorization required by each business use case. Joule continues to operate within these authorization boundaries. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 12: Configure Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

For Employee Central scenarios, review and configure the Quick Actions recommended by SAP. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 13: Validate Joule

Test Joule from the SAP SuccessFactors user experience.

Step 14: Validate business use cases

Test the actual supported employee and manager use cases required by your organization.

Step 15: Validate authorization boundaries

Confirm that Joule respects the underlying SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

17. Troubleshooting Approach

If Joule isn't working after configuration, troubleshoot the solution layer by layer instead of changing multiple components simultaneously.

Joule isn't available at all

First verify:

  • Joule entitlement
  • BTP landscape
  • Joule onboarding completion
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

User can't access Joule

Verify:

  • User identity
  • Relevant Cloud Identity Services configuration
  • Identity provisioning
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

Joule opens but a business request doesn't work

Verify:

  • Whether that particular Joule use case is supported
  • User's SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Required SuccessFactors business configuration
  • Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

This layer-by-layer troubleshooting method is my recommended implementation approach. The individual requirements above should still be validated against the current SAP onboarding documentation.

18. Final Implementation Checklist

Before declaring the solution ready, validate the following.

Licensing and Landscape

  • SuccessFactors license verified
  • Joule availability verified
  • Correct BTP Global Account identified
  • Correct landscape selected
  • Joule das-application entitlement available

Identity

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services available
  • Authentication requirements completed according to Joule onboarding
  • Identity provisioning requirements completed
  • User identity is consistent across the participating landscape

Joule

  • Official Joule onboarding completed
  • Required platform services provisioned
  • SuccessFactors integration completed

SuccessFactors

  • Access to Joule permission assigned
  • Target users correctly included in RBP roles
  • Underlying SuccessFactors permissions validated

Validation

  • Manager scenario validated where applicable
  • Restricted-user scenario validated

Conclusion

The most important point when implementing Joule for SAP SuccessFactors is understanding that this isn't simply a switch inside SuccessFactors.

The implementation spans multiple layers:

SAP SuccessFactors provides the HR business application and remains the system of record.

SAP Joule on SAP BTP provides the conversational AI and orchestration experience.

SAP Cloud Identity Services participates in the identity architecture.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions continue to control access to HR data and business functionality. [https://le...essfactors]

For users, however, the experience can remain straightforward: they interact with Joule from SAP SuccessFactors while the underlying BTP and identity landscape provides the services required to enable that experience.

For implementation teams, the safest sequence is therefore:

Most importantly, always use the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the tenant being implemented instead of relying exclusively on older manual configuration procedures. entry.title: Re: RAP Abstract Entity Optional Vs Mandatory fields issue
entry.content:
Hi @Vinay_Uniyal755,

I followed this in the code of an S/4HANA 2023 system (SAP_BASIS 758 SP01, one SP below yours), and I think two different things are mixed here: Nullable and optional.

Nullable="false" is expected. In CL_SADL_GW_V4_ACTION_BUILDER (method _CREATE_AC_PARAM_N_RETURN_TYPE), a parameter only gets Nullable when its type is Edm.Date, Edm.DateTimeOffset or Edm.Guid, because Gateway maps their initial value (like 00000000) to null. Every other type stays Nullable="false". ABAP has no null for a CHAR or a number.

Optional is a different flag. In V4 it becomes the annotation Core.OptionalParameter on the parameter (/IWBEP/CL_V4_MED_MODEL, method CREATE_ANNOS_FOR_PARAMS). The SADL builder sets it only for fields that have a %control flag, and only if they are not mandatory:execute. Without that, the RAP documentation is clear: "By default, the importing parameter fields of actions and functions are implicitly mandatory."

What surprised me: the list of %control fields is filled only when the parameter is deep. In CL_SADL_GW_V4_MODEL_ACTION it is set in _RESOLVE_PARAMS_FROM_DEEP and nowhere else. So with action myAction parameter ZA_PARAM every field stays mandatory, even if the abstract BDEF has with control.

What I would try:

// CDS: define root abstract entity ZA_PARAM { ... }

// abstract BDEF ZA_PARAM
abstract;
strict(2);
with hierarchy;

define behavior for ZA_PARAM with control
{
  field ( mandatory : execute ) field_you_really_need;
}

// in the behavior definition of the BO
action myAction deep parameter ZA_PARAM;

Then check $metadata for Core.OptionalParameter on the other fields, not for Nullable="true". In the implementation, %param-%control-<field> tells you whether the consumer sent the field.

I read the code and the documentation, I didn't build this in my system. I'm also not sure how a Fiori Elements dialog shows a deep parameter that has no child nodes, so that part is worth a quick test. Do you call the action from a Fiori Elements app or from another consumer?

entry.title: Update SAP Table Maintenance Generator (TMG) After Table Structure Changes Without Deleting It
entry.content:
Introduction

In SAP ABAP development, the Table Maintenance Generator (TMG) provides a standard way to maintain table entries through transaction SM30. It allows users to create, modify, and delete records without developing a separate maintenance program.

A common challenge occurs when a new field is added to a custom table that already has a TMG. The updated field may not appear in the existing maintenance screen.

One approach is to delete and recreate the TMG. However, if the existing maintenance dialog contains custom event logic or screen modifications, recreating it can introduce additional rework.

In this blog, we will explore how to update an existing TMG using the generation settings in SAP, without unnecessarily deleting the existing maintenance object.

Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure that:

  • You have an existing custom table with an active TMG.

  • The table is maintained through transaction SM30.

  • You have the required development authorizations.

  • Any existing TMG events or screen modifications have been documented.

Step 1: Check the Existing Table Maintenance Screen

Open transaction SM30 and enter the custom table or maintenance view name.

Choose Maintain to display the current maintenance screen. Note the existing fields and any custom functionality.

Step 2: Add the New Field to the Table

Open transaction SE11 and enter the custom table name.

Choose Change, add the required field to the table definition, maintain its data element and other relevant properties, and activate the table.

If the change requires a database adjustment, assess the impact and perform the necessary adjustment using the appropriate SAP tools and procedures.

Step 3: Open the Existing Table Maintenance Generator

While working with the table in SE11, navigate to:

Utilities → Table Maintenance Generator

Open the existing maintenance generator configuration and choose Change.

The objective is to adjust the existing generated maintenance dialog rather than delete the maintenance object and recreate it from scratch.

Step 4: Select the Appropriate Structure Change Option

In the generation settings, select the option corresponding to the structural change you have made.

For adding a field, select:

New field/sec. table in structure

If a field has been removed, choose the corresponding option for a field or secondary table removed from the structure.

Proceed to the next screen.

Step 5: Review the Field and Screen Settings

Continue through the generation wizard and verify the relevant settings.

Depending on your existing maintenance dialog, confirm:

  • Whether the new field is a key field or a non-key field.

  • Whether the maintenance dialog uses a one-step or two-step layout.

  • Whether the existing screen arrangement remains appropriate.

  • Whether any custom screen changes need to be preserved or reviewed.

Select the options that match your table design and proceed.

Step 6: Complete the Generation Adjustment

Continue through the remaining confirmation screens. Allow SAP to process the changes, then save the updated maintenance configuration.

Check the system messages and resolve any errors before moving to validation.

The exact screens and available options may vary depending on the SAP release and maintenance object configuration.

Step 7: Validate the Changes in SM30

Return to transaction SM30 and open the same table or maintenance view in change mode.

Verify that:

  1. The newly added field is available on the maintenance screen.

  2. Existing fields are displayed correctly.

  3. New and existing records can be maintained as expected.

  4. Relevant custom TMG events continue to behave correctly.

  5. Saving the entries updates the data as intended.

Important Considerations

  • Preserve custom logic: Review existing TMG events and screen modifications before changing generation settings.

  • Validate key changes carefully: Adding or removing key fields can affect maintenance behavior and existing records.

  • Test before transporting: Perform the required functional and regression testing in the development and quality systems.

  • Do not assume every modification is preserved automatically: Custom screen layouts, generated objects, and event implementations should be checked after the adjustment.

Conclusion

When a table structure changes, deleting and recreating the entire Table Maintenance Generator should not be the first option.

By reviewing the existing TMG configuration and selecting the appropriate structure-change settings, you can update the maintenance dialog while reducing unnecessary rework.

Always validate the resulting SM30 screen and existing custom functionality before transporting the changes to another system.

entry.title: Export SAPUI5 Table Data to Excel in SAP Fiori: Code Examples and Best Practices
entry.content:
Export SAPUI5 Table Data to Excel in SAP Fiori: A Practical Guide with Code Examples

Introduction

Exporting table data to Microsoft Excel is a common requirement in SAP Fiori applications. Business users often need to download data for reporting, offline analysis, reconciliation, and collaboration.

SAPUI5 provides the sap.ui.export.Spreadsheet API to generate Excel workbooks. Developers can define column headers, data types, file names, and which fields are included in the exported spreadsheet.

This blog explains how to implement Excel export in a freestyle SAPUI5 application using an employee-management example. It also covers exporting selected columns, using readable column headers, and handling common issues.

1. Prerequisites

  • An SAPUI5 freestyle application.
  • A table bound to a JSON model or another supported data source.
  • An export button in the table toolbar.
  • The sap.ui.export library available in the SAPUI5 runtime.

For API details and supported export settings, refer to the SAPUI5 Demo Kit.

2. Understand the export approach

The basic process consists of four steps:

  1. Retrieve the table data from the model.
  2. Define the Excel columns using readable labels and model property names.
  3. Configure the spreadsheet and file name.
  4. Generate the workbook and download the .xlsx file.

The column label becomes the Excel header, while property identifies the source field in each row.

3. Create a sample table in the XML view

This example uses an employee table with Employee ID, Employee Name, and Department columns.

<mvc:View
    controllerName="demo.controller.Employee"
    xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc"
    xmlns="sap.m">
    <Page title="Employee Overview">
        <content>
            <Table id="employeeTable" items="{/Employees}">
                <headerToolbar>
                    <OverflowToolbar>
                        <Title text="Employee List" />
                        <ToolbarSpacer />
                        <Button
                            text="Export to Excel"
                            icon="sap-icon://excel-attachment"
                            press=".onExportExcel" />
                    </OverflowToolbar>
                </headerToolbar>
                <columns>
                    <Column><Text text="Employee ID" /></Column>
                    <Column><Text text="Employee Name" /></Column>
                    <Column><Text text="Department" /></Column>
                </columns>
                <items>
                    <ColumnListItem>
                        <cells>
                            <Text text="{EmployeeId}" />
                            <Text text="{EmployeeName}" />
                            <Text text="{Department}" />
                        </cells>
                    </ColumnListItem>
                </items>
            </Table>
        </content>
    </Page>
</mvc:View>

The table binds to a model collection named Employees. The button invokes the controller method onExportExcel.

4. Configure the SAPUI5 export library

Declare the export library in the sap.ui5 section of manifest.json. Merge this dependency into your existing configuration rather than replacing other dependencies.

{
  "sap.ui5": {
    "dependencies": {
      "libs": {
        "sap.m": {},
        "sap.ui.core": {},
        "sap.ui.export": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

5. Implement Excel export in the controller

The following controller example defines the export columns explicitly, so only the selected fields are included in the Excel file.

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/core/mvc/Controller",
    "sap/ui/export/Spreadsheet",
    "sap/m/MessageBox"
], function (Controller, Spreadsheet, MessageBox) {
    "use strict";

    return Controller.extend("demo.controller.Employee", {
        onExportExcel: async function () {
            const oTable = this.byId("employeeTable");
            const oBinding = oTable.getBinding("items");

            if (!oBinding) {
                MessageBox.error("Unable to retrieve the table data.");
                return;
            }

            const aContexts = oBinding.getContexts(
                0,
                oBinding.getLength()
            );

            const aData = aContexts.map(function (oContext) {
                return oContext.getObject();
            });

            if (!aData.length) {
                MessageBox.information(
                    "There is no data available to export."
                );
                return;
            }

            const aColumns = [
                {
                    label: "Employee ID",
                    property: "EmployeeId",
                    type: "string"
                },
                {
                    label: "Employee Name",
                    property: "EmployeeName",
                    type: "string"
                },
                {
                    label: "Department",
                    property: "Department",
                    type: "string"
                }
            ];

            const oSpreadsheet = new Spreadsheet({
                workbook: { columns: aColumns },
                dataSource: aData,
                fileName: "Employee_Overview.xlsx"
            });

            try {
                await oSpreadsheet.build();
            } catch (oError) {
                MessageBox.error(
                    "Excel export failed. Please try again."
                );
            } finally {
                oSpreadsheet.destroy();
            }
        }
    });
});

How the code works

  • Table binding: Retrieves data associated with the table's item binding.
  • Column definitions: Specifies the Excel header and corresponding model property.
  • Data source: Supplies row objects to the spreadsheet generator.
  • File name: Sets the downloaded workbook's name.
  • Build and cleanup: Generates the workbook and destroys the spreadsheet instance afterward.

Note: This example is intended for a client-side collection whose required data is available in the binding. For large OData datasets, server-side paging, or growing tables, make sure all required records are fetched before exporting. The currently rendered rows may not represent the complete dataset.

6. Export only the required columns

A common issue is that the Excel file contains extra fields that are not intended for business users. This can happen when developers export entire model objects or derive columns from every property in the backend response.

For example, the backend may provide:

const oEmployee = {
    EmployeeId: "E1001",
    EmployeeName: "Alex Morgan",
    Department: "Finance",
    InternalReference: "REF-0048",
    CreatedBy: "TECH_USER"
};

If business users need only three fields, define only those fields in the export configuration:

const aColumns = [
    {
        label: "Employee ID",
        property: "EmployeeId",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: "Employee Name",
        property: "EmployeeName",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: "Department",
        property: "Department",
        type: "string"
    }
];

Only the properties listed in the export configuration are included. Backend-only fields such as InternalReference and CreatedBy are excluded.

7. Keep Excel headers consistent with the UI

Excel headers should be meaningful to end users rather than exposing technical property names.

UI column header Model property Excel header
Employee IDEmployeeIdEmployee ID
Employee NameEmployeeNameEmployee Name
DepartmentDepartmentDepartment

The label property determines the Excel header, while property identifies the source field.

For multilingual applications, labels can be retrieved from the i18n resource bundle:

const oBundle = this.getView()
    .getModel("i18n")
    .getResourceBundle();

const aColumns = [
    {
        label: oBundle.getText("employeeId"),
        property: "EmployeeId",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: oBundle.getText("employeeName"),
        property: "EmployeeName",
        type: "string"
    }
];

8. Export filtered or sorted table data

Applications often include search fields, status filters, and sorting options. Decide whether the export should contain the currently filtered data or the complete dataset.

For a client-side table binding, the binding can provide contexts for the current filter and sort configuration:

const oBinding = oTable.getBinding("items");

const aFilteredContexts = oBinding.getContexts(
    0,
    oBinding.getLength()
);

const aExportData = aFilteredContexts.map(function (oContext) {
    return oContext.getObject();
});

Pass the resulting objects to the spreadsheet as the data source. For server-side OData bindings, the number of records may be limited by paging or service configuration. To export every matching backend record, implement appropriate paging or a dedicated data-retrieval process.

9. Handle numbers and dates correctly

Choosing suitable data types helps Excel interpret values correctly.

const aColumns = [
    {
        label: "Employee ID",
        property: "EmployeeId",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: "Monthly Salary",
        property: "MonthlySalary",
        type: "number"
    },
    {
        label: "Joining Date",
        property: "JoiningDate",
        type: "date"
    }
];

Use string for identifiers that may contain leading zeros, number for numeric values, and date for valid date values. Verify supported types and formatting options for your SAPUI5 version.

10. Common issues and troubleshooting

Issue Recommended check
Export button does nothingVerify the event handler name and browser console errors.
Excel contains extra columnsReview the explicit workbook column definition.
Headers show technical namesSet the intended user-facing label for every column.
Some records are missingCheck binding length, paging, growing behavior, and OData retrieval.
Dates or numbers are incorrectVerify model data types and spreadsheet column configuration.
Export fails in the browserCheck library availability, SAPUI5 version compatibility, and console errors.

Conclusion

The sap.ui.export.Spreadsheet API provides a practical way to add Excel export to freestyle SAPUI5 applications. The most important considerations are to define the required columns explicitly, use meaningful labels, handle the table's actual data binding correctly, and account for filtering and server-side paging.

Following these practices helps deliver clean, consistent Excel files that meet business users' reporting needs.

entry.title: What If Joule Could Help You Complete the Business-Driven Configuration Questionnaire? Now It Can.
entry.content:
A successful SAP S/4HANA Cloud implementation starts with understanding how a business works—and translating that understanding into the right configuration. The Business-Driven Configuration Questionnaire (BDCQ), a structured accelerator within the SAP Activate methodology, helps make that connection. Line of Business (LoB) configuration experts use it to gather the configuration values that will ultimately be entered in SAP Central Business Configuration for the customer’s SAP S/4HANA Cloud development system tenants.

More than a questionnaire, the BDCQ is a bridge between SAP consultants and customer business users. It helps ensure that solution configuration reflects real business requirements, both before and during Fit-to-Standard workshops.

Why does the BDCQ matter?

  • It provides early insight into the customer’s business processes and configuration needs.
  • It offers prescriptive guidance on identifying configuration requirements aligned with the implementation scope.
  • It provides a secondary validation of whether SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (Public Cloud) is the right fit for the customer, complementing the Digital Discovery Assessment (DDA).
  • It brings greater structure to the planning and delivery of Fit-to-Standard Analysis workshops.
  • It supports productive conversations between implementation experts and business users during workshops.
  • It connects customer business processes directly to solution configuration activities, including references to specific SSCUI apps or SSCUI groups.

The BDCQ captures two levels of information at different stages of the project:

The value of the BDCQ goes beyond collecting configuration data. It also helps LoB configuration experts build relationships with customer LoB experts and introduces those experts to SAP S/4HANA Cloud early in the project. Ideally, the same customer experts who provide L2 responses will take part in Fit-to-Standard workshops and user acceptance testing before go-live. In this way, the BDCQ also supports the project’s broader change-management effort.

Not every BDCQ maps neatly to a traditional line of business. The implementation team should therefore confirm that all business processes selected in the Digital Discovery Assessment are covered across the available BDCQs. Any remaining processes—for example, Human Resources or Two-Tier ERP—should be assigned based on transferable expertise and team availability.

So, how can AI-assisted support make it easier to complete the BDCQ?

During the Prepare phase, open Perform Initial Business Process Assessment for SAP S/4HANA Cloud. You’ll find the ✦ AI-Assisted Procedure session there.

Open the session and follow the instructions for working with the BDCQ Experts.

For example, the BDCQ-FI Expert can guide you through the questionnaire in a conversational manner. Start the conversation, answer its questions, and review the highlights and key points that deserve attention. This provides structured support as you work through the information required for your BDCQ.

The result is a BDCQ populated with Critical Steps, Scope Items, open items, and potential blockers—as illustrated in the example below.
